modules.title: Clock gating, voltage domains and level conversion
modules.objective: Choose a low-power technique based on what state and performance must survive the transition.
modules.body:
### 3.2 Clock gating

SLIDE:m03_p011|Gating 90% of the flip-flops in an MPEG4 decoder cut power from 30.6 mW to 8.5 mW, about 70%, using a latch-based glitch-free gate.

**Clock gating** stops the clock to registers whose inputs are not changing. The clock tree and the flops' internal clock nodes have α = 1, so they often dominate dynamic power. In the MPEG4 decoder (Ohashi, ISSCC'02), 90% of the flip-flops are clock-gated, and clock gating alone gives a 70% power reduction (30.6 mW → 8.5 mW).

**The integrated clock-gating (ICG) cell** on the slide:

- `en` passes through a **latch that is transparent while clk is low**; its output `n` is ANDed with `clk` to form `g_clk`.
- Because the latch is opaque while clk is high, a glitch or late change on `en` during the high phase cannot reach `g_clk`. In the waveform, `n` changes only after clk falls, one tCQ later.
- Without the latch, AND(clk, en) would chop the clock pulse whenever `en` moved during the high phase and could clock a flop on a glitch.

!!! core "Core idea"
    Clock gating lowers α on the highest-α net on the chip. The latch + AND structure makes it safe: `en` is sampled only during the low phase, so `g_clk` cannot glitch.

!!! why "Why it matters for std-cell / ROM work"
    The ICG is itself a standard cell, characterized with a **clock-gating setup/hold check of `en` against clk**, not an ordinary data check. ROM and register-file macros gate their own internal clocks (precharge and wordline enables fire only on an access), and the `.lib` clock-pin internal-power tables for idle versus active come from exactly this behavior.


### 3.4 Multiple supply domains (multi-VDD, CVS)

SLIDE2:m03_p017|In clustered voltage scaling only non-critical gates move to VDDL, and paths may go from high to low voltage only, with level-shifting flops at the boundary.||m03_p018|Single-rail cells at VDDH and VDDL need N-well isolation, so they go in dedicated rows or dedicated regions.

**Multiple voltage domains** use the timing slack that most paths have: off-critical gates move to VDDL while the critical path stays at VDDH. Slide 12 lists the costs: DC-DC converters or extra off-chip supplies, and distributing several supplies on chip.

**Clustered Voltage Scaling (CVS), slide 17:**

- The low-VDD portion is shaded. Within a combinational cone, signals may go **from high to low voltage ONLY**.
- A VDDL gate driving a VDDH gate is the problem: its "1" is only VDDL, so the VDDH gate's PMOS sees VSG = VDDH − VDDL. If that exceeds |Vtp|, the PMOS is not off, and the gate draws static current or fails to switch cleanly.
- Low-to-high conversion therefore happens at the domain boundary, in the **level-shifting flip-flop** (marked FF on the slide).

**Physical implementation, slide 18.** The N-wells of VDDH and VDDL PMOS devices sit at different potentials, so they need **N-well isolation spacing**: (a) dedicated alternating VDDL/VDDH rows, or (b) dedicated VDDH and VDDL regions. Each costs area or placement freedom.

SLIDE2:m03_p019|With a shared N-well tied to VDDH, VDDL cells mix freely in a row, but their PMOS sees reverse body bias VSB = VDDL − VDDH.||m03_p020|A VDDL input cannot turn off a VDDH PMOS, so the level-converting flip-flop restores full VDDH swing inside the flop.

**Shared N-well, slide 19.** All cells share an N-well tied to VDDH, so VDDL and VDDH cells mix anywhere with no isolation spacing. The VDDL PMOS has its source at VDDL and its body at VDDH, so it sees **reverse body bias, VSB = VDDL − VDDH**. That raises |Vtp|, making those gates slower but less leaky (added).

**Level-Converting Flip-Flop (LCFF, Ishihara ISLPED'03), slide 20.**

- **Problem:** a 0-to-VDDL signal into a VDDH inverter leaves that PMOS at |VGS| = VDDH − VDDL when the input is "high", so the "PMOS does not turn off": static current and a degraded low.
- **Fix:** the low-domain driver feeds a clocked pass gate into a high-domain latch with a VDDH feedback inverter. The pull-down path (red, on/off) discharges the latch node, and the VDDH feedback restores the full high level.
- The conversion is absorbed into a flop that was already there, so a separate level shifter's delay and area leave the critical path.

!!! core "Core idea"
    Going down in voltage is free. Going up needs a level converter, because a VDDL "1" cannot shut off a VDDH PMOS. Put the converter where a sequential element already exists (the LCFF) and keep each cone strictly high-to-low.

!!! why "Why it matters for std-cell / ROM work"
    Multi-VDD appears in library work as **level-shifter cells** (single- and dual-rail), always-on cells, and the **N-well/row strategy** of a dual-rail library. SRAM/ROM macros with a separate array supply (often called VDDM or VCS) contain up-shifters on the wordline drivers, characterized on a 2-D grid of both supplies in the `.lib` (added).


### 3.5 Dynamic voltage scaling (DVS)

SLIDE:m03_p022|For a task needing only part of peak throughput, clock or power gating saves energy linearly with duty cycle, while just-in-time DVS saves roughly with its cube.

Two ways to run a task that needs only a fraction of peak throughput:

- **Clock/power gating (race to idle):** run at full VDD and f for t_on, then gate. Energy is linear in duty cycle.

    ```latex
    E = P_{Vdd}\, t_{on} = P_{Vdd}\, t_{task}\,(\text{duty cycle})
    ```

- **Just-in-time DVS:** lower f so the task finishes exactly at its deadline, and lower V with it (V ∝ f above threshold).

    ```latex
    E = P_{scaled}\, t_{task} = (f_{scaled} C_s V_{scaled}^2)\, t_{task} \propto f_{scaled}^3 \propto (\text{duty cycle})^3
    ```

- **Gain of DVS over gating:** ∝ (duty cycle)².

!!! guard "Common trap"
    The cubic saving assumes V tracks f and leakage is negligible. Near and below threshold, V stops dropping much while t_task keeps growing, so leakage energy grows. That is the reason for a minimum-energy point (next section), and why race-to-idle can win in leaky technologies or at low voltage (added).


### 3.7 Level converters: DCVS and pass-gate

Level converters are needed wherever a VDDL domain drives a VDDH domain. The asynchronous (unclocked) converters are covered here; the LCFF in 3.4 is the clocked option. Each slide labels every transistor ON/OFF and numbers the order of events.

SLIDE2:m03_p029|In a DCVS converter the VDDL-driven NMOS must overpower the cross-coupled VDDH PMOS (IN-ON > IP-ON) while the PMOS must beat NMOS leakage (IP-ON > IN-OFF), and both margins collapse as VDDL drops.||m03_p030|The pass-gate converter reduces contention because the fighting PMOS M3 loses VGS as IN rises and M1's VDS collapses once IN is high.

**Standard DCVS (Differential Cascode Voltage Switch) level converter, slide 29.**

- **Structure:** two NMOS pull-downs (M3, M6) driven by IN and its complement (from a VDDL inverter), two cross-coupled VDDH PMOS (M4, M5), and a VDDH output inverter.
- **Sequence for IN rising (0→VDDL):**
    1. M6 turns on (gate 0→L) while M3 turns off (gate L→0).
    2. M6 must pull its node down (H→↓) **while M5 is still fully on**. This is the **fight**.
    3. Once that node is low enough, M4 turns on.
    4. M4 pulls the other node to H, which shuts off M5, and the low node completes to 0.
    5. OUT goes 0→H.

**The two-sided constraint (the key interview point):**

- **IN-ON > IP-ON.** The NMOS, whose gate swings only to VDDL, must out-drive a PMOS whose |VGS| = VDDH. Otherwise the converter never flips: a **functional failure**. This pushes toward a large NMOS and a weak PMOS.
- **IP-ON > IN-OFF.** The PMOS must still hold the high node against the off NMOS's leakage. Otherwise the high node is not maintained. This forbids making the PMOS too weak.

**"Mingoo plot" (current ranges):**

| | VDDL = 0.8 V | VDDL = 0.3 V |
|---|---|---|
| IN-ON | 100 µA | 100 nA |
| IP-ON | 100 nA | 3 nA |
| IN-OFF | 100 pA | 100 pA |
| NMOS ION/IOFF range | 10⁶ | 10³ |
| Margin per constraint | 1000× each | 30× each |

At VDDL = 0.3 V the NMOS is subthreshold and its ION/IOFF collapses to about 10³. Only about 30× is left on each side, so IP-ON must sit inside a narrow window between IN-OFF and IN-ON, and variation can push it out either way. The slide's summary: **DCVS has a critical relationship between ION and IOFF, and the NMOS ION/IOFF ratio falls as VDDL falls.**

**Pass-gate (PG) level converter, slide 30.**

- **Structure:** IN (VDDL swing) drives M2, an NMOS pull-down on the internal node, and also passes through M1, an NMOS pass transistor with its gate at VDDL, to the gate of M3, the VDDH PMOS pull-up on the internal node. M4 is a VDDH PMOS feedback device, controlled by the internal node, that pulls M3's gate to full VDDH.
- **Sequence for IN rising:**
    1. M1 passes IN, so M3's gate rises 0 → L−Vth (M1 can only pass up to VDDL − Vth).
    2. M2 turns on (gate 0→L) and starts pulling the internal node down against the weakening M3.
    3. As the internal node falls (H→↓), M4 turns on.
    4. M4 pulls M3's gate the rest of the way, L−Vth → H, which shuts M3 off completely, and the node completes to 0.
    5. OUT goes 0→H.
- **Why it is more robust (reduced contention):**
    - **VGS of M3 shrinks as IN rises**, because its gate is being driven up, whereas a DCVS PMOS keeps full VDDH drive until the other side flips.
    - **VDS of M1 shrinks once IN is high**, so M4 pulling M3's gate above VDDL meets little opposition (M1 turns itself off).

!!! eq "Equation card"
    DCVS works only if **IN-ON(min) > IP-ON(max)** and **IP-ON(min) > IN-OFF(max)**.
    VDDL = 0.8 V: about 1000× margin each side. VDDL = 0.3 V: about 30× each side.
    Mnemonic: "N must win the fight, P must beat the leak."
takeaways: Clock gating, voltage scaling and power gating change different sources of energy.
Crossing a voltage domain requires an electrical interface and a safe control sequence.
checks: Explain why combinational clock gating can create a glitch and how an integrated gating structure avoids it.
Trace a low-to-high level shifter’s contention during a transition.
Choose a supply-domain strategy and identify isolation, retention and wake-up requirements.

modules.title: Track margin with replicas and in-situ monitors
modules.objective: Explain what an adaptive-voltage controller can observe and what its monitor can miss.
modules.body:
### 8.3 DVFS: design-time tables and safe switching

SLIDE2:m08_p010|To stay safe, always raise voltage before raising frequency and lower frequency before lowering voltage.||m08_p011|Intel SpeedStep on XScale (0.18 µm) ran 800 MHz at 1.65 V and 900 mW down to 200 MHz at 0.75 V and 50 mW, switching frequency by slow PLL relocking.

**DVFS (slide 9).** Adapt frequency to workload demand: software controls speed, lowers f when predicted demand is low, and adapts V to **match** f. The V/f pairs come from a **pre-silicon** look-up table generated at design time and stored once for all processors (ROM). First examples: AMD PowerNow, ARM IEM, IBM DPM, Intel SpeedStep / Enhanced SpeedStep, Transmeta LongRun/LongRun2.

**Safe sequencing (slide 10).** Frequency must never exceed what the present voltage supports:

- Going up: **increase V first**, wait for it to settle, then raise f.
- Going down: **decrease f first**, then lower V.

**SpeedStep numbers.** 1.65 V / 800 MHz / 900 mW; 1.3 V / 600 MHz / 450 mW; 0.75 V / 200 MHz / 50 mW. From 800 to 200 MHz, f drops 4X but power drops 18X, because P ∝ C·V²·f and V also drops (1.65 → 0.75 V gives (1.65/0.75)² ≈ 4.8X).

```latex
P_{dyn} = \alpha C V_{DD}^2 f, \qquad \frac{900\text{ mW}}{50\text{ mW}} = 18 \approx 4 \times 4.8
```

SLIDE2:m08_p012|IBM DPM avoids slow PLL relocking by running the PLL at fixed frequency and selecting divided clocks with a glitch-free mux, with VDD scaled externally from 0.9 to 1.95 V.||m08_p016|Design-time DVFS tables address none of the process, environmental or aging variations, because one table is used for every die.

**IBM DPM (2002, Nowka JSSC).** LDO-powered PLL on a constant 1.0 V supply; core supply VDVFS = **0.9–1.95 V**, set externally; software picks f and V. A **level shifter** moves the PLL clock into the variable core domain, then a clock divider and a **glitch-free (hazard-free) MUX** select the frequency, avoiding PLL relock time.

**Glitch-free MUX (slides 13–14).** A plain AND-OR mux, c·f1 + c̄·f2, can glitch when c changes while f1 = f2 = 1 (the classic static-1 hazard: one AND term turns off before the other turns on). Adding the consensus term **f1·f2** (the "added for glitch-free" gate) holds fout = 1 through the transition. For switching between f1 and f1/2, the control is resynchronized by a flop so the switch happens only when **both clocks are all '1' or all '0'**, so no runt pulse is created.

!!! guard "Common trap"
    A design-time DVFS table addresses **none** of the variations on the grid (slide 16). It is pure workload adaptation: every die gets the same worst-case V for a given f. Exam phrasing: DVFS = workload adaptation; AVFS = process and environmental adaptation.

!!! why "Why it matters for std-cell / ROM work"
    DVFS means every cell, flop and memory must work and be characterized across a voltage range, not one corner: .lib sets at several VDD points, level shifters on every domain crossing (as in the IBM DPM PLL path), and SRAM/ROM sense timing that tracks logic across V. A clock mux cell must be glitch-free by construction, which is why libraries ship dedicated clock-mux and clock-gating cells.


### 8.4 AVFS and post-silicon look-up tables

SLIDE2:m08_p018|AVFS gives each die, and each moment of its life, its own operating point, and needs a sensor, a knob and an algorithm.||m08_p022|Post-silicon tester tables address only variations fixed for the chip's lifetime, both global and local process.

**AVFS (slide 18).** Adjust V and f to process and environmental conditions:

- Instead of one operating point for all dies, use **different operating points per die**.
- Use **multiple operating points dynamically** over one die's life.
- Remove worst-case margins for better energy efficiency and performance.

Three requirements:

1. **SENSE**: performance/environment monitors (canaries, temperature sensors, in-situ measurements).
2. **KNOB**: frequency, supply voltage, body bias.
3. **ALGORITHM**: guarantee correct operation.

Two families (slide 19):

- **"Always correct"**: look-up tables, canary circuits, in-situ delay detection. Never fail; keep some margin.
- **"Let fail and correct"**: self-calibrating circuits tune until the point of failure, need a **recovery mechanism**, and remove margins for both global and local variation.

**Look-up table AVFS (slides 20–23).** Same as DVFS, but the table is **post-silicon**, generated on the tester, different for every chip.

- Advantages: very easy to design and deploy; exploits low-utilization epochs through DVFS; **addresses fixed WID variation (RDF, LER, …)**, because the tester measures the real critical path of that die, including its local variation.
- Disadvantages: only static variation (global and local process); worst-case margins for everything else (aging, V, T, noise); tester calibration across many frequency points is costly; must find and run worst-case vectors.

!!! core "Core idea"
    A per-die table measures the truth for that die at test time, so it captures both D2D and WID process variation. It cannot see anything that happens after test: aging, temperature, droop.

!!! guard "Common trap"
    (Practice exam P6.) Add a temperature sensor and three tester tables at −20, 25 and 85 °C. Now the tables also address **ambient temperature**, besides both process variations. They still do not address lifetime degradation, package effects, hot spots, or any fast-changing variation. At a sensor reading between table temperatures (e.g. 40 °C), pick the **worse** neighbor: above Vt that is the **hotter** table (mobility dominates, hot is slow); **below Vt pick the colder table** (Vt rise dominates, cold is slow). This is **temperature inversion** (added explanation): at low VDD the delay sensitivity to Vt, which rises as T falls, outweighs mobility loss.


### 8.5 Canary circuits: critical-path replicas and ring oscillators

SLIDE:m08_p031|A critical path replica is launched every reference cycle, and if its output arrives before the reference-clock sample the counter steps VDD down, otherwise up, so VDD settles where the replica just meets fref.

**Kuroda et al. (JSSC 1998), 0.4 µm.** The delay through a replica of the critical path sets the supply the processor runs at for a given frequency (fext).

Operation (from the timing diagram):

- A toggle flop launches a transition into the **critical path replica (CPR)** every fref cycle.
- At the next edge, two flops sample: **QCPR** (the CPR output) and **Qref** (the undelayed signal, a reference that always has the "correct" value).
- An XOR compares them. If the CPR output arrived in time, QCPR = Qref and the up/down counter counts **down** (lower VDD). If it was late, they differ and the counter counts **up**.
- The counter drives a **DC/DC converter** that sets Vcore; the loop dithers around the voltage where the replica delay equals one fref period. A frequency pick block chooses fcore.

This **eliminates the margin for global process variation** (and slow global V, T, aging, which the replica sees too).

SLIDE2:m08_p033|A tunable ring oscillator that tracks the critical path runs in a closed loop that adjusts the supply until the desired frequency is reached, saving 11% to 78% energy.||m08_p035|TI SmartReflex (45 nm) combines adaptive body bias (FBB for speed, RBB for leakage), DVFS and AVS, with modes that cut power to well below baseline.

**Burd et al. (JSSC 2002)**, 0.6 µm, 7.5 × 9 mm², 1.5M transistors: tunable **ring oscillator** tracks the processor critical-path delay; count and compare with the desired frequency, and the DC/DC adjusts Vcore until the ring runs at fcore. **11% to 78% energy savings** over no voltage/frequency scaling.

**Akui et al. (JSSC 2004), Sony PDA processor**, 0.18 µm eDRAM, **0.9–1.6 V, 8–123 MHz**: a DFC block picks frequency, a critical path monitor sets voltage, and a clock-thinning circuit gives **0.5 MHz** frequency steps.

**TI SmartReflex (Gammie, ISSCC 2008), 45 nm.** Power management by modes: High perf. (FBB + AVS), Mid and Low perf. (AVS + DVFS + RBB), No computation (AVS, DVFS, RBB, power-down). Body bias plot: forward bias up to ~+300–400 mV raises performance to ~125%; reverse bias down to ~−300 mV and below cuts leakage to below 75%.

!!! eq "Equation card"
    Body effect (added, standard): Vt = Vt0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF)).
    RBB (VSB > 0 for NMOS) raises Vt and cuts leakage exponentially; FBB lowers Vt and speeds up, at the cost of leakage and junction current. Body-bias effectiveness shrinks in FinFET (thin, undoped fin), which is why it survives mainly in FD-SOI (added).


### 8.6 Why canaries need margin: mistracking, local variation, fast changes

SLIDE2:m08_p039|A canary only tracks the real critical path across voltage approximately, and since the real critical path depends on the instruction, multiple canaries are needed to reduce the margin.||m08_p040|IBM Power6 uses 24 critical-path monitors with a time-to-digital converter that reads timing slack as a thermometer code and models Fmax across voltage within 3 FO2 delays.

Three sources of canary margin (slide 36): **(1) mistracking, (2) local variation, (3) fast-changing variation.**

**#1 Mistracking.** Ideal: the canary (CPM) delay vs V curve sits just above the core critical path everywhere. Actual: the core critical path is not one path; it **depends on the instruction**, and different paths (wire-dominated, gate-dominated, stacked, different Vt) scale differently with V and T. The curves cross, so a single canary fails at some voltages unless a big margin is added. Fix: **multiple CPMs** of different composition, take the worst, reduced margin.

**IBM Power6 CPM (Drake, ISSCC 2007), 65 nm.** Many CPR paths of different types feed a **TDC**: a delay line with 7 flops sampling the output at successive taps, giving a thermometer code (Fast: 1111110, Slow: 1000000). Results: CPM models Fmax across voltage **within 3 FO2 delays**; **24 CPMs** placed in expected high-activity areas to sense voltage transients and local hot spots. Limits: significant calibration effort during test; difficult to detect very fast voltage transients.

SLIDE2:m08_p041|Because the canary and the real critical path each vary locally, keeping tracking failures rare requires a 3σ margin on both distributions.||m08_p043|The first supply droop after a load step is fast (under 10 cycles) and can be highly localized, so a remote canary cannot see or react to it in time.

**#2 Local variation.** The canary is a different set of transistors from the critical path. With WID variation each has its own distribution; to keep the tracking failure region (overlap) small, the replica must be set about **3σ + 3σ** away from the critical path. Slide 42: histogram of replica path delay mistracking (% of original path delay), N = 1000; at **VDD = 1.2 V σ = 3%**, at **VDD = 0.7 V σ = 8%**. Local variation grows at low voltage, so canaries need more margin, waste energy, and need **multiple canaries to average** out variation (σ of the average falls as 1/√n).

```latex
\sigma_{mistrack} = \sqrt{\sigma_{canary}^2 + \sigma_{crit}^2}, \qquad \text{margin} \approx 3\,\sigma_{mistrack}
```

**#3 Fast-changing variation.** After a current step, VCC shows a deep **first droop** (Intel data: roughly from 1.2 V down toward ~1.1 V within the first few ns, then ringing settling over ~50 ns). The first droop (package L with on-die decap resonance) is **fast** (the canary loop needs **> 10 cycles**) and **highly localized**.

!!! core "Core idea"
    A canary is a copy, not the circuit. It tracks what copy and original share (global process, slow V, T, aging) and misses what they do not share (local variation, instruction-dependent paths, local fast droop).

SLIDE2:m08_p044|Itanium 2 regional voltage detectors spot a ~160 mV local droop and dither the regional clock from 2.272 GHz to 2.087 GHz for a droop lasting about 18 cycles.||m08_p048|Canary response takes a detection delay plus a response delay, during which the core keeps slowing at the environment's rate of change, so the restore margin must cover that interval.

**Itanium 2 local canary (Fisher, JSSC 2006).** Regional voltage detectors drive regional clock dividers. On a **~160 mV** local droop, frequency is reduced from **2.272 GHz to 2.087 GHz** (−8%) for a droop lasting **~18 cycles**. This is **di/dt adaptation**: instead of guardbanding the whole chip for the worst first droop, stretch the clock only where and when it happens. (Modern adaptive clocking / droop detectors on CPUs and GPUs follow this idea, added.)

**Response time margin (slides 45–48).** As core voltage (or 1/temperature) ramps at a rate (V/s), core delay and canary delay both rise. The canary takes one cycle to raise an alarm (**detection delay**) and the system needs several cycles to raise V or lower f (**response delay**). During that time the core keeps slowing, so a **restore margin / response margin** is required:

```latex
\text{margin} \;\geq\; \frac{\partial t_d}{\partial V}\cdot\frac{dV}{dt}\cdot(t_{detect} + t_{response})
```

(added formalization of the slide picture). Temperature changes in **ms**, voltage in **µs**: slow response + fast environment = more margin.

!!! why "Why it matters for std-cell / ROM work"
    Canaries and CPMs are built from library cells, so the designer must pick cells whose V/T sensitivity spans the real critical paths (wire-heavy, stacked NAND/NOR, high-Vt, flop-dominated). SRAM/ROM access paths scale with V and T differently from logic (bitline discharge vs gate delay), so a logic canary mistracks the memory: memories need their own replica (e.g. a replica bitline for sense timing) or a separate margin. Droop detectors and adaptive clocking reduce the IR/di/dt budget in signoff, but only if their reaction time is shorter than the first droop.
takeaways: A replica is useful only to the extent that it tracks the paths and operating changes that matter.
Safe adaptation requires a policy for fast disturbances and delayed control action.
checks: Separate design-time DVFS tables from feedback-based adaptation.
Name two ways a canary can mistrack the actual critical path.
Specify a safe response when the monitor indicates margin loss faster than the regulator can react.

modules.title: Compute near stored data: signal and efficiency limits
modules.objective: Compare memory-side computation by data movement, precision, signal margin and conversion overhead.
modules.body:
### 11.1 The memory wall and where CIM sits

SLIDE2:m11_p005|External memory access costs ~1000 fJ/bit, 20X an on-chip SRAM access (50 fJ/bit) and 167X a PE operation (6 fJ/bit), so data movement dominates system energy.||m11_p007|Architectures evolve from von Neumann (separate storage and processor) to near-memory compute to in-memory compute, trading transferred data for energy efficiency.

**Memory wall (slide 4).** In a von Neumann machine, weights and intermediate data travel through a hierarchy (NVM, DRAM, SRAM, PE controls, PE array) over a system bus. The result is long latency, high power and high hardware cost. The two responses are high-bandwidth memory, or an architecture beyond von Neumann.

**Energy numbers (Houshmand, IEDM 2020):**

```latex
E_{system} = E_{compute} + E_{on\text{-}chip\ access} + E_{external\ access}
```

| Operation | Energy (fJ/bit) |
|---|---|
| Off-chip memory | ~1000 |
| On-chip SRAM | 50 |
| PE operation | 6 |

So external access is >20X an on-chip SRAM access and >167X a PE operation. Even on chip (Wang, JSSC 2019), the **system bus** dominates: bus energy is **>26X the SRAM read energy** (slide 6 example: SRAM array read 1.6 pJ, network inside the cache macro 4.2 pJ, system bus 42 pJ vs a 32-bit add at 0.1 pJ).

**Three architectures (slide 7):**

- **Von Neumann**: memory array (storage) → read/write → data bus → processor.
- **Near-memory compute**: digital computing units placed right next to a storage array.
- **In-memory compute**: the array does storage and compute; mixed-signal or digital compute units are built into the macro.

Moving to the right reduces transferred data and raises energy efficiency.

**Device choices (slides 8–12):**

| Category | Devices | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-CMOS (off-chip NVM / DRAM PIM) | NAND flash, DRAM | reduces external memory access | memory processes are slow and inefficient for logic |
| CMOS volatile | SRAM, eDRAM | high throughput, compatible with existing architectures | lower memory density, utilization issues |
| CMOS nonvolatile (nvCIM) | MRAM, RRAM, PCRAM | eliminates weight movement, keeps whole network on chip, instant power-on (no reload) | limited capacity (~64 Mb), so only tiny edge models; device variation and reliability |

nvCIM's edge-AI pitch (slide 12): an SRAM-CIM edge chip must reload weights from NVM after every power-on, while an nvCIM chip wakes up with its weights in place. That gives low energy and short wake-up latency for duty-cycled devices.

**Metrics (slide 13):** performance in **TOPS** (10¹² operations per second, where one add or one multiply counts as one OP), energy efficiency in **TOPS/W**, area efficiency in TOPS/mm², **accuracy loss** of the network caused by CIM non-idealities, and memory capacity. Since precision changes everything, numbers are normalized:

```latex
TOPS_{N\,bit} = TOPS_{M\,bit}\cdot\frac{M_{input}}{N_{input}}\cdot\frac{M_{weight}}{N_{weight}},\qquad TOPS_{1b} = TOPS_{8b}\cdot 8\cdot 8
```

!!! guard "Common trap"
    CIM papers often quote 1-bit or 4-bit TOPS/W. Always normalize to the same input and weight precision before comparing. An 8b×8b operation is worth 64 binary operations.


### 11.4 Analog CIM: multiplier styles

SLIDE2:m11_p024|In-cell computing puts a multiplier in each bitcell (high parallelism, larger cell); in-array computing shares a local compute cell among a group of foundry 6T/8T cells (better density).||m11_p025|A current-domain multiplier is an AND: the cell sources Ion only when input X (on WL) and weight W are both 1; resistive memories use LRS/HRS currents instead.

**Why analog.** MAC (multiply-accumulate) is **>99% of the operations** in a neural network, Y = Σ Xi·Wi. Analog CIM uses the array as a matrix-vector multiplier: inputs X drive the wordlines (activation), weights W sit in the bitcells, and each bitline sums the products and is read by an ADC. Three mechanisms define a design: **multiplying, accumulating, and handling multi-bit inputs/weights**.

**In-cell vs in-array (slide 24, TSMC ISSCC'21/'22):**

- **In-cell local computing**: every bitcell can multiply. High parallelism (TOPS/mm²), but a larger bitcell (extra transistors).
- **In-array local computing**: uses the foundry's compact 6T/8T cells; a local computing cell (LCC) is shared by a group of cells (a sub-array). Good memory density (Mb/mm²), medium parallelism.

**Current-domain multiplier (slide 25).** 1-bit multiplication is AND (or NOR, depending on polarity). The SRAM cell with WL = X conducts I_on when X·W = 1 and I_off otherwise. In MRAM/RRAM the weight is a resistance: low-resistance state (LRS) gives I_LRS = "1", high-resistance state (HRS) gives I_HRS = "0".

Note (added) that the "0" is not zero current. The off cells still contribute I_off (SRAM) or I_HRS (RRAM/MRAM), and with N rows active the zero level is N·I_off. The on/off ratio of the cell therefore limits how many rows can be summed, which is a direct consequence of the leakage physics of L09.


### 11.5 Current-domain accumulation

SLIDE2:m11_p026|Cell currents add on the bitline by Kirchhoff's current law; a clamp holds the BL at VBL and a current ADC reads Isum = ΣIi.||m11_p028|Charge-domain multipliers deposit ΔQ = ION·tpulse (current-based) or ΔQ = C0·VWL (coupling-based) on the read bitline.

**Current-domain MAC.** With all rows active, the bitline current is

```latex
Y = \sum_{i=0}^{N}(X_i\times W_i) = \sum_{i=0}^{N} I_i = I_{sum}
```

A **clamping circuit** holds the bitline at a fixed V_BL, so each cell's current does not depend on how much the bitline has moved, and a **current ADC** digitizes I_sum. The I_BL waveform shows a "current developing" phase followed by readout, with levels MAC = 0, 1, … N.

- **Pro**: simple bitcell multiplier.
- **Cons**: **nonlinearity** in the current multiplication (each cell's current depends on its V_DS, set by the clamp, and on the series resistance as the sum grows), and **large power for constant current** (a DC current flows for the whole evaluation).

**Charge-domain (voltage-domain) multiplier (slides 28–29).** Each product deposits a fixed packet of charge on the bitline:

- **Current-based**: a WL pulse of width t_pulse lets the cell discharge ΔQ = I_ON·t_pulse when W = 1.
- **Coupling-based**: the cell drives a local capacitor C0 that couples onto RBL, so ΔQ = C0·V_WL.
- **Charge-sharing-based**: the product is stored on C0 and then shared onto RBL, again ΔQ = C0·V_WL.

The capacitor-based styles are more linear, because the packet is set by a capacitor (well matched, e.g. MOM) rather than by a transistor current (which varies with Vth). That is why they are popular (added).


### 11.7 Multibit weights and the signal-margin problem

SLIDE2:m11_p033|Multibit weights are built by separate columns plus a shifted adder tree, binary transistor sizing in the cell, multi-level cells, or binary-weighted charge sharing.||m11_p036|Signal margin is the worst-case gap between adjacent MAC levels, about range/levels minus variation, and reliable compute needs ADC offset below half of it.

**Multibit weights (slide 33):**

- **(a) Separate columns**: each weight bit in its own column with its own ADC; results are shifted (<<7 … <<0) and summed in an accumulator. This is the most common approach and is robust, but needs one ADC per column.
- **(b) Transistor sizing in the bitcell**: binary-sized read devices (1X, 2X) so one cell's current is weighted.
- **(c) Multi-level cell (MLC)**: e.g. RRAM conductance levels; the distributions must not overlap.
- **(d) BL charge sharing**: binary-weighted compute capacitors (1C, 2C, … 8C) combine column voltages before a single ADC.

**Signal margin (slide 36).** Each MAC value produces a distribution of BL voltages (cell-to-cell Vth variation, cap mismatch, noise). Definitions:

```latex
\text{Signal margin} \approx \frac{\text{total output range}}{\text{number of levels}} - \text{variation},\qquad |V_{os,ADC}| < \frac{\text{signal margin}}{2}
```

- Signal margin is the **minimum (worst-case) voltage gap between consecutive MAC levels**.
- The **ADC offset must be less than half the signal margin** for reliable compute.

This is the CIM version of the SRAM sense margin (added): in a normal read, the margin is between the "0" and "1" bitline distributions at high sigma, and the sense amp offset must fit inside it. In CIM there are N + 1 levels in the same voltage range, so each gap is about N times smaller, and each level's spread grows like √k·σ_cell as more cells contribute. High-sigma analysis now applies to every pair of adjacent MAC levels.

!!! core "Core idea"
    Analog CIM divides the bitline swing into N + 1 levels. Margin per level shrinks like 1/N while the variation of a level grows with the number of contributing cells, so precision is limited by bitcell current variation and ADC offset, exactly the quantities that limit an SRAM read.


### 11.8 Throughput vs margin, and nonlinearity

SLIDE2:m11_p037|Accumulating more rows per bitline raises throughput and energy efficiency but collapses the signal margin.||m11_p038|Measured transfer curves (Verma) bend away from the ideal line because cells move between operating regions across the MAC range.

**Trade-off (slide 37).** Plotted against the number of rows accumulated on the bitline (1 to 128): normalized throughput rises linearly (more MACs per access, low I_BL per row is good), while the voltage-domain signal margin falls from about 0.75 (a.u.) at 1 row to almost zero at 128. More accumulation means higher throughput and energy efficiency but lower compute accuracy. Practical macros activate a limited number of rows at a time (typically 16–64, added) and accumulate the partial sums digitally.

**Nonlinearity (slide 38, Verma, SSC Magazine 2019).** The MAC transfer curve is not linear, because the circuit moves between operating regions:

- (a) ΔV_BL vs WLDAC code: ideal vs nominal curve; the nominal curve bends and the spread grows with code.
- (b) Measured V_RBL vs input (XAC) value from −256 to 256: S-shaped saturation at the ends, with level spacing around zero of only tens of mV (0.28 V vs 0.32 V lines marked).

Sources (added): the bitcell current depends on V_DS, so as the BL discharges the current drops (and the access device can leave saturation); clamp and ADC finite gain; charge injection.

**Design space (slide 39):**

Analog CIM design space = target application × memory device × multiplication method × accumulation method × multibit input solution × multibit weight solution × system co-design.

The optimal point differs for each application.

!!! why "Why it matters for std-cell / ROM work"
    Every non-ideality of analog CIM is a familiar SRAM/ROM sign-off item: bitcell Ion variation at high sigma (local Monte Carlo on the read stack), Ioff accumulation from unselected rows (the bitline-leakage limit on rows per column), sense-amp/ADC offset, wordline pulse-width variation across PVT, and bitline coupling noise. An interviewer may ask how many cells you can hang on a bitline, or how you size a sense amp. The answer is the same σ-based margin argument as in 11.7, with two levels instead of N + 1.
takeaways: Analog accumulation trades conversion overhead and finite signal margin against data movement.
An efficiency number is incomplete without precision, workload, utilization and system boundary.
checks: Explain what operation is represented by current-domain multiplication and summation.
Identify how more active rows can increase useful throughput while shrinking an accuracy margin.
Define a fair comparison boundary between a memory macro and an end-to-end compute system.

modules.title: From transistor bias to gain: gm, ro and loading
modules.objective: Derive the gain of a loaded common-source stage and explain its bias, swing and bandwidth tradeoffs.
modules.body:
### Start with the operating point
An amplifier is a biased nonlinear circuit responding to a small change. First solve the DC operating point: drain current, gate overdrive, drain voltage and available swing. Only then replace the transistor by its incremental model. Transconductance converts a small gate-voltage change into drain-current change; output resistance describes how imperfectly the device holds current when its drain voltage changes. The external load participates in the same output-node current balance.

For an illustrative long-channel NMOS in saturation, with the source at AC ground and body effect neglected:

```latex
g_m \simeq \frac{2I_D}{V_{OV}},\qquad r_o\simeq\frac{1}{\lambda I_D},\qquad
A_v=-g_m\left(r_o\parallel R_D\parallel R_L\right)
```

### Work it through
Take a 1.8 V supply, 100 µA bias, 0.20 V overdrive, channel-length modulation 0.10 V⁻¹ and an 8 kΩ drain resistor. The DC drain voltage is 1.0 V, so the simple saturation condition has margin. Let a 100 kΩ load be connected through an ideal coupling capacitor, so it loads the signal without changing this DC bias. Then gm is 1 mS, ro is 100 kΩ, and the effective resistance is 6.897 kΩ. Gain is −6.897 V/V: a sufficiently small +1 mV input change produces approximately −6.897 mV at the output. The unloaded value gm·ro = 100 is not the gain of this loaded circuit.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why is the sign negative?** A rising gate voltage increases current through the drain resistor, reducing drain voltage. Write output-node KCL before writing a gain formula.

**L2 — Would doubling bias improve gain?** At fixed geometry in this square-law model, gm grows approximately with the square root of current while ro falls inversely with current. The resistor drop also grows. Recalculate bias and headroom; multiplying gm alone gives an incomplete answer.

**L3 — What does a larger load capacitance change?** It leaves ideal DC gain unchanged but moves the output pole downward. A one-pole estimate with 200 fF is about 115 MHz. Additional device capacitances, Miller multiplication and the input source resistance can introduce another dominant pole.

### Verify the mechanism
Use an operating-point report to check every device region, then compare the low-frequency AC gain with a tiny transient perturbation. Increase amplitude to identify distortion and clipping separately from bandwidth. Sweep load resistance and capacitance independently. In a compact model, use reported gm and gds rather than forcing square-law equations onto a short-channel transistor. [Primary reference: MIT single-transistor amplifier stages](https://live.ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-012-microelectronic-devices-and-circuits-fall-2009/18a2d9a52234f9e962d74b5599759767_MIT6_012F09_lec18.pdf).
takeaways: Bias first; incremental model second.
The gain uses every output conductance, including external loading.
Gain, swing and bandwidth must be evaluated together.
checks: Derive the negative sign from KCL.
Calculate the loaded resistance without dropping ro.
Explain why increasing current does not guarantee more gain.

modules.title: Differential pairs: signal gain and common-mode headroom
modules.objective: Separate differential gain from common-mode behavior and derive a plausible input range.
modules.body:
### Separate the two excitations
A differential pair responds to the difference between its inputs while a tail-current source sets their total current. Decompose both input voltages into a shared common-mode level and equal, opposite differential changes. For a matched pair with an ideal tail source and infinitesimal differential input, symmetry makes the common-source node an AC virtual ground. Each transistor sees half the differential voltage. That factor of two matters when moving between a single-ended and a differential output.

```latex
v_1=v_{CM}+\frac{v_{id}}2,\quad v_2=v_{CM}-\frac{v_{id}}2,
\qquad \Delta i_1=+g_m\frac{v_{id}}2,\quad \Delta i_2=-g_m\frac{v_{id}}2
```

With equal resistive drain loads, define the differential output as drain 2 minus drain 1. Its gain is positive gm·RD; the gain from differential input to drain 1 alone is negative gm·RD/2. State your output polarity rather than memorizing a sign.

### Work it through
Use a 1.8 V supply, 200 µA tail current, 0.20 V overdrive in each input device, threshold 0.40 V and 5 kΩ loads. At balance, each branch carries 100 µA, gm is 1 mS, and both drains sit at 1.3 V. A 10 mV differential input creates approximately +5 µA and −5 µA branch changes. The drains move by −25 mV and +25 mV; differential output changes by 50 mV, for gain 5 V/V.

If the tail source needs 0.15 V across it, the input common-mode lower bound is approximately 0.75 V: 0.60 V gate-source voltage plus tail headroom. Input-device saturation gives an upper bound near 1.70 V with these resistive loads. These are first-order limits, not a universal rail-to-rail specification.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why does common-mode gain vanish in the ideal model?** A perfectly constant tail current and perfect symmetry prevent equal input changes from changing either branch current.

**L2 — What breaks rejection?** Finite tail resistance changes total current; mismatched loads or devices convert a common-mode change into a differential output. Check single-ended common-mode gain separately from differential common-mode error.

**L3 — What happens for a large differential input?** Current steers toward one branch. The linear equations cease to apply, and output swing or device saturation can become the limiting factor first.

Verify with independent differential and common-mode sweeps. Log tail compliance, input-device saturation, branch currents and output levels at every point. A good gain number at one common-mode voltage does not establish a usable input range. [Primary reading: MIT differential amplifier stages and metrics](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-012-microelectronic-devices-and-circuits-fall-2009/pages/lecture-notes/).
takeaways: Distinguish single-ended gain from differential gain.
Input common-mode range comes from device headroom.
Finite tail resistance and mismatch are different error mechanisms.
checks: Explain the half-circuit factor of two.
Compute lower and upper common-mode bounds.
Predict branch current behavior for a large differential input.

modules.title: Current mirrors: ratio, compliance and finite output resistance
modules.objective: Predict mirror error and distinguish inadequate headroom from mismatch and channel-length modulation.
modules.body:
### A mirror copies a bias condition
A simple NMOS mirror ties two gates together and uses a diode-connected reference transistor to establish gate-source voltage. Equal gate voltage does not guarantee equal current under arbitrary drain voltages. The intended ratio follows geometry only when operating regions, threshold, temperature and relevant terminal biases are sufficiently matched. Treat compliance as a circuit requirement: the output node must remain high enough for the output transistor to behave approximately like a current source.

For matched long-channel devices in saturation, with equal lengths and a simple channel-length-modulation model:

```latex
\frac{I_{out}}{I_{ref}}\simeq
\frac{W_{out}}{W_{ref}}
\frac{1+\lambda V_{DS,out}}{1+\lambda V_{DS,ref}},
\qquad V_{out,min}\simeq V_{OV}
```

### Work it through
Let the reference current be 50 µA, intended width ratio 4, reference drain voltage 0.60 V, output drain voltage 1.20 V and lambda 0.10 V⁻¹. The ideal ratio predicts 200 µA. The finite-output-resistance model instead gives 200 multiplied by 1.12/1.06, or 211.32 µA: a +5.66% systematic error. No random mismatch was needed to produce it. If output voltage falls below an illustrative 0.20 V overdrive, this saturation expression stops being the right model; that is a compliance failure rather than simply a larger version of the same error.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why diode-connect the reference?** The reference current charges the shared gate until the transistor can conduct it. This creates a gate voltage corresponding to the desired bias.

**L2 — Why use longer devices or a cascode?** Longer devices can improve output resistance; cascoding reduces output-device drain-voltage variation. Both have costs. Length adds area and parasitic capacitance, and a cascode consumes voltage headroom and needs a bias network.

**L3 — What does layout fix?** Matched orientation, nearby placement and suitable common-centroid/interdigitated arrangements can reduce systematic gradients and layout asymmetry. They cannot eliminate finite output resistance, insufficient compliance or all random mismatch.

### Verify before trusting the ratio
Sweep output voltage while holding the reference current fixed. Plot current error and identify the compliance knee. Then repeat across corners and temperature; evaluate local mismatch separately with an appropriate statistical model. Check startup if the mirror is part of a self-biased loop: a zero-current equilibrium can be a real operating state. Inspect current density and device reliability limits as well as nominal accuracy. [Primary reference: MIT amplifier biasing and current mirrors](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-012-microelectronic-devices-and-circuits-fall-2009/e99a2858fa78c976288c042e10b9a06c_MIT6_012F09_lec17.pdf).
takeaways: Matched VGS is necessary but not sufficient for accurate current copying.
Compliance and finite output resistance produce different failure signatures.
A cascode buys output resistance with headroom.
checks: Calculate the error due to unequal VDS.
Identify the compliance knee in an Iout–Vout sweep.
Explain what layout matching can and cannot fix.

modules.title: Feedback: accurate gain requires a stable loop
modules.objective: Use loop gain to distinguish finite-gain error, stability and large-signal settling.
modules.body:
### Close the loop algebraically first
For a voltage-feedback amplifier, subtract a fraction of the output from the input and amplify the error. The ideal closed-loop gain emerges only when the loop gain is large enough. Its frequency-dependent phase also matters: an error correction delayed far enough can reinforce the disturbance instead. DC gain accuracy, phase margin and slew-limited settling are three different checks, even though a single step waveform can expose problems in all three.

```latex
v_o=A(s)\left(v_i-\beta v_o\right),\qquad
\frac{v_o}{v_i}=\frac{A(s)}{1+A(s)\beta},\qquad L(s)=A(s)\beta
```

For a conventional stable open-loop system with a single relevant unity-loop-gain crossing, phase margin is 180 degrees plus the loop phase at that crossing. This familiar shortcut does not replace a full stability analysis for an unusual multi-loop or multiple-crossing system.

### Work it through
Take A0 = 1000 and a frequency-independent feedback factor 0.10. The ideal closed-loop gain is 10, but the actual DC gain is 1000/101 = 9.901. The fractional error relative to 10 is 0.990%. Now suppose the measured unity-loop-gain crossing is at 1 MHz and loop phase there is −125 degrees. Phase margin is 55 degrees. These two calculations answer different questions: the first predicts DC accuracy; the second describes distance from a phase-instability boundary under the stated topology.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why does feedback improve accuracy?** A large loop gain suppresses the residual input error. The closed-loop result becomes less sensitive to changes in open-loop gain, provided the loop remains in its linear operating range.

**L2 — Why can a capacitive load hurt?** Output impedance and load capacitance introduce additional phase lag. Moving a pole toward crossover can reduce margin even if the DC gain is unchanged. Compensation or load isolation changes the loop and must be evaluated with its real loading.

**L3 — Why can a stable amplifier settle slowly?** A large input step may hit the available charging current. The slew interval is set by current and capacitance, after which the small-signal settling behavior dominates. Improving phase margin does not automatically remove slew limiting.

### Verify the whole claim
Measure return ratio with a method that preserves the DC operating point and both sides of the loop loading. Sweep output load, supply, temperature and device corners. Use small steps to inspect ringing and large steps to inspect slew and recovery. Do not equate overshoot with a unique phase margin without the model assumptions needed for that conversion. [Primary reading: TI basic op-amp stability](https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slyt858/slyt858.pdf).
takeaways: Loop gain controls finite-gain error.
Phase margin is evaluated at unity loop gain.
Small-signal stability and large-signal slew are separate.
checks: Derive the closed-loop transfer from the error equation.
Calculate gain error and phase margin.
Choose separate small-step and large-step tests.

modules.title: Noise and offset: density, bandwidth and error budgets
modules.objective: Build an input-referred noise budget without confusing random noise, deterministic offset and interference.
modules.body:
### Keep three different errors separate
Noise is a time-varying random process characterized statistically. Input offset is an equivalent differential input that produces a specified output error at a given operating point; across devices it can have a distribution, yet for one device it behaves like a largely static error over a short measurement. Interference is unwanted coupling from a particular source such as a clock or supply. Averaging, chopping, filtering, layout changes and calibration therefore solve different problems.

White voltage-noise density has units of volts per square-root hertz. Its power integrates over noise bandwidth. For independent input-referred terms and a brick-wall bandwidth approximation:

```latex
e_{rms}=e_n\sqrt{B},\qquad
e_{total}=\sqrt{e_{amp}^2+4kTRB+(i_nR)^2B}
```

For a shaped transfer function, integrate density squared times the squared transfer magnitude instead of inserting the signal bandwidth automatically. Correlated sources require cross terms; root-sum-square is not universal.

### Work it through
Assume amplifier white voltage noise of 8 nV/√Hz, a 10 kΩ source resistor at 300 K, negligible current noise and a 100 kHz brick-wall bandwidth. Amplifier noise is 2.530 µV rms. Resistor thermal noise is 4.070 µV rms using k = 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K. Their root-sum-square is 4.792 µV rms. A gain of 20 produces 95.85 µV rms at the output, assuming the same gain across that noise band. A separate 0.5 mV input offset would create 10 mV output error; adding that signed DC value inside the random-noise square root would mix two different specifications.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — What happens if bandwidth quadruples?** Integrated white-noise rms doubles. A deterministic offset does not become twice as large merely because bandwidth increased.

**L2 — Why is lowest voltage noise not always best?** Input current noise develops voltage across source impedance. A device with a smaller voltage-noise number may lose once its current-noise term is included.

**L3 — What dominates at low frequency?** Flicker noise, drift and interference can invalidate the flat-density approximation. Specify the lower integration frequency or measurement duration and examine the spectrum before blaming white noise.

Verify a noise budget against AC transfer functions and noise simulation, then compare transient or measured spectra using a stated window and bandwidth. Evaluate mismatch-driven offset with an appropriate statistical analysis separately. [Primary reference: Analog Devices MT-047](https://www.analog.com/MT-047).
takeaways: Density must be integrated over an explicit bandwidth.
Uncorrelated noise powers add; static offset is a separate error budget.
Source impedance can make current noise dominant.
checks: Convert nV/√Hz to rms noise.
Explain why offset is not another white-noise term.
Identify when root-sum-square is invalid.

modules.title: Sampling and ADCs: acquisition, aliasing and quantization
modules.objective: Distinguish sampling error from conversion error and budget a first-order acquisition path.
modules.body:
### Follow the signal into the capacitor
A sampled system must first acquire an analog voltage, then preserve enough information to represent it digitally. Sampling creates spectral replicas; signals or noise outside the intended input band can fold into that band. An analog anti-alias filter must therefore act before sampling. Quantization is a different operation: a continuous amplitude is assigned to one of finitely many codes. More bits do not repair aliasing, inadequate acquisition time or a saturated input.

For an ideal uniform converter with full-scale span VFS and N bits, using the usual uncorrelated uniform quantization-error approximation:

```latex
\Delta=\frac{V_{FS}}{2^N},\qquad v_{q,rms}=\frac{\Delta}{\sqrt{12}},\qquad
\mathrm{SNR}_{ideal}\simeq 6.02N+1.76\ \mathrm{dB}
```

The SNR expression assumes a full-scale sine wave and quantization-only error. Small periodic signals can produce correlated quantization error. Real SINAD also includes distortion and other noise.

### Work it through
For 10 bits across a 1.0 V input span, one LSB is 0.9766 mV and quantization noise is 0.2819 mV rms. The ideal full-scale-sine SNR is about 61.96 dB. Now model acquisition as a 1 kΩ source-plus-switch resistance charging 2 pF. The time constant is 2 ns. To settle a worst-case full-scale step below half an LSB, require an exponential error below 1/2048. Acquisition time must exceed ln(2048) time constants, or 15.25 ns. This ideal linear RC calculation excludes switch nonlinearity, driver recovery, charge injection and kickback.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Where does a 70 MHz tone appear when sampled at 100 MS/s?** It can alias to 30 MHz in the first Nyquist band. A digital filter cannot identify that it originally came from 70 MHz if the analog path already folded it into the desired band.

**L2 — Why does a larger sampling capacitor help and hurt?** Thermal sampling-noise variance scales approximately as kT/C in the simple equilibrated model, but larger capacitance takes more charge and more acquisition time from the driver.

**L3 — Why does a faster input demand lower aperture jitter?** Timing error becomes voltage error proportional to input slope. For a sinusoid, jitter-limited SNR depends on input frequency as well as rms jitter, not simply on the sample rate.

Verify acquisition settling at the worst preceding code or input transition, and analyze aliasing with the entire analog input spectrum. Separate DC linearity, dynamic distortion, random noise and clipping in the test plan. [Primary quantization reference: Analog Devices MT-001](https://www.analog.com/mt-001).
takeaways: Bits do not fix aliasing or acquisition errors.
Half-LSB settling needs a stated step size and RC model.
Larger sampling capacitance trades lower thermal noise for driver effort.
checks: Compute LSB and quantization rms error.
Derive the half-LSB settling requirement.
Explain why anti-alias filtering must precede the sampler.

modules.title: RTL that describes the registers you intend
modules.objective: Predict clocked behavior, avoid unintended storage and connect simulation semantics to synthesized hardware.
modules.body:
### Think in state and next-state functions
A clocked design has stored state and combinational logic that computes its next value. RTL is a language for describing that hardware, so procedural order in source code must not be confused with the passage of hardware clock cycles. Nonblocking assignments evaluate their right-hand sides when the process runs and schedule their updates for a later simulation scheduling region. This lets a set of registers observe the same old state at a clock edge.

```systemverilog
always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
  stage1 <= din;
  stage2 <= stage1;
end
```

At each edge, stage2 receives the old stage1. This is two registers, not an immediate copy from din through stage1 into stage2. Blocking assignments are appropriate for ordered temporary calculations in combinational logic, but replacing the two assignments above with blocking assignments changes their simulation meaning and can change inferred dataflow.

### Work it through
Start stage1 and stage2 at zero, and present inputs 1, 0, 1 at three consecutive active edges. The post-edge state pairs are (1,0), (0,1), then (1,0). The second register reflects the sample captured at the preceding edge. At a 200 MHz clock the edge spacing is 5 ns. That is a one-cycle separation between captures into the two registers; describe latency relative to the sampling edge rather than making an ambiguous claim about how long an arbitrary input transition waits.

```latex
q_1[k+1]=d[k],\qquad q_2[k+1]=q_1[k]
```

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why use complete combinational assignments?** If an output must retain its old value on a path through an otherwise combinational process, storage is implied. Supply defaults and cover every relevant branch when the intent is purely combinational.

**L2 — Does a missing else always infer a latch?** No. In an edge-triggered process, retaining the old value describes a flip-flop enable. In a level-sensitive combinational-style process, an incomplete assignment can infer a latch. The event control and data dependencies matter.

**L3 — Is simulation agreement enough?** No. Check inferred registers, widths, signedness, unintended latches and reset behavior. Two processes writing the same register can introduce races or illegal multiple drivers. A testbench that samples in the wrong scheduling region can also report a false failure.

Write a cycle-by-cycle reference trace before running a simulator. Compare it with waveforms and the synthesized netlist, then add assertions for the intended state transition. Keep code style rules tied to the hardware intent rather than treating punctuation as a circuit primitive. [Primary reference: Yosys synthesis primer](https://github.com/YosysHQ/yosys/blob/main/docs/source/appendix/primer.rst).
takeaways: Nonblocking updates let registers use the same old state.
A missing assignment means different hardware in clocked and combinational processes.
Check synthesized structure as well as waveforms.
checks: Trace three cycles of a pipeline.
Distinguish a flip-flop enable from an accidental latch.
Explain a testbench race at a clock edge.

modules.title: CDC protocols: move a transaction, not just individual bits
modules.objective: Choose a crossing protocol based on information rate, coherency and acknowledgement.
modules.body:
### Start with the information being transferred
An asynchronous crossing can violate a receiving register's timing aperture. A synchronizer gives a potentially metastable state more time to resolve before it is used, reducing failure probability. It does not guarantee detection of a short pulse or make a multi-bit word coherent. Decide whether the crossing carries a slowly changing level, an event, a bundled transaction or a stream. Each has a different correctness condition.

A request/acknowledge handshake can transfer a stable data word. The source writes a holding register, asserts a request, and keeps the data unchanged until the destination has captured it and acknowledged. Request and acknowledge pass through appropriate synchronizers in their receiving domains. The destination captures the bundled bus only under the protocol's stability guarantee; copying every bit through unrelated synchronizers is not the same guarantee.

### Work it through
Assume each control synchronizer has two stages, the destination clock is 100 MHz, and the source clock is 80 MHz. Ignoring metastability's rare extra latency and endpoint state-machine cycles, a changed request is observed in roughly 10–20 ns, depending on phase. The acknowledgement returns in roughly 12.5–25 ns. Control propagation for that outward and return transition is therefore about 22.5–45 ns. A four-phase return-to-zero handshake also needs the request and acknowledgement to return low before reuse, so its complete transaction cycle is longer. A two-phase toggle protocol has different bookkeeping; neither permits arbitrary event rate.

```latex
T_{dst}=10\ \mathrm{ns},\quad T_{src}=12.5\ \mathrm{ns},\qquad
t_{control,roundtrip}\approx[1,2]T_{dst}+[1,2]T_{src}
```

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why can a pulse disappear?** A pulse that starts and ends between destination sampling edges is never sampled high. Adding synchronizer stages cannot recover an event that never entered the chain.

**L2 — Why hold the bus?** Different bit arrival times and different metastability outcomes can otherwise combine bits from different words. The handshake creates a safe capture interval; implementation constraints must preserve that bundled-data assumption.

**L3 — What if transactions arrive continuously?** Backpressure is necessary when the source can outpace the crossing. An asynchronous FIFO can provide elasticity, but full/empty logic, pointer synchronization, reset and physical skew constraints still need verification.

Stress the interface with unrelated clock ratios, phase drift, back-to-back requests, destination stalls and independent reset events. Use CDC structural analysis alongside assertions for no loss, no duplication and stable data while a transaction is pending. [Primary protocol reference: AMD full-handshake bus synchronizer](https://docs.amd.com/r/2023.2-English/ug1344-versal-architecture-libraries/XPM_CDC_HANDSHAKE).
takeaways: A synchronizer reduces metastability risk; a protocol preserves meaning.
Short pulses and coherent words require more than per-bit synchronization.
Latency and throughput are different CDC requirements.
checks: Explain pulse loss without invoking a logic bug.
State precisely when the source may overwrite data.
Describe reset behavior for an in-flight handshake.

modules.title: Reset and verification: make initialization a protocol
modules.objective: Define reset behavior across clock domains and test recovery instead of only testing power-up.
modules.body:
### Reset is part of the interface contract
Specify what reset does to state, outputs and outstanding transactions. A synchronous reset is sampled by a clock; it cannot initialize a stopped domain merely by changing its pin. An asynchronous reset can assert independently of a clock, but its release can violate recovery/removal timing near an edge. A common approach is asynchronous assertion with a separately synchronized release in each clock domain, when that matches the technology and system requirements. Do not assume one domain's clean release is synchronous to every other domain.

### Work it through
Consider a two-stage reset-release synchronizer in a 100 MHz domain. Both stages clear asynchronously. After external reset is released, ones propagate through the two stages on successive rising edges. The release output therefore rises about 10–20 ns later, depending on phase, ignoring a possible extra resolution cycle. Downstream sequential logic may first perform normal work on the following edge because it sees the previous release state at the edge when that output changes. State whether latency refers to the reset output transition or the first accepted transaction.

```latex
T=\frac{1}{100\ \mathrm{MHz}}=10\ \mathrm{ns},\qquad
t_{release}\approx[1,2]T
```

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Must every register reset?** Reset control and validity state that establishes safe behavior. Large datapaths can sometimes remain uninitialized until their valid bit is set. This is an architectural decision: prove uninitialized data cannot influence a valid output, address, write enable or safety-critical control.

**L2 — What happens to an in-flight transaction?** If only one side of a handshake resets, the other may retain a request or acknowledgement. Define whether the transaction is flushed, replayed or completed and how the interface returns to an agreed idle state. Otherwise reset can create duplication or a permanent wait.

**L3 — What makes a verification result meaningful?** A property can pass vacuously if the event it checks never happens. Pair safety assertions with coverage that demonstrates reset, release, a request, a stall and eventual completion. For liveness, state assumptions about clocks and external readiness; no design can guarantee progress if the environment never permits it.

Write tests that assert reset during each protocol phase, release it close to edges, stop and restart clocks, and vary the order of domain releases. Run structural reset-domain checks and recovery/removal analysis in addition to RTL simulation. Use X-aware simulation or formal reasoning to find control paths that accidentally depend on uninitialized state. Device-specific reset guidance may differ, so verify the target library or FPGA architecture before choosing an implementation. [Primary reference: AMD reset methodology](https://docs.amd.com/r/2024.1-English/ug949-vivado-design-methodology/Synchronous-Reset-vs.-Asynchronous-Reset).
takeaways: Reset assertion and reset release have different timing concerns.
Each domain needs an explicit initialization and recovery contract.
A passing property needs coverage and meaningful environment assumptions.
checks: Distinguish release-output latency from first useful work.
List safe behavior for an in-flight reset.
Explain how a valid bit can protect an unreset datapath.

modules.title: Repair setup and hold without moving the failure elsewhere
modules.objective: Choose timing repairs from max/min path evidence and verify their side effects across corners.
modules.body:
### Diagnose the path before changing it
Setup asks whether the latest data arrives before a future capture requirement. Hold asks whether the earliest new data stays out of the current capture aperture. A repair changes a physical circuit shared by many paths, so a local slack improvement can create another violation. Separate cell delay, net delay, clock arrival, uncertainty and constraint validity before selecting a move. An incorrect exception or an unintended clock relationship is not repaired by inserting buffers.

Let capture-minus-launch skew be delta. With stated positive uncertainty allowances:

```latex
S_{setup}=T+\delta-t_{setup}-U_s-t_{cq,max}-t_{data,max}
```
```latex
S_{hold}=t_{cq,min}+t_{data,min}-\delta-t_{hold}-U_h
```

### Work it through
Use a 1000 ps period, +40 ps skew, 60 ps setup, 20 ps setup uncertainty, 90 ps maximum clock-to-Q and 850 ps maximum data delay. Setup slack is +20 ps. For the same endpoint, take 35 ps minimum clock-to-Q, 25 ps minimum data delay, 30 ps hold and 10 ps hold uncertainty: hold slack is −20 ps. A proposed delay cell adds 30 ps on the min path but 45 ps on the max path. It fixes hold to +10 ps while breaking setup to −25 ps if both paths traverse that cell. The repair needs a different location, another cell, a setup improvement elsewhere or an allowed architectural change.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why not lower the clock frequency for hold?** Period appears in the setup equation and is absent from this same-edge hold equation. Slowing the clock does not remove the short-path race.

**L2 — Where should a hold cell go?** Prefer a branch that affects the offending endpoint without unnecessarily delaying unrelated critical paths, while respecting slew, load, placement and routing constraints. Placement close to an endpoint is a useful starting intuition, not a proof of correctness.

**L3 — Why can resizing fail?** A stronger cell may reduce its own delay while increasing upstream input load, changing both min and max behavior. Clock skew adjustments likewise exchange setup and hold margin; they are not free time.

Verify all relevant modes and corners after routing-aware parasitic updates. Check electrical constraints, changed clock paths and functional equivalence. Record before/after path breakdowns and total violating endpoints rather than celebrating one repaired worst path. OpenROAD's timing repair documentation provides a concrete example of sequencing setup and hold repair while controlling their interaction. [Primary reference](https://openroad.readthedocs.io/en/latest/main/src/rsz/README.html).
takeaways: One repair can improve hold while breaking setup.
Use the actual skew sign convention and explicit uncertainty.
Recheck shared paths and all relevant modes/corners.
checks: Calculate both slacks for the worked endpoint.
Evaluate a delay cell using both min and max delay.
Explain why faster cells can increase upstream delay.

modules.title: Placement, routing and parasitics: why shorter is not always better
modules.objective: Explain routing-driven delay and select congestion fixes from physical evidence.
modules.body:
### Placement predicts a route; extraction measures one
Synthesis sees cell connectivity and a delay model. Placement chooses physical locations; routing must then realize those connections within metal, via, spacing and blockage constraints. Two equally short-looking placements can have very different pin accessibility or routing demand. A congested channel can force detours and extra vias, changing delay and power after the logic is already fixed. A timing estimate based only on straight-line distance can therefore miss the actual cause of a late path.

For a uniform distributed RC wire driven through resistance Rd and ending in a lumped load CL, a first-order Elmore moment is:

```latex
\tau_E\simeq R_d(C_w+C_L)+R_w\left(\frac{C_w}{2}+C_L\right)
```

This is a time-constant-like first moment, not an exact 50% crossing. A single-pole approximation may convert it to a rough crossing estimate, but a distributed network can require a waveform calculation.

### Work it through
Take Rd = 1 kΩ, wire resistance 200 Ω, wire capacitance 80 fF and load 20 fF. The moment is 100 ps + 12 ps = 112 ps. If a routing detour doubles wire length at unchanged cross-section and environment, both wire resistance and capacitance double. The new moment is 180 ps + 40 ps = 220 ps. The wire's own RC contribution grows quadratically with length, while driver loading also increases. This is why a modest physical detour can erase a gain achieved by gate sizing.

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — Why can lower utilization help?** It can provide whitespace for legal placement, buffering and routing access. But blindly spreading cells can also increase wire length and clock demand. Look at local congestion, not just the chip-wide utilization percentage.

**L2 — Why not put every critical net on upper metal?** Upper layers may offer lower resistance, yet access vias, scarce tracks, coupling, power-grid reservations and other critical nets constrain the choice. Evaluate the complete path and routing resource cost.

**L3 — Can a clean global route guarantee detailed-route success?** No. Global routing allocates coarse resources; detailed routing must satisfy actual geometry and design rules. Pin access, via enclosure and local blockages can fail even when a coarse congestion metric looks acceptable.

Compare placement estimates, global-route parasitics and extracted post-route delay for the same endpoint. Inspect layer usage, detours, pin access and coupling contributions. A useful repair hypothesis names the bottleneck, predicts which metric changes, and checks that no new electrical or routing violation appears. [Primary implementation reference: OpenROAD global routing](https://openroad.readthedocs.io/en/latest/main/src/grt/README.html).
takeaways: Routing topology and pin access matter beyond geometric distance.
Wire self-RC can grow quadratically with length.
A global congestion metric is not detailed-route signoff.
checks: Calculate a distributed-wire Elmore moment.
Predict which terms change when length doubles.
Name evidence that distinguishes congestion from a weak driver.

modules.title: Scan and at-speed test: controllability, observability and timing
modules.objective: Explain what scan makes testable and why structural coverage does not prove functional correctness.
modules.body:
### Separate functional operation from test operation
Scan makes internal sequential state accessible by connecting scan-capable registers into shift chains. In shift mode, a tester loads a starting state and unloads a response. In capture mode, functional logic computes a response that can be observed through those registers. This improves controllability and observability of internal faults; it does not replace verification that the intended algorithm and interface behavior are correct.

The scan input mux, scan-enable control and chain routing are physical circuit elements. Their delay, hold behavior, power and clock-domain relationships need design attention. Test mode is not an abstract exception from timing or electrical constraints.

### Work it through
Suppose 1200 scan registers are partitioned into four equal chains. Each chain contains 300 bits. At a 20 MHz shift clock, one parallel load of all chains takes 300 cycles, or 15 µs. A deliberately simple isolated pattern requiring a load, two capture cycles and a separate unload takes 602 cycles, or 30.1 µs if every cycle used the same clock. Real at-speed capture uses its required launch/capture spacing rather than the slow shift period. Test scheduling can overlap unloading one response with loading the next pattern, reducing the amortized shift cost; do not charge two full shifts per pattern automatically.

```latex
L_{max}=\left\lceil\frac{N_{FF}}{N_{chains}}\right\rceil,
\qquad t_{shift}=\frac{L_{max}}{f_{shift}}
```

### Three levels of drill-down
**L1 — What does a stuck-at test check?** It attempts to activate a modeled permanent logic value fault and propagate its effect to an observable point. High coverage of that model does not cover every possible manufacturing defect.

**L2 — Why use at-speed launch and capture?** A transition or path delay problem may produce the correct steady-state value but arrive too late. The test must create the relevant transition and capture under an appropriate timing interval. Slow scan shifting alone does not establish functional-speed timing.

**L3 — What changes physically?** Long scan routes can create hold and congestion problems; excessive simultaneous switching can cause supply droop during capture. Chain ordering, partitioning, test-clock controls and power-aware patterns must be coordinated. Domain crossings can require additional measures such as lockup elements, depending on clocks and library behavior.

Verify chain connectivity, scan-enable timing, capture clocks, reset/test isolation and unknown-state propagation. Interpret coverage with the fault model, exclusions and untestable categories visible. Report your actual contribution precisely: writing scan constraints, debugging chains, analyzing coverage and signing off a production flow are different claims. [Primary references: OpenROAD DFT](https://openroad.readthedocs.io/en/latest/main/src/dft/README.html) and [EECS 627 testability](https://www.eecs.umich.edu/courses/eecs627/testability.html).
takeaways: Scan improves internal access; it does not prove the specification.
At-speed capture checks timing behavior that slow shifting cannot.
Test insertion has real timing, routing and power costs.
checks: Calculate maximum chain length and shift time.
Distinguish stuck-at activation from delay-fault capture.
Explain why scan hold and capture power still need analysis.

questions.title: Repair a hold violation
questions.prompt: For a same-edge hold check with unchanged clock skew, which change directly improves negative hold slack?
questions.answer:
!!! analogy "Picture it"
    Setup and hold are a **photographer's shutter**: the subject (data) must be still a moment **before** the click (setup) and a moment **after** (hold). Taking photos less often (a slower clock) doesn't help if someone jumps into the frame right at the click.

DIAGRAM:timing

> **Hold time** is the minimum time the data input must stay **stable after the capturing clock edge**, so the flop reliably captures the **old** value. A **hold violation** means **new data arrives too early**, through a path that's too fast, and corrupts the value being captured. **Setup time** is the mirror image: data must be stable **before** the edge.
>
> The key difference: the **hold check compares launch and capture on the same clock edge**, so the **clock period doesn't appear**. That's why you **can't fix hold by slowing the clock**. You fix it by **adding delay to the short data path** (buffers or slower cells), **reducing clock skew**, or using a flop with a smaller hold requirement. Setup, by contrast, gets better with a longer period.

!!! eq "Hold and setup slack (S = capture clock arrival − launch clock arrival)"
    ```latex
    \text{Setup slack} = T + S - t_{cq,max} - t_{pd,max} - t_{setup}
    \qquad
    \text{Hold slack} = t_{cq,min} + t_{cd,min} - S - t_{hold}
    ```
    **Remember:** setup races the **next** edge (T is in it); hold protects the **same** edge (no T). **Later capture clock (S > 0) helps setup, hurts hold.**

!!! core "Core memory"
    **Setup = old data arrives in time. Hold = new data stays away long enough. Period only helps setup.**

- **Follow-up: "Where does hold come from inside the flop?"** In a TG master–slave flop, the master's input gate closes a little **after** the clock edge (clock buffering, CLK/CLKB overlap). Data changing inside that window can leak through (Q7).
- **Follow-up: "Can setup or hold be negative?"** Yes. They're measured at the **external pins**. If the internal clock is delayed relative to data, data can arrive after the edge and still be captured (negative setup), and vice versa.
