questions.title: ROM folding and address allocation
questions.prompt: A 4K×32 memory is organized as 512 physical rows by 256 columns. How many column choices per output bit and how many row-address bits are needed?
questions.answer:
Why they ask: it tests whether you can turn "4K×32" into rows, columns, a mux and a decoder with numbers, and whether you see the delay and energy consequences.

FIG:D_org.png|For 128 Kb, BL development delay grows with rows and WL RC with columns squared; their sum has a minimum near 256–512 rows

**Opening question.** "You need a 4K×32 memory (128 Kb). How do you organize the array?"

**Answer.** Not 4096 rows × 32 columns. A 4096-cell BL is about 780 fF and takes about 3 ns to develop 100 mV. Instead, **fold** the words with a **column mux** so the array is closer to square: 512 rows × 256 columns (mux 8) or 256 × 512 (mux 16). Then weigh:
- **BL C ∝ rows**, which sets read time
- **WL R and C ∝ columns**, so WL RC ∝ columns²
- mux ratio, which sets SA pitch
- decoder size
- energy

Go to **banks** when the capacity grows. Draw: the array, the row decoder on the left, the column mux and SAs at the bottom, I/O, and the control block.

**Worked numeric problem.** Per cell: BL 0.19 fF, WL 0.3 fF and 2 Ω. I_cell = 25 µA and ΔV = 100 mV.

| rows × cols | mux | C_BL | t_BL (100 mV) | WL 0.5·R·C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4096 × 32 | 1 | 778 fF | 3.1 ns | 0.3 ps |
| 1024 × 128 | 4 | 195 fF | 778 ps | 4.9 ps |
| 512 × 256 | 8 | 97 fF | 389 ps | 19.7 ps |
| 256 × 512 | 16 | 49 fF | 195 ps | 79 ps |
| 128 × 1024 | 32 | 24 fF | 97 ps | 315 ps |

In this model the delay sum is lowest near **256 × 512**. Many designs still choose **512 × 256**, because of energy, SA pitch and layout aspect (next follow-up).

**▸ Follow-up 1.** "Where does the energy go, and does the mux ratio matter?"

**Answer.** Every cell on the selected row turns on, so **all columns swing**, not just the 32 you read. Energy per access = cols × C_BL × V_DD × ΔV = bits × c_cell × V_DD × ΔV ≈ **2.2 pJ**, regardless of aspect. The **useful fraction is 32/cols**: mux 16 wastes 15/16 of it. To cut energy you need a **divided/segmented WL** (only the needed columns' local WL goes high) or **banking** (only one bank is active), not a different aspect ratio.

**▸ Follow-up 2.** "Size the row decoder with logical effort."

**Answer.** Take a 9:512 decoder (512 rows × 256 columns).
- Each address line (true or complement) drives half of the 512 ANDs, so **B = 256**.
- WL load = 256 × 0.3 fF = 76.8 fF. With address C_in = 2 fF, **H = 38.4**.
- A 9-input AND built as NAND3 + NOR3 has **G = (5/3)(7/3) = 3.89**.

```latex
F=G\,B\,H=3.89\cdot256\cdot38.4\approx3.8\times10^{4},\qquad N=\log_4F\approx7.6\Rightarrow 8,\qquad f=F^{1/8}\approx3.74
```

Delay ≈ N·f + P ≈ 29.9 + 8 ≈ **38 τ** (with p ≈ 1 per stage; N = 8 beats 7 or 9). **Predecoding** (three 3:8 predecoders whose outputs are ANDed at each row) cuts the branching per address bit and the number of large gates. The final WL driver is a large inverter chain sized for the WL RC.

**▸ Follow-up 3.** "Why does WL delay go as columns², and how do you fix it?"

**Answer.** R and C both grow with length, so the distributed RC ∝ L². The Elmore value is 0.5·R·C (the 50 % point is about 0.38·RC). Fixes:
- **strap** the poly WL with metal
- a **divided WL**: a global WL plus local WL drivers per segment, which also saves energy
- drive the WL from the middle (halves L, quartering the RC)

You cannot put repeaters inside the cell pitch, so segmentation is the way to "repeat".

**▸ Follow-up 4. What if the spec were 1K×128 instead of 4K×32 (same 128 Kb)?**

**Answer.** Physically it can be the **same 512 × 256 array**:
- **4K×32**: 9 row bits + 3 column bits, **mux 8**, 32 SAs.
- **1K×128**: 9 row bits + 1 column bit, **mux 2**, **128 SAs** and I/Os.

The wide word has **4× the bandwidth** per access and wastes fewer columns (1 of 2 instead of 7 of 8 in each mux group), so energy per useful bit is lower. The costs are 4× the SAs and I/O, an SA pitch of only **2 columns** (tight), and higher peak current per access.

**▸ Follow-up 5. What if capacity grows 16× (2 Mb)?**

**Answer.** Don't stretch one array. Use **banks** of about 128 Kb, plus bank decode, an H-tree or balanced global data and address routing, and activate only one bank per access. **Leakage ∝ total bits** no matter how you organize it, so add retention or power-gating of idle banks. For ROM, rows per local BL also set the **(N−1)·I_off** leakage (D3), which is another reason for hierarchy.

**▸ Follow-up 6.** "Any other reason to use a column mux besides aspect ratio?"

**Answer.** **Soft errors**: interleaving bits of different words means one multi-cell upset hits different words, so per-word **ECC** (SECDED) can correct each one. The cost is half-select during writes (D2).

!!! guard "Trap"
    "Make it square for minimum delay" without mentioning that every column on the row swings (energy), SA pitch, or the mux's effect on half-select. Another trap is forgetting that BL delay is set by the **number of rows**, not by total capacity.

!!! core "One-line takeaway"
    Rows set C_BL and read time, columns set WL RC (∝ cols²), and mux ratio sets SA pitch and wasted energy. Fold the words to balance these, then use banks and a logical-effort-sized decoder (here about 8 stages, ≈ 38 τ).

questions.title: Average and RMS pulse current
questions.prompt: An ideal current is 2 mA for 10% of each period and zero otherwise. What are its average and RMS values?
questions.answer:
Why they ask: the interviewer has EM-flow background. They want to see that you separate the voltage problem (IR) from the reliability problem (EM), and that you can do the numbers.

FIG:D_ir_rail.png|Static IR along a 100 µm, 200 Ω rail carrying 0.5 mA spread uniformly, fed from one end vs both ends

**Opening question.** "What's the difference between IR drop and EM, and how would you check a standard-cell power rail?"

**Answer.**
- **IR drop** is voltage lost across grid resistance, so cells see a lower V_DD. That means slower timing and less SRAM/ROM margin. It has a **static** part (average current) and a **dynamic** part (L·di/dt and resistive drop during switching bursts, buffered by decap).
- **EM** is a **wear-out** mechanism: the electron wind transfers momentum to metal atoms, which grows **voids** (opens, rising resistance) and **hillocks** (shorts). It depends on **current density J** and **temperature**, and it is checked per wire and via against foundry limits for average, RMS and peak current.

So: IR is a voltage at time zero, EM is a lifetime. Draw: a rail with tap currents and the V(x) parabola.

**Worked numeric problem (static IR).** The rail is 100 µm long and 0.1 µm wide, with R_s = 0.2 Ω/□. That is 1000 squares, so R = **200 Ω**. A total current I = 0.5 mA is spread uniformly along it.

```latex
V(x)=V_{DD}-\frac{IR}{L^2}\Big(Lx-\frac{x^2}{2}\Big)\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta V_{max}=\frac{IR}{2}\ \text{(one end)},\qquad \frac{IR}{8}\ \text{(both ends)}
```

- Fed from one end: 0.5 mA × 200 Ω / 2 = **50 mV**.
- Fed from both ends: **12.5 mV**.
- With **straps every 20 µm** (each segment 40 Ω, 0.1 mA, both ends fed): **0.5 mV**.
- Doubling the width halves R, so the one-end drop becomes 25 mV.

The lesson: IR drop goes as **I·R/2 for distributed current**, not I·R, and strap pitch is the strongest lever.

**▸ Follow-up 1.** "What is dynamic droop, and what does decap do?"

**Answer.** Model the package and bump path as series R and L feeding the on-die decap C, and apply a load step I. The first droop is roughly I·√(L/C), followed by ringing at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) with Q = √(L/C)/R. **Numbers:** L = 20 pH, R = 2 mΩ, C = 200 nF, 10 A step:
- √(L/C) = 10 mΩ, so the estimate is about 100 mV; the simulation gives **105 mV**.
- f₀ = **80 MHz**, Q = 5.

**What if decap is 4× (800 nF)?** The droop **halves** to about **55 mV** (∝ 1/√C) and f₀ halves to 40 MHz. The DC level is still 0.9 − 10 A × 2 mΩ = 880 mV. Decap only buys **time** for the regulator and package; it cannot fix the resistive (DC) drop.

FIG:D_droop.png|Simulated RLC response to a 10 A load step with 200 nF vs 800 nF on-die decap

**▸ Follow-up 2.** "For EM, which current do you check: average, RMS or peak?"

**Answer.** Take a 2 mA pulse with 10 % duty cycle:
- **I_avg = 0.2 mA**
- **I_rms = 2 × √0.1 = 0.63 mA**
- **I_peak = 2 mA**

**Power rails** carry mostly unidirectional current, so the **average** J limit applies (Black's equation). **Signal wires** are **bidirectional**: they charge and then discharge, so the average is about 0, and damage partly heals when current reverses. Their limits are **RMS** (Joule self-heating, which raises temperature and accelerates EM in nearby wires) and **peak**. For bidirectional ±2 mA pulses of 10 % each, I_rms = 2√0.2 = **0.89 mA**.

FIG:D_em_pulse.png|Average, RMS and peak current of one pulse train: each maps to a different EM/self-heating rule

**▸ Follow-up 3. What if current doubles, or temperature rises 20 °C?**

**Answer.** Black's equation:

```latex
\text{MTTF}=A\,J^{-n}\exp\!\Big(\frac{E_a}{kT}\Big),\qquad n\approx 1\text{–}2
```

- **J × 2 with n = 2** gives MTTF ÷ **4** (with n = 1, ÷2).
- **105 → 125 °C** with E_a = 0.9 eV: exp[(E_a/k)(1/398 − 1/378)] = **0.25**, also ÷4.
- **Both together** give ÷16 (0.062).

This is why EM limits are quoted at a temperature (often 105–125 °C), and why self-heating (RMS) feeds back into the average-current EM rule.

**▸ Follow-up 4.** "How do vias come in?"

**Answer.** Vias are EM weak points: current crowds at the via edge, and the via-to-line interface is where voids nucleate. Each via has its own current limit. With an illustrative 0.1 mA per via, a 1.2 mA rail tap needs **≥ 12 vias**, so use **via arrays**. Arrays also add **redundancy** (one voided via doesn't open the path) and improve yield. **Blech effect**: if J·L is below a critical product, back-stress halts EM. Short segments between vias are therefore effectively immune, which EM tools exploit.

**▸ Follow-up 5.** "List the fixes for IR and EM."

**Answer.**
- **Wider / parallel / stacked rails**: R ↓ and J ↓, which fixes both.
- **More straps and vias**.
- **Decap** near hot spots, for dynamic droop only.
- Place high-current cells near straps.
- Spread switching activity: stagger precharge, skew clock edges.
- Power-switch sizing.
- For signal EM: non-default width rules, a smaller driver (slower edge, lower peak), or splitting the load.

For memories, **all BLs precharging at once** gives a large peak current, so stagger precharge or use segmented arrays.

**▸ Follow-up 6. What if temperature rises 20 °C: does IR drop change too?**

**Answer.** Yes. Cu resistivity rises about 0.4 %/K, so R goes up about 8 % and IR drop goes up about 8 % (50 → 54 mV in the example) (added). Hot is also the leakage corner, so static current rises as well. Hot is therefore bad for IR and EM together.

!!! guard "Trap"
    Checking a signal wire's EM with average current (≈ 0, so it "passes") and missing the RMS/peak limits. Or treating EM as a voltage-drop problem. EM is lifetime, ∝ J^−n·e^(E_a/kT), so 2× current or +20 °C each cost about 4× MTTF.

!!! core "One-line takeaway"
    IR = I·R/2 for distributed load (I·R/8 fed from both ends); droop ≈ I·√(L/C), so decap scales as 1/√C and can't fix DC drop. EM uses average current for rails and RMS/peak for signals, and Black's equation makes 2× J or +20 °C roughly a 4× lifetime hit.

questions.title: What do zero Monte Carlo failures prove?
questions.prompt: For 1,000 independent trials with zero observed failures, what is the approximate one-sided 95% upper bound on failure probability?
questions.answer:
Why they ask: every memory margin above (bump, SNM, write trip, SA offset, ROM leakage) is meaningful only at a sigma target. They want the yield arithmetic and why brute-force Monte Carlo can't reach it.

FIG2:D_pelgrom.png|Pelgrom scaling: σ(ΔVt) = A_VT/√(WL)||D_tail.png|Normal tail with 3, 4.5 and 6σ markers, and array yield vs per-cell sigma for 128 Kb, 1 Mb and 16 Mb

**Opening question.** "How do you verify that a bitcell is robust? Why aren't corners enough?"

**Answer.**
- **Global variation** (die-to-die and wafer; the SS/FF/SF/FS corners) moves **all** devices together.
- **Local random mismatch** (random dopant fluctuation, line-edge roughness, metal grain) is **independent per transistor**, with σ_Vt = A_VT/√(WL).

Bitcells use **minimum-size** devices, so their σ is large, and there are **millions** of cells. A cell fails on **differences** (AX vs PD, left vs right) that corners never create. So you verify global corners **plus** local Monte Carlo at **about 6σ** per cell, which needs special statistical methods. Draw: a normal curve with the tail beyond kσ shaded.

**Worked numeric problem.**
- **Pelgrom**, with A_VT = 1.5 mV·µm:
  - 0.1 × 0.05 µm gives σ_Vt = 1.5/√0.005 = **21.2 mV**.
  - 0.2 × 0.1 µm (4× the area) gives **10.6 mV**, half as much.
- **Yield:** a 1 Mb array (N = 2²⁰ cells) at 99.9 % yield with no repair:

```latex
Y=(1-p)^N\approx e^{-Np}\ \Rightarrow\ p\le\frac{-\ln Y}{N}=\frac{1.0005\times10^{-3}}{1\,048\,576}=9.5\times10^{-10}\ \Rightarrow\ k=\Phi^{-1}(1-p)\approx 6.0\sigma
```

For reference, the tails are: 3σ → 1.3 × 10⁻³, 4.5σ → 3.4 × 10⁻⁶, 6σ → 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁰ (one-sided). Even 3σ, in 1 Mb, means about **1400** failing cells.

**▸ Follow-up 1.** "Why can't you just run Monte Carlo?"

**Answer.** Estimating p ≈ 10⁻⁹ to ±10 % needs about 100 failures, i.e. **100/p ≈ 10¹¹ simulations**. Running 1000 samples with zero failures only shows p < 3 × 10⁻³, which is about **2.7σ**. **Importance sampling** fixes this: sample from a distribution **shifted toward the failure region** (centred near the most-probable failure point in V_t space), then weight each sample by the likelihood ratio f(x)/g(x). That gives an unbiased p estimate from about 10³–10⁴ simulations. Related methods: statistical blockade, and minimum-norm (most-probable-point) search.

**▸ Follow-up 2. What if the array is 16× larger (16 Mb)?**

**Answer.** p ≤ 1.0 × 10⁻³ / 2²⁴ = 6.0 × 10⁻¹¹, which is **6.44σ**: only **+0.44σ** for 16× the bits. The tail is so steep that capacity costs little extra sigma. **Redundancy** (spare rows/columns) and **ECC** relax the requirement much more. For example, with SECDED on 39-bit codewords (32 data + 7 check) in a 1 Mb array, a word fails only with ≥ 2 bad bits. p_word ≈ C(39,2)·p², and 32768 words × 741 × p² ≤ 10⁻³ gives p ≤ 6.4 × 10⁻⁶ ≈ **4.4σ** per cell. In practice ECC is usually reserved for soft errors, so this is an upper bound on the benefit.

**▸ Follow-up 3.** "How does σ map into the memory margins we discussed?"

**Answer.** Each metric has a mean and a spread, and you need roughly μ − kσ > 0:
- **Read SNM**: a 3σ AX/PD skew already took read SNM from 216 to 128 mV (D1/D2).
- **SA**: required ΔV = 5σ × 15 mV + noise (D4).
- **ROM**: I_off is **lognormal**. One σ_Vt (21 mV) changes I_off by exp(0.0212/(1.35 × 0.0259)) ≈ **1.8×**, so a 6σ low-V_t leaker is huge. Summed over N−1 cells it averages out somewhat, but the weak-I_on read-0 cell sits at the far tail.

Metrics like SNM are **nonlinear** in V_t, so sample in V_t space. Do not fit a Gaussian to SNM and extrapolate it.

**▸ Follow-up 4. What if you combine global corners with local variation?**

**Answer.** Run local high-sigma MC **at** the worst global corner for each failure mode. Read stability is typically worst at **FS** (fast NMOS AX, slow PMOS) and write at **SF** (slow NMOS AX, fast PMOS). ROM read-1 is worst **hot** (leakage) and read-0 is worst **slow / low V_DD** (I_on). Low V_DD makes all of these worse, because σ_Vt stays fixed while the margins shrink.

**▸ Follow-up 5.** "What breaks the Gaussian assumption?"

**Answer.** V_t mismatch is close to Gaussian, but the far tail is not guaranteed. Random telegraph noise and aging (BTI) add time-dependent shifts, and layout-dependent effects add systematic offsets. So high-sigma signoff often includes **aging-aware** and **end-of-life** margins, plus silicon V_min correlation.

!!! guard "Trap"
    "We ran 1000 Monte Carlo runs and none failed, so it's fine." That shows only about 2.7σ. A 1 Mb array needs about 6σ per cell, which takes importance sampling or a similar method. Another trap is using global corners alone for a bitcell, whose failures come from **mismatch between neighbouring devices**.

!!! core "One-line takeaway"
    σ_Vt = A_VT/√(WL) makes bitcells the worst-matched devices on the chip. N cells at yield Y need p ≤ −ln Y/N per cell (about 6σ for 1 Mb, +0.44σ for 16×), which you verify with importance sampling and recover with redundancy or ECC.

questions.title: Transient evidence and state retention
questions.prompt: In a hardened latch, a transient fault disables both strong paths to Q while Q’s stored charge initially preserves the correct value. What would be an unjustified robustness claim?
questions.answer:
7. **(Exam 1 P7.3) SEU-hardened latch.** TG1 writes D onto Q and TG2 writes D onto INT2. INT2 and INT3 form a cross-coupled inverter pair (I2: INT2→INT3, I1: INT3→INT2). INT1a is driven by MP3 (gate INT2) and MN3 (gate Q). INT1b is driven by MP4 (gate Q) and MN4 (gate INT2). Q is driven by the stack MP1 (gate INT1a) + MP2 (gate INT3) to Vdd and the stack MN2 (gate INT3) + MN1 (gate INT1b) to ground. PMOS and NMOS have equal on currents and equal off currents. The posted solutions for this part are blank, so all answers below are (derived).
    - **(A) Q = 0 is stored and a strike drives INT3 1 → 0 for several FO4. Sketch INT2, INT1a, INT1b and Q. Does the latch survive?** Stored state: INT2 = 0, INT3 = 1, INT1a = 1, INT1b = 1, Q = 0. The strike sets INT3 = 0. I1 then drives INT2 0 → 1, which turns MP2 on and MN2 off. Q loses both paths (MP1 is off because INT1a = 1, MN2 is off), so **Q floats at 0**. INT2 = 1 turns MP3 off while MN3 stays off (Q = 0), so **INT1a floats at 1**. MN4 turns on while MP4 stays on, so **INT1b fights to about ½**. Q stays at 0 because pulling it up needs INT1a and INT3 to both go low, and INT1a can only fall if Q first rises. The output stage acts like a C-element. **Yes, the latch resists** at Q. The INT2/INT3 pair stays flipped until the next transparent phase rewrites it through TG2.
    - **(B) Same case, but the strike holds INT3 at 0 indefinitely. Can MP1–4 and MN1–4 be sized so Q is unaffected?** Yes, through leakage ratios. Q is floating between MP1 (off) and MN2 (off), so make the pull-down leakage win: **MN2 (and MN1) wider than MP1**. INT1a is floating between MP3 (off) and MN3 (off), so make **MP3 wider than MN3** to keep INT1a high and MP1 off.
    - **(C) Can it be sized so it also survives the mirror case: Q = 1 and a held 0 → 1 strike on INT3?** In the mirror case INT2 falls, so MP2 and MN1 are off, Q floats at 1, INT1b floats at 0 and INT1a fights. Holding Q = 1 needs **MP2 wider than MN1** and **MN4 wider than MP4**. These are different devices from case B, so on paper both sets of ratios can be met at once. In practice the retention is purely leakage-based, sensitive to PVT and to TG1 leakage from D, and holds only for a limited time. Hardening is meant for transient strikes.

questions.title: Can reducing frequency fix hold?
questions.prompt: A short data path violates a capture flop hold requirement by 25 ps. Clock arrivals and the input waveform do not change when frequency is reduced. Which repair directly targets the violation?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** Hold checks whether new data arrives too soon after the same capture edge. Extra minimum data delay can move that arrival beyond the hold window. Recheck maximum delay because the same change consumes setup slack, and check across fast corners and routing variation. A changes the next-cycle setup budget but not the same-cycle hold equation under the stated assumptions. B addresses a different constraint. D usually makes the path even faster. Clock-tree changes may also repair hold, but they must be evaluated on all affected paths.
questions.hint: Hold is a minimum-delay constraint referenced to one clock edge.
questions.followup: Why can a delay buffer have different hold benefit at FF and SS?
questions.trap: Frequency reduction fixes many setup failures but does not inherently fix hold.
choices: Double the clock period.
Reduce only the capture setup time.
Insert delay on the short data path and verify its setup impact.
Remove data buffers to reduce congestion.

questions.title: Why a keeper slows a ROM read
questions.prompt: A precharged NOR-style ROM column is stable against noise after increasing keeper size, but programmed discharge reads become slower. What mechanism best explains both results?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** The weak feedback pull-up replenishes leakage and small negative glitches while the bitline is logically high. On a valid falling read it initially sources current against the selected nMOS discharge path. The net discharge current drops until feedback turns the keeper off, increasing delay and transient contention energy. A reverses its action, C invents isolation, and D confuses retention with resetting the next access. Choose strength from noise/leakage and legitimate-read constraints over PVT, pattern, slew and variation; one nominal waveform is insufficient.
questions.hint: Write net bitline current as pull-down current minus keeper current.
questions.followup: Which PVT combination makes keeper contention most dangerous?
questions.trap: Treating keeper sizing as a monotonic robustness improvement.
choices: The keeper increases pull-down current directly.
The keeper strengthens restoration of a high bitline but fights a legitimate discharge.
The keeper permanently disconnects bitline capacitance.
A keeper removes the need to precharge.

questions.title: ROM decoder hazard
questions.prompt: A dynamic ROM occasionally returns a discharge when changing addresses while evaluation is active. Individual address bits have unequal delays. Which design measure addresses the likely cause?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Decode glitches can briefly activate an unintended wordline. A dynamic bitline may discharge irreversibly for that evaluation phase even if the decoder later settles correctly. Separate address capture/settling from evaluation, use suitable gating or a verified decoder protocol, and check worst-case bit transitions. A may hide a small glitch but also fights intended reads and is no functional guarantee. C leaves stale data. D may mask some pulses but does not prevent corrupted stored charge. Confirm the diagnosis by viewing all wordlines, bitline and evaluation controls together.
questions.hint: A dynamic node cannot generally recover a lost high during evaluation.
questions.followup: How would you test 0111→1000 and other many-bit address changes?
questions.trap: A final one-hot decoder truth table does not prove transient one-hot behavior.
choices: Make every keeper stronger until the glitch disappears.
Guarantee address settling and hazard-free wordline selection before evaluation.
Remove precharge to preserve the prior result.
Use a slower output inverter without checking the wordlines.

questions.title: SRAM stability versus writability
questions.prompt: You strengthen the 6T SRAM access transistors while keeping pull-downs and pull-ups fixed. Which simultaneous trend is plausible?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** During a write, stronger access devices better overpower the cell pull-up through a low bitline. During a read, the precharged high bitline couples through the same access device into the stored-zero node; a stronger access path can raise that node and reduce read stability. Quantify read SNM and a clearly defined write metric separately. A reverses the tradeoff, B ignores it, and D confuses wordline-off hold with wordline-on read. In advanced processes fin quantization and assist circuits further limit simple continuous width tuning.
questions.hint: Compare which side of the access device is trying to win in read versus write.
questions.followup: How can wordline underdrive help reads but hurt writes?
questions.trap: A single cell ratio cannot summarize every read and write condition.
choices: Read stability improves and writing gets harder.
Both read and write margins necessarily improve.
Writing improves, but the read-zero storage node can be disturbed more.
Hold stability disappears whenever access width changes.

questions.title: Sense-amplifier startup timing
questions.prompt: A latch sense amplifier has 25 mV input-referred offset in the unfavorable direction. At enable, the desired bitline differential is only 15 mV before adding noise. What is the defensible conclusion?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Before regeneration, the differential decision includes the desired signal, mismatch offset and noise. In this example the unfavorable 25 mV offset exceeds the 15 mV signal, so the initial effective sign can be wrong. A and C confuse amplification with accuracy: high gain amplifies whichever sign wins. D ignores the differential input, although common mode affects device operation and available gain. Increase signal-development time within the access budget, improve the sense amplifier or use an appropriate offset-mitigation scheme, then verify distributions and failure tails.
questions.hint: Compute desired differential minus unfavorable offset before regeneration.
questions.followup: Why does simply delaying sense enable increase bitline energy and latency?
questions.trap: An ideal offset-free latch waveform is not a statistical read-margin result.
choices: Correct sensing is guaranteed because regeneration has large gain.
Regeneration may amplify the wrong sign; develop more differential or reduce offset.
Gain cancels all device mismatch.
Only the common-mode bitline voltage matters.

questions.title: Characterization pin sensitivity
questions.prompt: For an AOI21 cell Y = NOT(A + B·C), which setup sensitizes the A→Y propagation arc without blocking it?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** With B·C = 0, the expression reduces to Y = NOT(A), so an A transition produces an output transition. B = 0, C = 1 is one valid condition; other BC = 0 states may have different internal charge histories and deserve separate tests. A forces Y = 0 and blocks the A arc. C combines causes and cannot isolate one propagation arc. D characterizes B rather than A. Sensitization is necessary, but the characterization flow must also choose states, history, input slew, output load and the correct output edge.
questions.hint: First simplify the Boolean function under each proposed static condition.
questions.followup: Which BC = 0 states could have different A-arc delays after extraction?
questions.trap: A Boolean arc condition alone does not establish a worst-case transistor history.
choices: B = 1 and C = 1.
B = 0 and C = 1.
B and C both toggle with A.
A held fixed while B toggles.

questions.title: A suspicious delay-table point
questions.prompt: One delay-table entry drops sharply as output load rises, while neighboring entries follow the usual trend. What is the best first action?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** An isolated reversal is a QA signal. Check that the input/output crossings belong to the same intended transition, that the output settled, that load and units are correct, and that the simulator converged. Reproduce the suspect point before modifying the cell or data. A overstates a heuristic as a physical law; nonlinear circuitry and measurement definitions can produce real unusual behavior. B can hide a failure or valid feature. D changes the design before finding the cause. Compare a small local sweep to distinguish a genuine effect from a bad extraction.
questions.hint: Ask what waveform crossing actually produced the tabulated number.
questions.followup: How would you detect a measurement that accidentally used the second output edge?
questions.trap: QA should flag anomalies for diagnosis, not manufacture smooth results.
choices: Delete the point automatically because delay must always be monotonic.
Smooth the entire table and release it.
Inspect the measured waveforms, transition indices, initialization and convergence for that run.
Increase every device size to avoid table noise.

questions.title: Negative setup time
questions.prompt: A characterized flip-flop has a small negative setup value under one documented clock/data-slew condition. What interpretation is valid?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** External 50% clock and data reference crossings are not the instant every internal device responds. Clock buffering and internal transparency can allow data after the external clock reference while still satisfying the chosen output-delay or functional criterion. This does not imply unlimited late arrival. A rejects a valid possibility, C incorrectly removes hold, and D confuses a small timing window with permanently transparent operation. State the measurement thresholds, degradation criterion, slew/load conditions and associated setup/hold tradeoff before using the number in STA.
questions.hint: External clock pin timing and internal latch-closing timing differ.
questions.followup: Why should setup and hold be characterized as a coupled boundary?
questions.trap: A negative table value does not mean negative physical propagation time.
choices: The characterization must be invalid because all setup times are positive.
The data can arrive slightly after the external clock reference and still meet the specified clock-to-Q criterion.
The cell has no hold constraint.
The internal latch never closes.

questions.title: Why LVS passing is insufficient
questions.prompt: A standard-cell layout passes LVS. Which statement is still true?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** LVS compares recognized devices and connectivity to the reference schematic/netlist. DRC checks legal geometry; extraction derives physical R/C; circuit characterization checks behavior; integration checks pin access and cell boundary compatibility. A conflates geometry and connectivity. B ignores parasitics. D assigns routability to a connectivity check. A clean LVS result is necessary evidence for layout correctness, but it cannot prove every independent release criterion. If the comparison uses black boxes or waived mismatches, document those limitations as well.
questions.hint: List each check by the distinct question it answers.
questions.followup: How could two LVS-equivalent layouts have different output slew?
questions.trap: Do not report LVS as complete electrical signoff.
choices: It automatically passes all foundry geometry rules.
Its extracted delay must match the schematic delay.
Its connectivity matches the reference under the LVS comparison, but DRC, extraction and performance checks remain.
Its pins are necessarily easy for a router to access.

questions.title: Finger count is not free
questions.prompt: Two inverter layouts have equal total transistor width. One uses more fingers. Why can their extracted timing differ?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Equal total width gives a similar ideal channel drive under the same model, but the layouts can have different diffusion area/perimeter, source/drain sharing, contact resistance, gate routing and output metal. These change extracted resistance and capacitance, and thus delay and slew. A confuses geometry with logic. C ignores the extraction network. D turns a possible diffusion-capacitance benefit into a universal claim, overlooking added routing and contacts. Compare legal candidate layouts with consistent extraction and characterization conditions rather than infer the best topology from finger count alone.
questions.hint: Trace the actual output diffusion and metal in each candidate.
questions.followup: Which parasitic dominates at light output load?
questions.trap: Equal W/L does not imply equal post-layout behavior.
choices: Finger count changes the Boolean function.
Shared diffusion, contact placement, gate resistance and wiring capacitance can differ.
Equal width makes every physical parasitic identical.
More fingers always reduce all capacitances.

questions.title: Power grid average versus transient
questions.prompt: A ROM power rail has acceptable average IR drop, but reads fail after a large simultaneous precharge event. Which investigation is most relevant?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Simultaneous switching creates a rapidly changing current demand. Local voltage can drop from resistive loss and inductive L·di/dt effects even if average current is acceptable. Examine the local VDD/GND waveform at the failing devices and align it with wordline, precharge and sense events. A misses transient behavior. C selects a cause without evidence. D usually removes charge support and can worsen the transient, although decap placement and resonance need careful analysis. Verify any staggered switching, grid or decap repair against functional timing and wakeup requirements.
questions.hint: Average current and peak current derivative are different quantities.
questions.followup: How could staggering precharge reduce droop while changing access latency?
questions.trap: A chip-level supply waveform may miss a local array droop.
choices: Only rerun a DC analysis with the same average current.
Check transient local droop, package/grid inductance, current waveform and decoupling.
Assume temperature inversion is the sole cause.
Remove all decoupling to speed rail recovery.

questions.title: Which EM current metric?
questions.prompt: A metal segment carries narrow unidirectional current pulses. You have only its average current and want to claim reliability signoff. Which response is correct?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** Average directional current is relevant to material transport; RMS current relates to Joule heating; peak limits can constrain acute stresses or vias. Which metrics, averaging windows and temperature derating apply comes from the qualified process rules and signoff methodology. A ignores heating and peak constraints. B discards duty-cycle and thermal information. D wrongly treats pulses as harmless. Also inspect vias, current crowding, return paths and local temperature; dividing current by a nominal cross-section is only a first-order screening estimate.
questions.hint: Average of I and average of I² describe different effects.
questions.followup: Why can two pulse trains with the same average current have different RMS currents?
questions.trap: Use a teaching calculation as screening, not a foundry-specific signoff rule.
choices: Average current alone universally determines all reliability limits.
Peak current alone universally replaces all other limits.
Use applicable foundry limits and waveform-derived average, RMS and peak metrics as required.
Pulsed current cannot produce electromigration or heating.

questions.title: Aging with an idle input
questions.prompt: A CMOS inverter input is held low for a long duty fraction at elevated temperature. Which device stress deserves particular attention?
questions.answer: **Choose A.** With input low and source near VDD, the pMOS sees negative VGS while on. Its bias and temperature history can produce BTI degradation, shifting threshold and later slowing a rising output. B substitutes a transition-related mechanism for a static-bias concern. C and D overlook static electric-field stress; TDDB also depends on bias/field and lifetime conditions. Actual dominant mechanisms and aging models depend on process. Evaluate both logic states, workload duty factors and aged timing/noise margins rather than claim a universal degradation rate.
questions.hint: Write VGS for each transistor when input is low.
questions.followup: How could asymmetric aging change duty cycle in a clock buffer chain?
questions.trap: Toggle rate and signal probability measure different stresses.
choices: PMOS negative-bias temperature instability while its gate is below its source.
Only NMOS switching-related hot-carrier stress, despite no transitions.
No aging is possible when the input is static.
The metal oxide cannot see an electric field in a static circuit.

questions.title: Clock gating enable glitch
questions.prompt: A rising-edge clock is ANDed directly with an enable that can change during the high clock phase. Which concern motivates an integrated clock-gating cell?
questions.answer: **Choose A.** If enable rises while clock is already high, the AND output gains a new rising edge. If enable falls during high, the pulse is shortened. A latch-based gating structure holds the enable stable through the active clock phase and imposes its own enable timing checks. B ignores the Boolean waveform. C ignores sequential sensitivity. D wrongly removes downstream timing requirements. Use a qualified clock-gating implementation with test support as needed; verify enable protocol, gating checks, generated-clock constraints and minimum pulse width.
questions.hint: Sketch clock high while enable changes in both directions.
questions.followup: Why is a low-level latch natural for gating a rising-edge clock with an AND?
questions.trap: A correct cycle-level enable truth table can still produce a dangerous pulse.
choices: An enable transition can truncate a pulse or create an extra rising edge.
ANDing can never change a clock edge.
The enable only affects dynamic power, not functionality.
A clock-gating cell removes all downstream setup/hold checks.

questions.title: DVFS transition ordering
questions.prompt: A block must move from a low-voltage/low-frequency state to a higher-performance state, then return. Which sequencing is generally safe after allowing supply settling?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** The current frequency must remain supported by the actual voltage throughout the transition. Raise and settle voltage before requesting a higher clock. On the way down, reduce frequency before lowering voltage. A temporarily demands performance unsupported by the supply in both directions. C ignores transient timing safety. D directly violates the characterized voltage/frequency envelope. Practical transitions also require regulator acknowledgement, clock-source protocol, interface handling and worst-case droop margins; the simple order is a necessary starting rule, not a complete controller specification.
questions.hint: At each intermediate state, ask whether present VDD supports present f.
questions.followup: How would you represent supply-ready and clock-ready acknowledgements in a controller?
questions.trap: Target-state validity does not guarantee a safe transition path.
choices: Increase frequency, then voltage; decrease voltage, then frequency.
Increase voltage, then frequency; decrease frequency, then voltage.
Change either quantity in any order because average power is unchanged.
Keep frequency fixed while lowering voltage below its characterized operating point.

questions.title: Global and local variation
questions.prompt: Two nearby nominally identical devices share a die-wide threshold shift but have independent local mismatch. Which quantity cancels the ideal common global term?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Write d1 = μ + G + L1 and d2 = μ + G + L2. Their difference is L1 − L2, so a common additive global draw cancels. Their sum includes 2G. A therefore retains global variation; C generally retains it too; D confuses common-mode cancellation with removing independent local terms. Cancellation is exact only for the stated equal additive sensitivity. Different cells, operating points or spatial gradients can leave a residual correlated contribution. Use covariance rather than treating all variations as independent by default.
questions.hint: Write the same symbol G in both device equations.
questions.followup: What happens if one device has twice the global sensitivity?
questions.trap: Identical corner values cannot represent local mismatch.
choices: The sum of their delays.
The difference of their delays, assuming equal sensitivity to the global term.
The maximum of their delays in every case.
Every local mismatch sample.

questions.title: Zero failures in a small Monte Carlo
questions.prompt: A simulation reports zero failures in 100 independent trials. What can you responsibly conclude about a one-in-a-million failure target?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** No observed failures is useful screening evidence, but a small sample barely constrains a rare tail. For a binomial model, the one-sided 95% upper bound after zero failures is 1 − 0.05^(1/N), about 2.95% for N = 100. This is many orders above 10^-6. A and B confuse observation with proof; D invents a statistical percentile from the sample maximum. Plan validation around the target and model assumptions using validated high-sigma or importance-sampling methods where appropriate, with independent checks of failure mechanisms.
questions.hint: Estimate the rule-of-three upper bound: 3/N.
questions.followup: How many zero-failure independent trials roughly bound p below 10^-6 at 95%?
questions.trap: A Monte Carlo count is not meaningful without a confidence level and target.
choices: The target is proven because there were no failures.
The true failure probability is exactly zero.
The sample is far too small to demonstrate that tail target; report a confidence bound and use suitable tail methods.
The worst simulated waveform is automatically the six-sigma point.

questions.title: CDC bus coherence
questions.prompt: Eight data bits cross from an unrelated clock domain. Each bit gets its own two-flop synchronizer, and the destination assembles the word. What remains wrong?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Independent synchronizers lower metastability propagation risk for each bit but do not preserve the temporal relationship of a multi-bit transition. Some bits can settle one destination cycle earlier than others. Use a coherent transfer protocol such as stable-data request/acknowledge or a properly designed asynchronous FIFO; Gray coding is useful for appropriate counters/pointers with additional constraints. A confuses metastability mitigation with atomicity, C imposes an unnecessary frequency identity, and D does not solve uncontrolled phase or data coherence.
questions.hint: Imagine source word 01111111 becoming 10000000.
questions.followup: Why does an asynchronous FIFO synchronize pointers rather than each payload bit?
questions.trap: A synchronizer is not a general data-transfer protocol.
choices: Nothing: two flops guarantee coherent words.
Individual bits can be captured on different cycles, creating a word that was never transmitted.
Two-flop synchronizers require identical clock frequencies.
The destination must sample faster to make every bit atomic.

questions.title: A SPICE timestep illusion
questions.prompt: A pulse appears to violate a cell specification at one simulation setting, then disappears when the maximum timestep is reduced. What should you do before deciding the circuit is fixed?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** A change in numerical resolution can expose or remove interpolation/measurement artifacts, but can also reveal a genuine short transient. Check the stimulus definition, accepted solver timepoints, output-data compression, crossing selection and tolerances; demonstrate that the measured quantity stabilizes as settings are tightened enough for its timescale. A substitutes appearance for evidence. C masks behavior by changing the experiment. D ignores discretization and nonlinear convergence. Keep settings and models in the run record so a result can be reproduced.
questions.hint: What is the shortest relevant edge or pulse compared with solver and saved-data spacing?
questions.followup: Why can a dense plotted interpolation still conceal sparse solver output?
questions.trap: A visually smooth waveform does not prove measurement convergence.
choices: Accept the prettier waveform immediately.
Compare convergence, saved-point resolution, measurement crossings and stimulus breakpoints with tighter settings.
Increase the output load until the pulse is hidden.
Treat simulator settings as irrelevant to transient analysis.

questions.title: Robust simulation-log parser
questions.prompt: A corner-sweep log contains valid delays, a failed convergence run, and a missing measurement. What should an automated summary do?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** A trustworthy parser separates simulation status from metric values and carries the run identity, corner, units and failure reason. Missing, NaN or failed measurements must remain invalid, not numerically excellent. A turns failure into an apparent best case, B loses coverage evidence, and D compares text rather than physical values. Normalize to a common unit, verify the expected sweep matrix and report coverage as well as extrema. A result is usable only when its provenance and measurement validity are known.
questions.hint: Distinguish a valid zero from an absent measurement.
questions.followup: How would you detect a corner that never produced any log file?
questions.trap: Silent data cleaning can turn incomplete simulation into false signoff.
choices: Convert missing values to zero delay and include them in averages.
Discard failures silently because only successful values matter.
Retain explicit run status, validate units and completeness, and exclude invalid measurements with visible reasons.
Sort strings alphabetically to identify the slowest delay.

questions.title: Cold is unexpectedly slow
questions.prompt: At low VDD a characterized cell is slower at the cold corner than at the hot corner. What is the strongest next step?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** Mobility usually degrades as temperature rises, but threshold voltage also changes. Near threshold, increased cold threshold can outweigh improved cold mobility; the balance is process and operating-point dependent. Check qualified models, convergence and measurement settings, then characterize the specified voltage/temperature range rather than assume one universal slow temperature. A turns a common trend into a law, B discards a potentially real corner, and D treats supply lowering as a cure despite its strong delay sensitivity. Temperature inversion is a possibility to validate, not an automatic explanation for any anomalous run.
questions.hint: Compare mobility and overdrive effects at the actual VDD.
questions.followup: How could the worst temperature change when VDD is raised?
questions.trap: Do not hard-code hot equals slow across all supplies.
choices: Reject the result because hot is always slower.
Exclude the cold corner from signoff.
Check for temperature inversion and validate the corner data.
Lower VDD further because it always improves cold speed.

questions.title: RC propagation-delay estimate
questions.prompt: Use t50≈0.69ReqCtotal. A falling transition has Req=2.0 kΩ, fixed load=32 fF and output parasitic=8 fF. What is t50?
questions.answer: **55.2 ps.** 1. Sum the capacitances at the output: C_total = 32 + 8 = 40 fF. 2. Form RC = 2000 Ω × 40 × 10^-15 F = 80 ps. 3. Multiply by ln(2) ≈ 0.69 to get 55.2 ps. This is a one-pole step-response estimate with a constant effective resistance. Finite input slew, voltage-dependent device current and distributed wiring require transistor-level verification. Omitting output diffusion would predict 44.16 ps and understate the delay.
questions.hint: Sum every capacitance on the output before forming RC.
questions.followup: What happens if width doubles so R halves but the 8 fF parasitic doubles?
questions.trap: Ω·F gives seconds; do not mix fF with pF.
choices: 80 ps
choiceExplanations: 80 ps is RC before applying the 50% crossing factor.
This includes only the 8 fF parasitic, omitting the fixed load.
Total capacitance is 40 fF, RC=80 ps, and 0.69RC=55.2 ps.
This leaves out output parasitic capacitance.
questions.mcqExplanation: For the stated one-pole step model, t50=0.69×2000×40×10⁻¹⁵ s. Real finite slew and device-current variation require separate validation.
questions.oralPrompt: Use t50 ≈ 0.69 R_eq C_total. A falling transition has R_eq = 2.0 kΩ, fixed load 32 fF, and output parasitic 8 fF. Estimate the 50% propagation delay in ps.

questions.title: Distributed wire moment
questions.prompt: An RC wire has Rw = 100 Ω and Cw = 80 fF, driven by Rd = 200 Ω with endpoint CL = 20 fF. What is Rd(Cw + CL) + Rw(Cw/2 + CL), the Elmore first moment?
questions.answer: **26 ps.** 1. The driver charges all wire and load capacitance: 200 Ω × 100 fF = 20 ps. 2. Wire resistance sees half its own distributed capacitance plus all endpoint load: 100 Ω × (40 + 20) fF = 6 ps. 3. Add the terms: 26 ps. This is the Elmore first moment, not a claim of a 26 ps exact threshold crossing. A detailed distributed step response or transient simulation is needed for t50; a universal 0.69 multiplier on the whole expression is an approximation.
questions.hint: Separate capacitance seen by the driver from capacitance weighted by the wire.
questions.followup: Which term grows quadratically if wire length doubles?
questions.trap: A first moment and a 50% propagation delay are different metrics.
choices: 30 ps
26 ps
24 ps
choiceExplanations: This places all wire capacitance at the endpoint.
Driver contribution is 20 ps and wire contribution is 6 ps.
This omits the wire resistance charging CL.
This multiplies the correct moment by 0.69, which the question does not request.
questions.mcqExplanation: 200 × 100 fF + 100 × 60 fF = 26 ps. The first moment is not an exact 50% threshold-crossing time.
questions.oralPrompt: An RC wire has total Rw = 100 Ω and Cw = 80 fF. Its driver has Rd = 200 Ω and its far-end load is CL = 20 fF. Compute the Elmore first moment Rd(Cw + CL) + Rw(Cw/2 + CL), in ps. Do not convert this first moment to a 50% delay.

questions.title: Logical-effort delay calculation
questions.prompt: A three-stage path has F=64, P=6 and τ=8 ps. With continuous equal-effort sizing, use D=3F^(1/3)+P. What delay follows?
questions.answer: **144 ps.** 1. Equal stage effort is f = 64^(1/3) = 4. 2. The effort-delay sum is Nf = 3 × 4 = 12. 3. Add parasitics: D = 12 + 6 = 18 normalized units. 4. Convert with τ = 8 ps: t = 144 ps. This assumes the selected topology, branching and input/output capacitance constraints permit the optimal sizes. It does not include a separate wire-delay term or discrete legal cell sizing. If real sizes are quantized, evaluate neighboring choices with circuit or timing models.
questions.hint: Path effort is a product; equal stage effort is its Nth root.
questions.followup: How would branching effort change F if one stage also drives an off-path load?
questions.trap: Do not multiply the parasitic sum by N again.
choices: 192 ps
144 ps
560 ps
96 ps
choiceExplanations: 192 ps double-counts the parasitic contribution relative to the given formula.
560 ps adds total path effort directly rather than distributing it across stages.
96 ps omits the six units of parasitic delay.
questions.oralPrompt: A three-stage path has path effort F = 64 and total parasitic delay P = 6. All stages can be sized continuously for equal effort, and τ = 8 ps. Use D = N·F^(1/N) + P. Estimate delay in ps.

questions.title: Setup slack with uncertainty
questions.prompt: A same-edge flop path has T=500 ps, capture-minus-launch skew=+20 ps, tcq,max=55 ps, data delay=350 ps, setup=35 ps and setup uncertainty=20 ps. What is setup slack?
questions.answer: **60 ps.** 1. Available time is T + s − uncertainty = 500 + 20 − 20 = 500 ps. 2. Required launch-to-data-and-setup time is 55 + 350 + 35 = 440 ps. 3. Slack = 500 − 440 = 60 ps. Positive capture-minus-launch skew delays the next capture edge and helps setup. The uncertainty here is a specified setup margin, not an additional physical path delay. A positive slack under these assumptions says this particular check passes; other corners, hold and clock-gating checks still need their own analysis.
questions.hint: Keep skew’s sign convention and uncertainty’s conservative direction explicit.
questions.followup: What is the new slack if capture-minus-launch skew becomes −20 ps?
questions.trap: Always state the skew convention; do not count uncertainty twice.
choices: 20 ps
100 ps
60 ps
80 ps
choiceExplanations: This uses negative rather than positive capture skew.
This adds uncertainty instead of subtracting it.
This omits setup uncertainty.
questions.mcqExplanation: Available time is 500 ps after skew and uncertainty; required data-plus-setup time is 440 ps. This setup check passes with 60 ps slack.
questions.oralPrompt: A same-edge flop path has T = 500 ps, capture-minus-launch skew s = +20 ps, tCQ,max = 55 ps, maximum data delay = 350 ps and setup = 35 ps. Subtract 20 ps setup uncertainty. What is setup slack in ps?

questions.title: Minimum hold-repair delay
questions.prompt: For a same-edge check, tCQ,min = 18 ps, data contamination delay = 12 ps, capture-minus-launch skew = 22 ps, hold = 15 ps and hold uncertainty = 10 ps. What added minimum data delay makes slack zero?
questions.answer: **17 ps.** 1. Earliest new data arrives at 18 + 12 = 30 ps after launch. 2. The capture hold deadline is s + tH + uncertainty = 22 + 15 + 10 = 47 ps. 3. Current hold slack is 30 − 47 = −17 ps, so at least 17 ps extra minimum delay is needed in this simplified check. Actual repair should include appropriate margin and corner-dependent delay of the inserted element. Recheck setup and all paths affected by the placement/routing change.
questions.hint: Subtract existing earliest arrival from the capture-side hold deadline.
questions.followup: If the delay element adds 40 ps maximum delay, what setup slack is consumed?
questions.trap: A clock period is absent from this same-edge hold equation.
choices: 17 ps
47 ps
−3 ps
7 ps
choiceExplanations: Existing arrival is 30 ps; required hold deadline is 47 ps.
This is the full deadline, not the additional delay.
This uses the wrong sign for one of the timing requirements.
This omits the 10 ps uncertainty.
questions.mcqExplanation: Hold slack = 18 + 12 − 22 − 15 − 10 = −17 ps. A real repair also needs corner-appropriate margin and a setup recheck.
questions.oralPrompt: For a same-edge path, tCQ,min = 18 ps, data contamination delay = 12 ps, capture-minus-launch skew = 22 ps, hold = 15 ps and hold uncertainty = 10 ps. With clock arrivals fixed, what minimum extra data delay is needed to make hold slack zero?

questions.title: Dynamic switching-power calculation
questions.prompt: A node has C=40 fF, VDD=0.8 V, f=1.5 GHz and α=0.12 counting charging events per cycle. Using P=αCV²f, what power is predicted?
questions.answer: **4.608 µW.** 1. One charging event draws CV² = 40 fF × 0.64 V² = 25.6 fJ from the supply. 2. The event rate is αf = 0.12 × 1.5 GHz = 180 MHz. 3. Multiply: 25.6 fJ × 180 MHz = 4.608 µW. This activity definition already counts charging events, so no extra factor of 1/2 is applied. The estimate excludes short-circuit power and leakage, and assumes the stated capacitance switches through the full supply swing.
questions.hint: Keep the charging-event activity definition fixed when applying the energy formula.
questions.followup: What changes if VDD drops to 0.7 V while event rate and capacitance remain fixed?
questions.trap: The energy stored is CV²/2, while a full charging event draws CV² from an ideal supply.
choiceExplanations: 38.4 µW ignores the activity factor.
5.760 µW uses only one factor of V rather than V².
An extra one-half is not used when α already counts charging events.
questions.oralPrompt: A node has C = 40 fF, VDD = 0.8 V and f = 1.5 GHz. Its activity α = 0.12 counts 0→1 charging events per cycle. Use P = αCV²f. What is dynamic switching power in µW?

questions.title: Ideal charge-sharing voltage
questions.prompt: A 30 fF node at 0.9 V connects to a 10 fF node at 0 V. Assume complete instantaneous equilibration, no threshold limit, leakage, keeper or external conduction. What voltage do they share?
questions.answer: **0.675 V.** 1. Initial total charge is 30 fF × 0.9 V + 10 fF × 0 V = 27 fC. 2. The final connected capacitance is 40 fF. 3. Charge conservation gives Vfinal = 27 fC / 40 fF = 0.675 V, a 225 mV droop. Compare this with the receiver trip/noise boundary, not merely with zero. The ideal redistribution estimate excludes keeper replenishment, channel charge and threshold-limited conduction; those affect the real waveform and its recovery.
questions.hint: Conserve total charge on the combined capacitance.
questions.followup: What if the internal node started at 0.3 V instead?
questions.trap: Capacitances share charge; their voltages do not average equally unless C values match.
choiceExplanations: Initial charge is 27 fC and total capacitance is 40 fF.
0.225 V is the droop from 0.9 V, not the final voltage.
The initially empty capacitance requires charge from the charged node.
0.45 V assumes equal capacitances.
questions.mcqExplanation: Vfinal=(30×0.9+10×0)/(30+10)=0.675 V. Compare this retained voltage with the actual receiver’s decision margin.
questions.oralPrompt: A 30 fF dynamic node is initially at 0.9 V and connects instantaneously to a 10 fF internal node initially at 0 V. Ignore leakage, keeper, transistor threshold limits and external conduction. What final shared voltage is obtained in V?

questions.title: Keeper-limited bitline discharge
questions.prompt: A 120 fF bitline must fall 0.30 V. Assume constant selected pull-down current 20 µA opposed by a constant 5 µA keeper. What is the discharge time?
questions.answer: **2.4 ns.** 1. Required removed charge is CΔV = 120 fF × 0.30 V = 36 fC. 2. Net discharge current is 20 − 5 = 15 µA because the keeper opposes the selected pull-down. 3. Time is 36 fC / 15 µA = 2.4 ns. Without the keeper this constant-current estimate would be 1.8 ns. Real keeper feedback can turn off during the transition, and both currents vary with voltage, so integrate the net current or simulate for an accurate access delay.
questions.hint: Identify the current direction of the keeper.
questions.followup: What happens as keeper current approaches selected pull-down current?
questions.trap: Do not add contention current to useful discharge current.
choices: 7.2 ns
2.4 ns
1.8 ns
choiceExplanations: This uses only the keeper current as the discharge current.
Removed charge is 36 fC and net discharge current is 15 µA.
This incorrectly adds keeper current to pull-down current.
This ignores keeper contention.
questions.mcqExplanation: t = CΔV/(Ipull-down − Ikeeper) = 36 fC/15 µA = 2.4 ns. Real voltage-dependent currents require integration or simulation.
questions.oralPrompt: A ROM bitline has 120 fF capacitance. During the relevant interval, selected pull-down current is constant at 20 µA and keeper current is constant at 5 µA. Estimate time to fall by 0.30 V in ns.

questions.title: Bitline discharge time
questions.prompt: One 100 fF SRAM bitline discharges at constant 30 µA while the other stays fixed. How long to develop a 60 mV differential?
questions.answer: **200 ps.** 1. Only the discharging line changes under the given assumption, so its 60 mV drop is the differential. 2. Removed charge is 100 fF × 60 mV = 6 fC. 3. Time is CΔV/I = 6 fC / 30 µA = 200 ps. Do not double C just because the array has two bitlines: the stated model holds the other line fixed. Cell current changes as bitline/storage voltages evolve, and required sensing signal includes offset, noise and yield margin.
questions.hint: Use the voltage change and capacitance of the line that actually moves.
questions.followup: How would equal and opposite bitline currents change the differential growth rate?
questions.trap: Differential voltage is not always the voltage drop of either individual line.
choices: 400 ps
100 ps
2 ps
200 ps
choiceExplanations: Doubling capacitance for both lines is incorrect because the other line is fixed in this model.
There is no half-swing division when only one line develops the entire differential.
This is a factor-of-100 unit error.
questions.oralPrompt: During the initial SRAM read, one bitline discharges with approximately constant 30 µA while the other remains fixed. Each bitline has 100 fF capacitance. How long does it take to develop a 60 mV differential, in ps?

questions.title: Initial coupling glitch
questions.prompt: A quiet initially low victim has 24 fF to ground and 8 fF coupling to an aggressor. The aggressor steps +0.8 V faster than the victim holder responds. Ignoring other caps, estimate the initial victim bump.
questions.answer: **200 mV.** 1. During the fast edge, treat the weak holding path as effectively inactive. 2. The capacitive-divider ratio is Cc/(Cg + Cc) = 8/32 = 0.25. 3. Initial bump is 0.25 × 0.8 V = 0.2 V = 200 mV. A restoring driver later removes the injected charge with a time constant. An aggressor ramp slow relative to that recovery produces a smaller peak. The calculation screens amplitude only; functional impact also depends on pulse width, receiver state and timing.
questions.hint: Use the total capacitance at the temporarily floating victim node.
questions.followup: Why could the same bump be harmless in one static path and destructive in a dynamic ROM?
questions.trap: Peak amplitude alone does not decide whether a digital noise pulse causes a failure.
choices: 600 mV
800 mV
200 mV
267 mV
choiceExplanations: This uses the ground-capacitance fraction instead of the coupling fraction.
Full tracking neglects the 24 fF to ground.
The divider ratio is 8/(24+8)=1/4.
This uses Cc/Cg rather than Cc/(Cg+Cc).
questions.mcqExplanation: ΔVvictim=0.8×8/32=0.2 V. Later recovery and receiver sensitivity depend on pulse width and driver impedance.
questions.oralPrompt: A quiet, initially low victim has Cg = 24 fF to ground and Cc = 8 fF to one aggressor. The aggressor steps by +0.8 V faster than the victim holder can respond. Ignore all other caps. Estimate initial victim glitch in mV.

questions.title: Ideal local-decap charge budget
questions.prompt: A decap alone supplies an extra 6 mA for 200 ps with at most 30 mV droop. Ignore ESR, ESL and grid replenishment. What capacitance is needed?
questions.answer: **40 pF.** 1. Extra charge demand is ΔQ = ΔIΔt = 6 mA × 200 ps = 1.2 pC. 2. Use C = ΔQ/ΔV = 1.2 pC / 0.030 V = 40 pF. This is an ideal charge budget, not a placement-complete decap design. ESR contributes an instantaneous I·ESR step, ESL contributes L·di/dt and the power grid can replenish some charge. Verify the actual distributed transient and allowable droop at the devices, including leakage, area and resonance tradeoffs.
questions.hint: Calculate demanded charge before choosing capacitance.
questions.followup: How would ESR = 1 Ω consume part of the 30 mV droop budget?
questions.trap: Capacitance value without placement and impedance does not establish transient support.
choices: 40 pF
400 pF
4 pF
1.2 pF
choiceExplanations: C = IΔt/ΔV = 1.2 pC/0.03 V = 40 pF.
This adds a factor of ten to the required charge budget.
This misses a factor of ten in the droop conversion.
1.2 is the charge in pC, not the capacitance in pF.
questions.mcqExplanation: This is a lower-level ideal charge estimate, not a complete distributed decap design; real impedance can add droop.
questions.oralPrompt: A local decoupling capacitor must supply an extra 6 mA for 200 ps while limiting droop to 30 mV. Ignore ESR, ESL, replenishment and baseline load. What minimum capacitance is required in pF?

questions.title: Static IR-drop calculation
questions.prompt: An array draws 8 mA through a 2.5 Ω effective supply path. Ignoring return resistance and dynamic effects, what DC drop follows?
questions.answer: **20 mV.** 1. Apply Ohm’s law: ΔV = IR = 0.008 A × 2.5 Ω = 0.020 V. 2. Convert to 20 mV. If the source is 0.8 V, the local supply becomes approximately 0.78 V under this DC model. Do not silently assume the return path is ideal in a real design: ground rise also reduces the voltage across the circuit. Spatial current distribution, temperature-dependent resistance and switching transients require a more complete grid model.
questions.hint: Use Ohm’s law and convert volts to millivolts only at the end.
questions.followup: What changes if the ground-return path adds another 1 Ω?
questions.trap: Absolute VDD and effective VDD minus local ground are not interchangeable.
choices: 20 mV
3.2 mV
200 mV
choiceExplanations: Dividing current by resistance does not give voltage drop.
This is a factor-of-ten overestimate.
0.020 is the value in volts, not millivolts.
questions.oralPrompt: An array draws 8 mA through a 2.5 Ω effective supply path. Ignore ground return resistance and dynamic effects. What supply drop is predicted in mV?

questions.title: Inductive droop from a current ramp
questions.prompt: A supply loop has L=150 pH. Current rises linearly by 20 mA in 100 ps. Using |ΔV|=L|di/dt|, what is the inductive drop magnitude?
questions.answer: **30 mV.** 1. Current slope is 0.020 A / 100 ps = 2 × 10^8 A/s. 2. Multiply by 150 pH = 150 × 10^-12 H: ΔV = 0.030 V = 30 mV. The estimate isolates the inductive term; resistive and capacitive behavior also shape the actual rail transient. Effective inductance belongs to a complete current loop, including return paths, not just one visible metal segment. Slowing or staggering the demand edge reduces di/dt but must preserve functional timing.
questions.hint: Convert both picoseconds and picohenries before converting volts to millivolts.
questions.followup: What is the estimated droop if the same current step takes 200 ps?
questions.trap: Peak current and current slope are different inputs.
choices: 300 mV
30 mV
3 mV
choiceExplanations: This adds one factor of ten.
0.030 V equals 30 mV, not 0.03 mV.
This loses one factor of ten in the unit conversion.
questions.mcqExplanation: The estimate isolates the inductive term of the complete current loop. Rail resistance and decoupling shape the actual waveform too.
questions.oralPrompt: A supply path has effective inductance 150 pH. Its current increases by 20 mA in 100 ps with an approximately linear ramp. Use |ΔV| = L|di/dt|. Estimate droop magnitude in mV.

questions.title: RMS of a pulsed current
questions.prompt: Current is 16 mA for 25% of each period and zero otherwise, with negligible edge durations. What is its RMS value?
questions.answer: **8 mA.** 1. Average squared current is duty × Ipeak² = 0.25 × (16 mA)² = 64 mA². 2. Take the square root: Irms = 8 mA. The arithmetic average current is only 0.25 × 16 = 4 mA, so substituting average for RMS underestimates Joule heating. For a constant resistance R, average resistive heating is Irms²R. Reliability rules may separately constrain average, RMS and peak metrics with process-specific definitions and temperature limits.
questions.hint: Average the square, then take the square root.
questions.followup: What peak current at 6.25% duty gives the same RMS current?
questions.trap: RMS is Ipeak times sqrt(duty), not Ipeak times duty.
choices: 16 mA
64 mA
4 mA
8 mA
choiceExplanations: This is the peak current.
64 is the mean-square current in mA², not its square root.
This is the arithmetic average.
questions.mcqExplanation: Average heating in a constant resistance is Irms²R, so substituting the 4 mA average underestimates it by four.
questions.oralPrompt: A current is 16 mA for 25% of a repeating period and zero for the remaining 75%. Ignore rise/fall intervals. What is RMS current in mA?

questions.title: Shared and local delay variation
questions.prompt: Four gate delays are μ+G+Li. Shared G has σG=6 ps, independent Li have σL=4 ps, and G is independent of them. What is total-path σ?
questions.answer: **25.30 ps.** 1. The path is 4μ + 4G + L1 + L2 + L3 + L4. 2. Shared global variation contributes variance (4σG)² = 24² = 576 ps². 3. Independent local terms contribute 4σL² = 4 × 16 = 64 ps². 4. Total σ = sqrt(640) = 25.298 ps. Treating all global contributions as independent would incorrectly give sqrt(4 × (36 + 16)) = 14.42 ps. This model assumes identical additive global sensitivity and no local spatial correlation.
questions.hint: Sum the shared random variable before calculating its variance.
questions.followup: What happens to relative local variation σ/mean as path length grows?
questions.trap: Root-sum-square is valid for independent components, not identical shared draws.
choices: 8 ps
40 ps
choiceExplanations: 8 ps includes only the independent local terms and drops global variation.
Adding all standard deviations assumes every local term is perfectly correlated too.
The shared term is 4G: variance is (4×6)²+4×4²=640 ps², giving √640=25.30 ps.
14.42 ps incorrectly treats the four global contributions as independent.
questions.mcqExplanation: The shared term is 4G: variance is (4×6)²+4×4²=640 ps², giving √640=25.30 ps.
questions.oralPrompt: Each of four identical gates has delay μ + G + Li. G is one shared zero-mean global draw with σG = 6 ps; independent Li each have σL = 4 ps, independent of G. What is the standard deviation of total path delay in ps?

questions.title: Extra metastability resolution time
questions.prompt: Hold event rates and aperture fixed in MTBF∝exp(Tresolve/τ). If resolution time grows by 200 ps and τ=50 ps, what is the improvement factor?
questions.answer: **54.60×.** 1. Form the ratio rather than evaluate two large MTBF values: MTBFnew/MTBFold = exp(ΔT/τ). 2. ΔT/τ = 200/50 = 4. 3. exp(4) = 54.598. This exponential benefit holds only if the assumed regeneration constant, aperture and event rates remain valid. Adding a stage does not provide a full period of extra resolution if clock-to-Q, routing and setup consume part of it. Bus coherence and pulse capture are separate protocol issues even with excellent single-bit MTBF.
questions.hint: Compute how many regeneration time constants are added.
questions.followup: What added resolution time gives a 10× improvement at τ = 50 ps?
questions.trap: MTBF improvement is probabilistic; a synchronizer does not eliminate metastability.
choices: About 7.39×
About 54.6×
About 1.02×
choiceExplanations: 7.39 is exp(2), corresponding to only 100 ps extra resolution.
The ratio is exp(200/50)=exp(4)≈54.6.
Four is the exponent, not the multiplicative result.
This is not the exponential ratio for four time constants.
questions.mcqExplanation: Take the ratio directly: MTBFnew/MTBFold=exp(ΔT/τ). This does not address multi-bit coherence or pulse-capture protocols.
questions.oralPrompt: Use the illustrative relation MTBF ∝ exp(Tresolve/τ), holding event rates and aperture constant. If resolution time increases by 200 ps and τ = 50 ps, by what multiplicative factor does MTBF improve?

questions.title: Specify a faster NAND before sizing
questions.prompt: A request says “make this NAND2 faster at the same cell height.” What should be established first?
questions.answer: **Start with the operating and integration contract.** 1. Fix logic/pin ordering, legal height/width, voltage range, PVT models, input-slew/output-load grid, pin accessibility and rise/fall behavior. 2. Specify what faster means: a critical arc, a path metric, or improvement across the table; bound area, leakage, switching/internal power and reliability. 3. Compare schematic candidates with controlled stimuli, including both last-arriving inputs and internal histories. 4. Implement legal layouts, run DRC/LVS, extract parasitics and remeasure. 5. Release consistent layout, netlist, Liberty and physical abstract views with QA and reproducible evidence. A nominal win that fails the intended corner or pin-access requirement does not satisfy the request.
questions.hint: “Faster” requires a measurement context and constraints.
questions.followup: How would you compare a loaded-delay win with increased input capacitance?
questions.trap: An isolated SPICE delay is not a complete standard-cell specification.
choices: The target arcs, slew/load/PVT conditions and allowable area, power and integration tradeoffs.
Only the nominal unloaded falling delay at typical process.
A transistor-width increase applied equally to all devices before choosing a metric.
A schematic timing improvement with layout and pin access left outside release criteria.
choiceExplanations: A measurable contract defines what qualifies as a useful improvement.
One nominal metric may miss the actual critical arc or load.
Sizing before defining the objective can worsen the wrong terms.
Physical integration and extracted performance are part of the delivered cell.
questions.mcqExplanation: Specify the operating contract, compare controlled candidates, then verify legal layout, extracted behavior and consistent release views.
questions.oralPrompt: You receive a request for a faster NAND2 with the same cell height. Before resizing devices, define a compact design and release plan.

questions.title: AOI21 matched-drive sizing
questions.prompt: For Y=NOT(A+B·C), match an N1/P2 reference using the equal-resistance model. Which choice is correct?
questions.answer: **Use complementary dual networks.** 1. Pull-down: nMOS A in parallel with series B and C. Pull-up: pMOS A in series with parallel B and C. 2. The A-only nMOS path needs width 1. Use width 2 for each BC nMOS, making two half-resistances sum to the reference nMOS resistance. 3. Each pull-up path contains two pMOS. Use width 4 for A, B and C, versus reference width 2, making each series device half the reference pMOS resistance. 4. Verify input capacitance, internal charge, stack/body effects, discrete fins and extracted wiring. These are starting estimates, not guaranteed equal real rise/fall delay or optimal energy.
questions.hint: Derive dual pull-up and pull-down networks before assigning widths.
questions.followup: Which pin has the largest estimated input capacitance?
questions.trap: Matching resistance does not match every delay or parasitic.
choices: NMOS A=1, B=C=2; PMOS A=B=C=4
NMOS A=2, B=C=1; PMOS A=2, B=C=4
NMOS A=B=C=2; PMOS A=B=C=2
NMOS A=B=C=1; PMOS A=B=C=2
choiceExplanations: The A-only pull-down uses N1; B/C share a series path and need N2; every pull-up path has two PMOS and needs P4 each.
This widens the single-device NMOS path while leaving the BC stack weak and fails equal pull-up path resistance.
Uniform N2 overdrives A while P2 leaves the series pull-up at twice reference resistance.
The series pull-down and pull-up paths remain too resistive without compensation.
questions.mcqExplanation: The A-only pull-down uses N1; B/C share a series path and need N2; every pull-up path has two PMOS and needs P4 each.
questions.oralPrompt: Construct static CMOS for Y = NOT(A + B·C). A reference inverter has nMOS width 1 and pMOS width 2. In an equal-resistance model, propose widths matching its worst-case pull-up and pull-down resistance.

questions.title: Pin-specific post-layout failure
questions.prompt: An extracted NAND3 misses delay only when input C arrives last. Which controlled experiment best separates parasitic effects from testbench/history effects?
questions.answer: **Preserve the failing experiment.** 1. Record models, extraction version, PVT, slew, load, thresholds, active pin and prior state. 2. Plot inputs, output, internal stack nodes and local supplies. 3. Compare schematic and extracted cases under identical stimuli. Inspect added diffusion and routing RC. 4. Exercise all three last-arriving inputs with settled sensitizing states and relevant histories. 5. Tighten transient resolution to verify crossing stability and reproduce the run. 6. Try a targeted ordering or layout repair and evaluate other arcs, leakage, pin access and reliability. Improvement only after changing initialization suggests a testbench issue rather than a demonstrated circuit repair.
questions.hint: Keep the failing stimulus fixed while isolating extraction and input-order effects.
questions.followup: How would you distinguish a slow crossing from ringing with multiple crossings?
questions.trap: Map a last-arriving input to its physical stack position.
choices: Average delays from A, B and C and release if the average passes
Change initial state, load and extraction settings together until C passes
Compare schematic and extracted circuits with matched PVT, loads, slews, initial states and thresholds; sweep last-arriving pins and inspect internal nodes
Ignore internal nodes because LVS proves all timing arcs are identical
choiceExplanations: A failing required arc is not repaired by averaging with faster arcs.
Changing several variables at once cannot identify the cause.
Matching conditions and varying one dimension exposes pin/history and extraction contributions.
LVS verifies connectivity, not equivalence of parasitic timing across pins.
questions.mcqExplanation: Preserve the failing run and compare controlled waveforms. Verify crossing stability with appropriate transient resolution before crediting a physical repair.
questions.oralPrompt: A post-layout NAND3 only fails delay when input C toggles last. Write an experiment distinguishing pin ordering, parasitic and measurement causes.

questions.title: Find coupled setup and hold limits
questions.prompt: A characterization flow finds minimum setup with very generous hold, then minimum hold with very generous setup. What is its main blind spot?
questions.answer: **Map the coupled boundary.** 1. Define edges, voltage thresholds and pass criteria: correct output plus an allowed clock-to-Q degradation under stated slew/load. 2. Sweep two data-transition positions around capture, controlling the last pre-edge and first post-edge transitions independently. 3. Record pass/fail, clock-to-Q and metastable or ambiguous trajectories. 4. Refine near the boundary to expose setup/hold tradeoff and separate functional failure from an excessive-delay criterion. 5. Repeat clock/data slews, output loads and PVT. Independent remote cuts can give individually attractive limits that are unsafe together; the release representation needs a consistent boundary and waveform QA.
questions.hint: Two one-dimensional cuts need not intersect inside the safe region.
questions.followup: Why can a 10% clock-to-Q criterion differ from functional failure?
questions.trap: Do not combine independently optimized timing limits without joint verification.
choices: The two separately found limits may be unsafe when used together.
Hold can be omitted once the setup sweep is accurate.
A correct final logic value makes clock-to-Q degradation irrelevant.
The two sweeps automatically reveal the entire two-dimensional safe boundary.
choiceExplanations: Setup and hold interact through the internal state at capture.
Post-edge data behavior still matters.
An excessively late correct result can violate the release timing criterion.
Two remote cuts cannot map the full coupled surface.
questions.mcqExplanation: Sweep the last pre-edge and first post-edge transitions independently, applying explicit functional and clock-to-Q criteria across required conditions.
questions.oralPrompt: A script sweeps setup with hold fixed very large, then hold with setup fixed very large. What does this miss, and how would you improve it?

questions.title: Verifying a high-impedance output
questions.prompt: A tri-state output is disabled but its loaded bus voltage barely changes. What can be concluded from that waveform alone?
questions.answer: **Separate data propagation, enabling and release.** With enable active, measure data rise/fall delay and slew over the load/input-slew grid. For enable assertion, precondition the bus to relevant levels and measure enable-to-driven transitions. For disable, define how loss of drive is measured: a floating loaded node can retain voltage and never create a normal crossing. Use the supported three-state characterization method with a controlled load/holder. Check enable polarity, overlapping drivers, contention, disabled leakage and startup states.
