Validate timing sense and integration. An unchanged bus voltage after disable proves neither continued drive nor successful release.
questions.hint: A node voltage and the impedance driving that node are different observables.
questions.followup: How would you detect overlap during driver handoff?
questions.trap: A missing voltage edge does not define disabled state.
choices: The cell is definitely still enabled
Neither continued drive nor successful release is proven; stored charge can preserve the voltage
Disable timing equals zero because there was no threshold crossing
The cell is definitely high-impedance under every bus condition
choiceExplanations: Voltage retention can occur without active drive.
A floating capacitive bus can retain charge; release needs an appropriate controlled load or supported characterization method.
No ordinary voltage crossing does not imply instantaneous release.
One voltage trace without a probing condition does not prove output impedance.
questions.mcqExplanation: A floating capacitive bus can retain charge; release needs an appropriate controlled load or supported characterization method.
questions.oralPrompt: What experiments does a shared-bus tri-state cell need beyond ordinary input-to-output delay tables?

questions.title: Release choice for crowded pins
questions.prompt: Two DRC/LVS-clean cell layouts implement the same function. One is narrower but has crowded boundary pins. What evidence should decide whether its width reduction is useful?
questions.answer: **Measure integration cost with cell performance.** Compare legal access points and routing obstructions, representative abutments and orientations. Route benchmark contexts and inspect failed connections, detours, congestion and added wire capacitance. Characterize both extracted candidates and include routing overhead in path comparisons. Check boundary diffusion/well/power-rail conventions and post-integration antenna/DRC. The narrow layout may need whitespace or detours that erase its area win and hurt timing. Choose against a measured integration objective and document the area/timing/power/access tradeoff. Keep isolated geometry distinct from effective placed-and-routed density.
questions.hint: Ask what the router must add to use the smaller layout.
questions.followup: Which pin-access metric would accompany your density comparison?
questions.trap: LVS correctness and minimum isolated area do not prove routability.
choices: Isolated cell width alone
Only the schematic delay, because clean LVS removes routing effects
The number of drawn pins, regardless of legal access points
Representative placement/routing, pin-access and extracted path results including detours and required whitespace
choiceExplanations: Width does not measure effective routed density or accessibility.
LVS does not remove parasitic RC or access constraints.
Equal pin counts can have very different routability.
Integration can erase an apparent width win through congestion and wire overhead.
questions.mcqExplanation: Evaluate effective integrated area and PPA with legal access and abutment contexts, not isolated cell geometry alone.
questions.oralPrompt: Two clean layouts implement the same cell. The narrower one has crowded boundary pins. How would you decide which to release?

questions.title: Choose a ROM organization
questions.prompt: A 2,048-row ROM has excessive bitline capacitance and unselected leakage. Which proposal most directly reduces rows attached to each active local bitline, with an explicit cost?
questions.answer: **Start from 65,536 bits and the access contract.** A long 2048-row bitline has many attached devices and wiring, increasing capacitance, unselected leakage and recharge cost. Banking shortens active columns but repeats periphery and adds decode/output selection. Column muxing reduces sense/output circuitry at the cost of array width, mux loading and selection delay; it is different from banking. Estimate wordline fanout, bitline C, selected current, keeper requirement, precharge time and output load for candidates. Compare full extracted access/cycle time, energy, area and noise margin across PVT and contents patterns. Specify latency and sustained throughput before declaring an optimum.
questions.hint: Separate the number of rows on a bitline from the number of output columns selected.
questions.followup: What changes if latency can increase but throughput stays one read per cycle?
questions.trap: Capacity alone does not define a feasible timing architecture.
choices: Use a stronger keeper, assuming both read-zero speed and read-one margin improve together.
Only multiplex more output columns, assuming rows per bitline automatically shrink.
Bank the array, accepting repeated periphery and bank/output selection.
Keep the organization and compare only total bit count.
choiceExplanations: A stronger keeper opposes selected discharge even if retention improves.
Column selection and row segmentation are distinct decisions.
Banking can shorten local columns but adds support circuitry.
Equal capacity can have very different RC, leakage and timing.
questions.mcqExplanation: Compare banking, column muxing and hierarchy using actual access/cycle, energy, area and margin requirements; none is an unconditional optimum.
questions.oralPrompt: A 2048-word × 32-bit ROM could use one 2048-row array or banking and column multiplexing. Compare organizations before committing.

questions.title: ROM retained-high leakage test
questions.prompt: A ROM passes random contents at TT. Which additional experiment most directly tests retained-high failure from aggregate off leakage?
questions.answer: **Stress distinct mechanisms.** Test retained-high columns for unselected leakage and noise; also test heavily populated columns for attached-device load. Exercise weak legitimate discharge paths at unfavorable PVT and maximum keeper contention. Change many address bits and select physically distant rows to stress decode/distribution. Arrange adjacent columns with opposite or synchronized activity to probe crosstalk and current bursts. Run consecutive accesses demanding maximum recharge and residue removal. State the bit-to-transistor programming convention because 0/1 polarity varies by architecture. Collect precharge completion, bitline limits, read delay and correctness, rather than only a final truth-table pass.
questions.hint: Keep the programming convention explicit and maximize the leakage mechanism rather than nominal read speed.
questions.followup: Why is all-zero contents ambiguous without programming polarity?
questions.trap: Random vectors may miss a structured worst case.
choices: Only a zero-load output delay measurement
A column with many connected unselected cells, evaluated at an appropriate high-leakage corner and long valid hold interval
Only an empty column with minimal attached cells at nominal temperature
Only a strong selected discharge with the keeper removed
choiceExplanations: Output load timing alone does not isolate internal bitline retention.
Many off devices can aggregate leakage on a retained-high bitline, especially under leakage-stressing conditions.
That removes much of the mechanism the test is meant to stress.
A strong read-zero path tests a different side of the keeper window.
questions.mcqExplanation: Many off devices can aggregate leakage on a retained-high bitline, especially under leakage-stressing conditions.
questions.oralPrompt: A ROM compiler passes one random contents file at TT. Propose directed contents and address patterns for timing and margin.

questions.title: ROM local/global segmentation
questions.prompt: A long ROM bitline is slow and leakage-limited. What must be included when evaluating a local/global segmentation proposal?
questions.answer: **Evaluate the complete hierarchy.** Shorter local lines reduce attached load and leakage. Local sensing/buffering or selection then drives a global line. Estimate whether saved local RC and current margin outweigh the added stage, global wiring and repeated periphery. Check local/global precharge sequencing, isolation, prior-bank residue, keeper contention, charge sharing and coupling. Ensure inactive segments cannot discharge the selected global result. Measure address-to-output delay and minimum cycle time, not only local bitline delay. Report energy and area from repeated circuits and statistical margin if extra sense stages are introduced.
questions.hint: Follow the result all the way from selected address to the final output.
questions.followup: When would a static local buffer beat a second dynamic stage?
questions.trap: A shorter local line need not improve end-to-end access.
choices: Only the faster local-bitline edge
Only the number of removed local cells, assuming global wiring is ideal
Only steady-state leakage, because sensing delay cannot change
Saved local capacitance/leakage plus added sensing, global wiring, sequencing and isolation costs
choiceExplanations: A fast local node can still feed a slower global path.
Global capacitance and added stages are real loads.
Segmentation changes sensing stages and timing.
The complete hierarchy determines address-to-output delay, cycle time and correctness.
questions.mcqExplanation: Short local lines can improve margin, but check inactive-segment isolation, precharge order, charge sharing and global-path overhead.
questions.oralPrompt: A ROM bitline is slow and collects unselected leakage. Discuss local/global segmentation, including new failure modes.

questions.title: Diagnose a slow ROM read with a current spike
questions.prompt: A broad supply-current spike coincides with wordline rising near precharge-off, and the bitline falls slowly. What is the best first diagnostic?
questions.answer: **Look for temporary supply-to-ground contention.** Plot precharge gate, wordline, bitline, keeper control, supply current and local rail. Confirm whether precharge pMOS still conducts while the nMOS read path turns on. Sweep phase, slew and PVT, including extracted control-distribution skew. Trace device currents to separate overlap from capacitive charging and keeper contention. Introduce verified nonoverlap/gated evaluation while preserving adequate precharge and address settling. Recheck cycle time, retention exposure and droop. Excessive dead time can reduce throughput and leave a dynamic node floating longer, so choose the window from worst-case evidence.
questions.hint: Look for simultaneous source and sink paths on the same bitline.
questions.followup: How could overlap droop increase the observed read delay?
questions.trap: Ideal digital nonoverlap does not prove analog nonoverlap.
choices: Check whether precharge PMOS and selected NMOS discharge path overlap in conduction.
Assume the spike is ordinary capacitive charging and ignore control timing.
Weaken the sense amplifier before plotting bitline and control waveforms.
Increase the precharge size without checking whether it remains on during evaluate.
choiceExplanations: Temporary supply-to-ground contention explains both current and slow discharge.
The correlation with evaluation onset calls for device-current and phase checks.
The symptoms point upstream of the sense decision.
A stronger overlapping precharge device can worsen the fight.
questions.mcqExplanation: Inspect gate and device-current waveforms with extracted skew, then create verified nonoverlap without excessive dead time.
questions.oralPrompt: A ROM shows a broad current spike and slow falling read when wordline rises near precharge-off. Diagnose and repair it.

questions.title: Dynamic ROM read protocol
questions.prompt: A dynamic ROM address is stable, but the array is in precharge. Which interface rule is appropriate?
questions.answer: **Relate validity to access phases.** Precharge resets internal lines, evaluation develops signal, and data is valid only after a bounded read interval. Specify address capture/change rules, precharge/evaluation windows, output-valid timing and whether a register holds prior data outside that window. Verify back-to-back reads, idle/restart, boundary address changes, clock stretching and output loading over corners. A valid/ready signal must follow a worst-case completion bound or qualified detector, not an optimistic nominal waveform. Ensure consumers cannot sample transitional or stale values as the current result.
questions.hint: Tie validity to the access sequence, not merely to address stability.
questions.followup: What changes if the clock pauses during evaluation?
questions.trap: Stable address and valid output are separate properties.
choices: Assert valid from a typical-corner delay regardless of PVT or load
Let the consumer sample any time because precharge only changes internal nodes
Treat a stable address as sufficient for continuous current-data validity
Declare data valid only after the specified evaluation/completion interval, with defined behavior outside that window
choiceExplanations: A nominal delay is not a worst-case validity guarantee.
Internal transitions can leave outputs stale or transitional unless explicitly held by the interface.
Address stability alone does not complete precharge and evaluation.
Dynamic operation resets and develops internal state by phases; the interface must bound when the current result is valid.
questions.mcqExplanation: Dynamic operation resets and develops internal state by phases; the interface must bound when the current result is valid.
questions.oralPrompt: An interface designer assumes a dynamic ROM output is continuously valid whenever address is stable. Define a better contract.

questions.title: SRAM read assist can hurt writes
questions.prompt: A 6T SRAM has read-disturb failures and weak write-0 ability at low VDD. Which use of wordline underdrive is most defensible?
questions.answer: **Identify failure mechanism first.** Read failure may be cell disturb, insufficient signal, sense offset or timing. Write failure may be inability to defeat the pull-up within the pulse. Wordline underdrive can reduce read disturb but also reduce read current and worsen writing. Write-only supply lowering or bounded wordline/bitline assist can improve writing; separate read-port topologies decouple read disturb with area cost. For each proposal verify selected and half-selected cells, retention, driver timing, rail transients, terminal-voltage limits and recovery. No assist amplitude is universally safe without qualified process limits and statistical margins.
questions.hint: Compare what the access transistor must accomplish during read and write.
questions.followup: How can write supply lowering affect other cells on the rail?
questions.trap: Do not reuse a read assist unchanged during write.
choices: Evaluate it as a read-only assist, while checking reduced read current and using a separately verified write assist
Apply it identically to every read and write because weaker access improves both
Raise its amplitude beyond qualified terminal limits until all sampled cells pass
Use it without checking half-selected cells or recovery
choiceExplanations: Weakening access can reduce read bump but also opposes writing and reduces sensing current.
Read stability and writeability make opposing demands on access strength.
Functional pass does not establish voltage reliability.
Assists can disturb neighboring states and sequencing.
questions.mcqExplanation: Identify the failure mechanism first. Verify operation-specific assists across selected/half-selected states, timing, PVT, mismatch and process voltage limits.
questions.oralPrompt: A low-voltage 6T SRAM meets hold stability but fails some reads and writes. Propose different assists and verification.

questions.title: Read SNM passes but a read fails
questions.prompt: A cell has acceptable DC read SNM but fails with a short wordline pulse and early sense enable. Which explanation should be tested first?
questions.answer: **Static stability is different from timely sensing.** DC read SNM describes tolerance to a defined sustained read disturbance; it does not promise enough bitline differential before sense enable. Plot storage nodes, bitlines, wordline and sense controls. Determine whether the cell flips or the sense circuit resolves an insufficient/wrong differential. Sweep wordline duration and sense enable with offset, PVT, supply transients and parasitics; check storage-node recovery after wordline falls. A short tolerated exposure also does not excuse poor DC stability during stalled/long accesses. Define result correctness, non-disturb and latency separately.
questions.hint: Check whether the stored bit flips or only the observed output is wrong.
questions.followup: Why can a longer wordline aid sensing but worsen disturbance?
questions.trap: SNM alone is not a dynamic timing guarantee.
choices: The failure proves that the DC butterfly calculation is mathematically invalid.
Only write margin can affect a sense-enable timing failure.
The cell may remain stable while the bitline differential is still too small for correct sensing.
Passing DC SNM guarantees every finite-time read produces enough differential.
choiceExplanations: Different metrics can give different outcomes without either calculation being invalid.
Read development, offset and sensing timing are directly relevant.
Static storage stability and time available for signal development are different requirements.
SNM does not impose the transient current/time needed by the sense circuit.
questions.mcqExplanation: Plot storage nodes and bitlines to distinguish a cell upset from an incorrect sense decision, then sweep pulse width and sense timing.
questions.oralPrompt: Read SNM is acceptable, yet transient reads fail with a short wordline pulse and early sense enable. Reconcile these results.

questions.title: Wordline overdrive and half-select cells
questions.prompt: An SRAM wordline-overdrive write assist succeeds on a selected cell. What is the next array-level concern?
questions.answer: **Enumerate partially affected cells.** A selected-row/unselected-column cell sees wordline assertion with different bitline biases. A cell sharing a reduced supply can lose retention without active wordline. Derive half-select cases from actual array and mux topology. Test both stored polarities, neighboring patterns, assist assertion/release, repeated operations and PVT/local mismatch. Include preconditioning, grid parasitics, coupling and driver activity. Track selected write success separately from half-select disturb and retention. If assist is localized, verify isolation and recovery in the extracted array.
questions.hint: Enumerate which cells share the assisted resource without receiving the intended write bitline pattern.
questions.followup: How could more column muxing change half-select exposure?
questions.trap: Selected-cell success does not establish array safety.
choices: Whether a stronger access device removes all retention requirements
Whether all unselected cells automatically see zero gate voltage
Read disturb in selected-row/unselected-column cells whose bitlines remain precharged
Only whether the written cell can be written a second time with the same data
choiceExplanations: Retention and read stability remain separate checks.
Cells sharing the selected wordline see its assertion even if their columns are not written.
Half-selected cells can see a read-like condition with strengthened access, increasing low-node disturbance.
Repeating one selected-cell case misses partially affected neighbors.
questions.mcqExplanation: Half-selected cells can see a read-like condition with strengthened access, increasing low-node disturbance.
questions.oralPrompt: A write assist succeeds on one selected bitcell. Array cells share wordline and supply resources. What must be verified next?

questions.title: Schematic passes, extracted timing fails
questions.prompt: A cell passes schematic simulation and LVS but narrowly misses extracted delay. Which sequence best identifies a real physical fix?
questions.answer: **Make the comparison controlled.** Match models, corner, stimulus, supplies, load, initial state and measurements. Check extraction port mapping, units, coupling treatment and reduction settings. Locate the earliest waveform divergence. Inspect output diffusion/metal C, input/gate R, internal stack C and local supply/return resistance. Use targeted parasitic removal or scaling only as diagnostic experiments; retain the full extracted case as acceptance reference. Repair the dominant physical bottleneck and rerun DRC/LVS/extraction plus characterization. Do not idealize the acceptance model merely to regain the pass.
questions.hint: Separate experiments used to locate a cause from the model used to accept a design.
questions.followup: When can input-wire resistance dominate a high-capacitance pin?
questions.trap: Clean LVS does not imply negligible parasitics.
choices: Remove all wire capacitance from the acceptance model and keep the passing result
Match all simulation conditions, locate the earliest waveform divergence, isolate candidate parasitics diagnostically, then validate the repair with full extraction
Change measurement thresholds only in the extracted run
Conclude the extracted result is impossible because LVS passed
choiceExplanations: An idealized acceptance model hides the physical delay.
Controlled comparisons identify the physical bottleneck without weakening final acceptance.
Different thresholds make the comparison inconsistent.
LVS correctness does not imply zero parasitic performance cost.
questions.mcqExplanation: Parasitic removal can be a diagnostic experiment, but the repaired cell must meet requirements in the complete qualified model.
questions.oralPrompt: A cell passes schematic simulations and LVS, but extracted timing narrowly misses specification. Provide a focused diagnostic sequence.

questions.title: Debug SPICE operating-point failure
questions.prompt: A testbench cannot converge at its DC operating point. What is the most defensible first response?
questions.answer: **Inspect the DC model and setup.** Read solver diagnostics, verify models and terminal order, check supplies/inputs, floating nodes, conflicting ideal sources and missing physical leakage. Confirm intended startup conditions. Apply supported convergence aids deliberately and record them; an added high-value path must be physically justified and its leakage effect checked. Compare plausible initial states in bistable circuits rather than force one arbitrary state as proof of robustness. Separate operating-point initialization from transient startup and show that measurements stabilize after diagnostic changes.
questions.hint: First determine whether the simulator is solving the intended circuit.
questions.followup: Why can a latch have multiple valid operating points?
questions.trap: Artificial conductance or forced initial state can alter the phenomenon.
choices: Force a single initial condition and claim all bistable states are verified.
Inspect diagnostics, terminal/model connections, biases, floating nodes and conflicting ideal sources.
Add an arbitrary low-value resistor until it converges and keep the new result without disclosure.
Treat nonconvergence as a failed timing measurement with zero delay.
choiceExplanations: One forced startup state does not demonstrate all relevant behavior.
The model or topology should be understood before applying targeted, documented aids.
A hidden circuit change can alter both behavior and leakage.
A missing measurement is not a valid zero.
questions.mcqExplanation: Separate DC initialization problems from transient startup and validate that any physically justified convergence aid does not change the intended measurement.
questions.oralPrompt: A transistor testbench fails to converge before transient simulation. How do you debug without silently changing the circuit?

questions.title: Simulation provenance
questions.prompt: Which run record best supports rerunning a characterization sweep after a model update?
questions.answer: **Make every run self-identifying.** Store design/netlist hashes, extraction/model identifiers, simulator version/options, corner, supply/temperature, slew/load, sensitizing state, prior sequence, random seed when used and measurement definitions. Generate unique directories from a structured manifest and retain the exact deck, command, log, raw measurements and status. Validate the expected coverage matrix, retries and missing outputs. Normalize units while preserving raw text and run identity. Link summary anomalies to waveforms and compare a documented baseline. Parallel runs must not share writable filenames. Preserved inputs and a manifest matter more than merely printing fastest and slowest delay.
questions.hint: A reproducible result must identify both what was simulated and how its number was measured.
questions.followup: How should a model-library change invalidate cached results?
questions.trap: A filename containing TT is not complete provenance.
choices: Exact netlist/model identifiers, corner/stimulus/measurement manifest, commands, logs and raw results
Only the simulator executable path, with all parallel jobs overwriting one deck
Only a CSV of rounded final delays without run IDs
Only the source schematic name and the engineer’s initials
choiceExplanations: Versioned inputs and measurement definitions connect each result to a reproducible experiment and reveal changed assumptions.
The executable alone is insufficient and shared writable decks can corrupt parallel run identity.
Rounded summaries cannot reconstruct stimuli, models or missing coverage.
A name is not an immutable record of circuit, extraction and measurement versions.
questions.mcqExplanation: Versioned inputs and measurement definitions connect each result to a reproducible experiment and reveal changed assumptions.
questions.oralPrompt: Design metadata and workflow for an automated cell sweep another engineer can rerun months later.

questions.title: Parse units and validity before ranking
questions.prompt: A delay summary contains 0.085 ns, 90 ps, failed and a missing field. Which normalized result is correct?
questions.answer: **Parse validity and units before ranking.** Convert 0.085 ns to 85 ps and retain 90 ps as 90 ps using a documented numeric grammar and unit whitelist. Keep failed and missing as distinct invalid states, never zero. Carry cell, arc, transition, corner, slew/load and run ID. Flag unknown units, nonfinite values, conflicting duplicates and missing required coverage. Compute extrema only over valid comparable records while displaying exclusions. Test scientific notation, whitespace, malformed values, mixed units, failed convergence and no measurement. A complete pass requires coverage as well as acceptable successful values.
questions.hint: Do unit conversion and status validation before taking a minimum or maximum.
questions.followup: How would you handle a possible negative delay under a stated crossing reference?
questions.trap: Numeric-looking text is not necessarily a valid measurement.
choices: 85 ps and 90 ps are valid; failed and missing are silently removed from coverage
0.085 ps, 90 ps, 0 ps and 0 ps are all valid
85 ns and 90 ns are valid; failures are assigned the largest numeric value
85 ps and 90 ps are valid; failed and missing remain distinct invalid states
choiceExplanations: Silently dropping invalid runs hides missing required work.
This misreads ns and invents zero-delay measurements.
Both units and invalid-status representation are wrong.
Unit normalization and explicit validity preserve both numerical order and coverage.
questions.mcqExplanation: Compare valid records with matching arc/corner/conditions; the smaller valid delay here is 85 ps, but the run set is incomplete until invalid coverage is addressed.
questions.oralPrompt: A summary mixes 0.085 ns, 90 ps, failed and a missing field. Describe parser behavior and tests that prevent false best cases.

questions.title: Avoid double-counting process variation
questions.prompt: A selected global corner already shifts every device coherently. Which Monte Carlo setup best avoids counting the same global effect twice?
questions.answer: **Match the model to the metric.** Offset compares competing branches; ideal common-mode global terms can cancel with equal sensitivities, while local mismatch remains. Path delay adds stages, so shared global variation adds coherently and must not be drawn independently per device. Use qualified corners and local-mismatch methodology. Do not add another full global random term if the same effect is already represented by the selected corner/model. Include spatial correlation and unequal sensitivities when relevant. Check failure probability with appropriate confidence/tail methods, not just mean and sigma. State correlations explicitly so another engineer can reproduce and challenge the assumptions.
questions.hint: State which random variables are shared and which are local.
questions.followup: How could different device stacks make global variation contribute to offset?
questions.trap: Independence is an assumption, not an inherent property of Monte Carlo.
choices: Draw a separate independent copy of the global shift for each path stage.
Add another full independent global random shift to every device and call it local mismatch.
Add the qualified local-mismatch model while preserving stated correlations and corner meaning.
Remove local mismatch because a global corner already covers branch-to-branch differences.
choiceExplanations: A shared die-level component must not be randomized independently per stage.
It duplicates or mislabels the global effect.
This separates common process displacement from local device differences.
Common shifts do not reproduce all local branch mismatch.
questions.mcqExplanation: Choose the statistical model for the metric: offset compares branches, while path delay sums stages and coherent global terms.
questions.oralPrompt: Assess sense-amplifier offset and cell-path delay. Explain how global corners, local Monte Carlo and correlation differ between these metrics.

questions.title: Safe power-domain wake-up
questions.prompt: When waking a power-gated block while its controller remains on, when should output isolation normally be released?
questions.answer: **Sequence around state and signal validity.** Before power-off, finish or safely abort transactions, stop traffic, save necessary state into qualified retention and establish isolation before outputs become invalid. Keep controls on a valid supply and respect cell timing. Turn off the switch and verify collapse/standby. Wake with controlled inrush, wait for power-good/settling, restore or initialize state, make clocks/reset safe, then release isolation only when outputs and protocol state are valid. Exact save/clock/isolation order depends on implementation specifications. Verify stale handshakes, unknowns, back-powering and simultaneous-wakeup droop.
questions.hint: The always-on consumer needs valid signals, not just an instruction that power should return.
questions.followup: Which crossings can back-power an off domain?
questions.trap: Clock gating does not disconnect power or require identical sequencing.
choices: Only according to a fixed nominal delay that ignores inrush and corner behavior
Immediately when the power-switch enable changes
Before restoring or initializing any required state
After power is settled and state, clocks/reset and protocol outputs meet the implementation’s validity contract
choiceExplanations: A delay must be qualified against actual worst-case settling and sequencing requirements.
Switch-enable assertion does not mean the supply or logic is already valid.
Uninitialized or stale state can expose invalid outputs to the live controller.
Release must follow valid electrical and protocol behavior; exact sequencing is implementation-specific.
questions.mcqExplanation: Release must follow valid electrical and protocol behavior; exact sequencing is implementation-specific.
questions.oralPrompt: A block is power-gated while an always-on controller remains active. Design the isolation, retention and wakeup contract.

questions.title: Stalled low-voltage level shifter
questions.prompt: A cross-coupled level shifter works nominally but stalls as input-domain VDD falls. Which observation most directly supports a contention-limited failure?
questions.answer: **Check whether low-side devices overturn the high-side latch.** In a common topology, low-voltage nMOS inputs must pull down a node against a pMOS supplied by the high rail. Reduced input-domain overdrive weakens discharge, increasing contention or blocking regeneration. Plot branch currents and internal nodes over both supplies, slew, load and PVT; test both transitions and startup. Consider a qualified wider-range topology, changed contention ratio or staged conversion, with area/power/delay costs. Verify all terminal-voltage and oxide/junction limits. A functional repair can still violate reliability, and a low-driven ordinary high-domain buffer is not automatically a valid substitute.
questions.hint: Examine the transition before positive feedback takes over.
questions.followup: Why can stronger low-side devices worsen input loading?
questions.trap: One successful supply pair does not define a safe conversion range.
choices: The low-domain NMOS cannot pull its internal node past the regeneration threshold against the high-domain PMOS
The expected input transition never reaches either low-domain gate
Internal nodes regenerate promptly but the external output crosses late only with a large load
The output waveform completes correctly but the measurement selects the wrong edge
choiceExplanations: Reduced low-side overdrive can prevent the initiating pulldown from winning the current fight.
This points to input stimulus or connectivity rather than demonstrated current contention.
This points toward output loading after successful regeneration, not a failed initial current fight.
This points to a measurement error rather than a physical failure to regenerate.
questions.mcqExplanation: Plot internal nodes and branch currents across both supplies and corners. Verify any ratio or topology repair for startup, both transitions and terminal-voltage reliability.
questions.oralPrompt: A cross-coupled level shifter works nominally but stalls at lower input-domain VDD. Explain a likely cause and validation plan.

questions.title: Repair a contact EM hotspot
questions.prompt: EM fails at a driver via array even though the nearby wide rail has low average current density. What action targets the reported bottleneck?
questions.answer: **Current density is spatially nonuniform.** A wide rail may feed a narrow neck, small via array or crowded transition. Trace extracted currents and waveform, inspect contact/via geometry and resistance, and confirm the report metric, temperature and operating assumptions. Add legal contact/via capacity or improve local geometry and current sharing. Check whether the hotspot moves. Re-extract and rerun electrical, EM/IR and layout checks, including delay/slew and pin access. Dividing current by the widest visible rail area cannot dismiss a hotspot at a different bottleneck.
questions.hint: Follow the current through its narrowest transition.
questions.followup: Why can redundant vias still carry unequal current?
questions.trap: Nominal rail width is not the effective area at every bottleneck.
choices: Use average current alone even if the rule flags a different waveform metric.
Dismiss the violation using current divided by the widest rail area.
Inspect local current crowding and add legal via/contact capacity or improve current sharing, then re-extract.
Only widen metal far from the failing via array.
choiceExplanations: The reported rule’s metric and temperature conditions must be checked.
That calculation uses the wrong local area.
The limiting cross section can be the connection rather than the visible rail.
Remote widening may not relieve the actual bottleneck.
questions.mcqExplanation: EM is local and waveform-dependent. Verify whether a repair moves the hotspot or changes electrical timing and layout legality.
questions.oralPrompt: EM flags a driver contact/via region while its nearby wide rail has low average current density. Explain and propose a repair.

questions.title: Aged keeper and read margins
questions.prompt: A ROM keeper ratio passes at time zero. Why is it unsafe to assume aging preserves both read-zero and retained-high margins?
questions.answer: **Aging can shift either side of the margin.** Keeper, selected pull-down, precharge and sensing devices experience different bias, temperature, duty and switching history. A weakened discharge relative to keeper raises contention delay; weakened keeper relative to leakage/noise reduces high retention. A changed sensing threshold moves the decision boundary. Use qualified aged models with documented workloads, then repeat discharge, leakage, coupling, precharge and sense checks over PVT. Add repetitive-address and long-idle directed cases. Do not assume every device loses equal strength or one time-zero keeper ratio preserves lifetime balance.
questions.hint: Compare the stress experienced by the keeper, selected cell and decision circuit.
questions.followup: How could repetitive access create asymmetric degradation?
questions.trap: A universal percentage delay penalty is not a lifetime margin model.
choices: Every device necessarily loses exactly the same fraction of drive
Keeper, cell and sense devices can age differently because their stress histories differ
Aging affects only metal and cannot alter transistor decisions
A fixed ROM code eliminates all bias and switching stress
choiceExplanations: Equal fractional degradation is not guaranteed across different biases, duties and device types.
Unequal degradation can change contention, retention and sense thresholds, so both sides need aged-model checks.
Device aging can change threshold and drive as well as interconnect reliability.
Fixed stored data can create persistent asymmetric stress, while access circuitry still switches.
questions.mcqExplanation: Unequal degradation can change contention, retention and sense thresholds, so both sides need aged-model checks.
questions.oralPrompt: A ROM is stable and fast at time zero. Why revisit keeper balance with aging and workload assumptions?

questions.title: Same glitch, different logic outcome
questions.prompt: The same 150 mV negative glitch appears on a driven static net and a precharged ROM bitline. Why can the static path pass while the ROM fails?
questions.answer: **Amplitude alone does not define failure.** A static driver restores charge, gates may attenuate a narrow pulse, and functional impact depends on logical sensitization and sampling aperture. A dynamic node may lack strong recovery during evaluation, so lost charge and sense timing can produce a lasting error. Compare glitch width, impedance, keeper response, receiver threshold/gain, state and sampling window. Plot downstream propagation and local supply effects as well as the original bump. A DC noise-margin screen must match the operating condition and is not a complete transient correctness test.
questions.hint: Ask what restores the disturbed voltage before the receiver makes its decision.
questions.followup: Why can a glitch far from a sample edge still corrupt a dynamic node?
questions.trap: Voltage amplitude alone is not a complete noise budget.
choices: The static driver can restore charge, while the evaluating dynamic node may retain the loss until sensing
Equal glitch amplitude guarantees equal logical outcome in every circuit
A precharged bitline always has an ideal low-impedance restoring source during evaluate
Static noise margin alone fully specifies every transient failure
choiceExplanations: Impedance, recovery, pulse width and sensing window determine the effect of injected charge.
Amplitude alone ignores temporal and circuit-state dependence.
Precharge is normally released during evaluation, leaving limited recovery.
DC margin does not fully characterize a time-dependent disturbance.
questions.mcqExplanation: Compare waveform width, keeper response, receiver threshold and sampling time; dynamic history can turn a short disturbance into a lasting wrong value.
questions.oralPrompt: The same 150 mV negative glitch appears on a static net and a precharged ROM bitline. Static logic passes; ROM occasionally fails. Explain the difference.

questions.title: Audit an SRAM capacity claim
questions.prompt: A group report lists 16 SRAM instances, each 512 words × 64 bits, but states total capacity as 256 Kbit. What conclusion is justified from the dimensions alone?
questions.answer: **Show arithmetic and preserve uncertainty.** The dimensions imply 16 × 64 × 512 = 524,288 bits = 512 Kibit = 64 KiB. That does not match 256 Kbit under common decimal/binary rounding. Check whether there were eight active instances, effective 32-bit words, different depth or a report mistake; these are hypotheses. Reconcile instance inventory, macro views, synthesis hierarchy and slides before choosing a definitive value. Say, “The listed dimensions compute to 512 Kibit; the report total needs reconciliation.” This is group-authored evidence, and personal ownership must be supported separately.
questions.hint: Check units and separate arithmetic from speculation about the report.
questions.followup: Which artifact establishes instantiated macro count/configuration?
questions.trap: Do not silently correct project numbers or invent ownership.
choices: They prove only eight instances were actually active.
They imply 256 Kibit because a 64-bit word contains two bytes.
They imply 524,288 bits = 512 Kibit; the report total needs reconciliation.
They imply 512 KiB because bits and bytes use the same conversion.
choiceExplanations: Eight active instances is a hypothesis requiring evidence, not a deduction.
A 64-bit word contains eight bytes, and the multiplication still gives 512 Kibit.
Multiply instance count, depth and word width; do not invent an explanation for the mismatch.
Divide bits by eight to get 64 KiB.
questions.mcqExplanation: 16 × 512 × 64 = 524,288 bits. Preserve the discrepancy until inventory, macro views or source records resolve it.
questions.oralPrompt: The group report states 16 SRAMs, each 64 bits × 512 words, but calls total storage 256Kb. Check and explain it without inventing a fix.

questions.title: Read-bandwidth utilization
questions.prompt: A report gives read capacity 1.8 GB/s, write capacity 1.8 GB/s and combined 3.6 GB/s. A workload demands 4.4 GB/s of reads. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.answer: **Compare each direction separately.** A 4.4 GB/s read demand is not served by 1.8 GB/s reads merely because concurrent writes lift the combined rate. Stated read capacity is about 41% of demand before efficiency/burst effects. Clarify sustained versus theoretical rates, interface aggregation and workload. Investigate wider reads, more transfers per cycle, buffering/reuse, scheduling or feasible frequency increases; each has physical/protocol costs. Verify actual implementation before claiming stall-free behavior, and label these report values and estimates rather than measured post-layout achievements.
questions.hint: Match the direction and definition of capacity to the workload’s actual demand.
questions.followup: How might twiddle reuse reduce external demand without widening AXI?
questions.trap: Write bandwidth cannot satisfy a read-only demand.
choices: Read and write capacities can always be added to serve an all-read workload
The read deficit proves a measured post-layout failure independent of workload details
Read capacity is only about 41% of demand before efficiency effects; combined bandwidth does not fill the read deficit
The read demand is met because 3.6 GB/s combined rounds up to 4.4 GB/s
choiceExplanations: Separate directional resources require architecture evidence before reallocating capacity.
These are report-based capacity/demand figures, not proof of a particular measured implementation outcome.
1.8/4.4≈0.409; the write channel contributes to combined traffic, not automatically to read service.
The values do not meet demand even numerically, and rounding cannot create bandwidth.
questions.mcqExplanation: 1.8/4.4≈0.409; the write channel contributes to combined traffic, not automatically to read service.
questions.oralPrompt: The NTT report lists 1.8 GB/s reads, 1.8 GB/s writes, 3.6 GB/s combined and about 4.4 GB/s worst-case read demand. Explain the bottleneck.

questions.title: Describe project ownership with an evidence boundary
questions.prompt: An interviewer asks whether you personally signed off the NTT chip. The group report includes incomplete results. Build a truthful answer framework.
questions.answer: **Lead with actual scope and status.** Use: “I owned [documented block/flow/debug task], produced [artifact] and verified it with [actual checks]. The group top-level status was [documented status]; I would not call unfinished DRC/LVS or missing post-layout results completed signoff.” Then explain one concrete decision, alternatives and measured result within your scope. Prepare an evidence sheet listing source, date, metric basis and ownership for every claim. Fill brackets only from your own records. A group result can provide context without becoming a personal verified achievement.
questions.hint: Separate I did, team did and report estimates.
questions.followup: What would you check first when joining a team to finish signoff?
questions.trap: Projected metrics and completed checks are different evidence.

questions.title: Choose an adder for the actual path
questions.prompt: For a critical 32-bit addition with tight routing and area budgets, which evaluation is most defensible?
questions.answer: **Compare implemented paths, not only logic depth.** Ripple is compact with local connectivity but serial carry propagation. Carry-select computes sums for both carry-in values and selects, reducing dependency with duplicate logic and mux/input loading. Prefix computes group propagate/generate with logarithmic Boolean depth, but topology changes fanout, wires, congestion and area. Compare legal candidates using actual arrival times, loads, extraction and PVT. Consider hybrid block or bypass options. Specify whether critical output is sum/carry and whether objective is latency, energy or throughput. A shallower tree can lose its advantage to wiring.
questions.hint: A shallower Boolean network can still have a worse routed path.
questions.followup: Why might a fewer-level prefix tree be slower after layout?
questions.trap: O(log N) depth is not a post-layout timing guarantee.
choices: Select prefix solely because its Boolean depth is logarithmic.
Compare legal ripple, carry-select and prefix candidates with actual arrival times, loads and extracted wiring.
Select carry-select without accounting for duplicate logic and mux loading.
Select ripple solely because each stage has local wires.
choiceExplanations: Routing and fanout can erode a depth advantage.
The optimum depends on physical delay and the design’s constraints.
Its speed benefit has concrete area and load costs.
Local wiring does not remove serial carry delay.
questions.mcqExplanation: Match the arithmetic representation and topology to the critical sum/carry output and implemented PPA objective.
questions.oralPrompt: A 32-bit ripple adder is critical, with tight area/routing budgets. Compare ripple, carry-select and parallel-prefix choices.

questions.title: Carry-save numerical representation
questions.prompt: A Booth multiplier returns two carry-save vectors before its final adder. What should an arithmetic scoreboard compare with the exact product?
questions.answer: **Test the contract and boundaries.** Fix width, signedness, output width and overflow policy. Compare an independent exact signed reference before truncation. Exercise zero, ±1, minimum negative, maximum positive, minimum-negative squared, alternating bits and long runs of ones. Check implicit low zero bit, upper sign extension, negative partial-product correction, shift widths and final carry-propagate addition. Carry-save outputs are two vectors whose weighted sum is the value; neither alone is the product. Exhaustive small-width versions can catch structural errors. Scoreboard pipeline latency and valid alignment to separate arithmetic from sequencing failures.
questions.hint: A redundant arithmetic representation must be decoded before comparing numeric values.
questions.followup: Why do positive-only tests miss recoding extension errors?
questions.trap: Unsigned correctness does not prove signed correctness.
choices: Their correctly weighted sum, with the design’s carry alignment and signed width convention
Either vector alone, because each is a complete product
Only their lowest bit, because sign extension affects no other bit
Their bitwise OR, because carries cannot overlap sums
choiceExplanations: Carry-save representation encodes a value across sum and carry vectors; weighting/alignment and signedness are part of the contract.
Neither vector generally equals the full product by itself.
Sign extension and correction affect upper bits and boundary cases substantially.
Carry and sum fields can overlap in significance and require arithmetic addition, not OR.
questions.mcqExplanation: Carry-save representation encodes a value across sum and carry vectors; weighting/alignment and signedness are part of the contract.
questions.oralPrompt: A signed multiplier uses Booth recoding and carry-save reduction. Define directed tests catching sign-extension/representation bugs.

questions.title: Transmission-gate mux-chain viability
questions.prompt: A long transmission-gate mux chain reduces device count. Which analysis is necessary before declaring it electrically superior?
questions.answer: **Track resistance, capacitance and noise.** Transmission gates pass both rails better than a lone nMOS but have no restoring gain. Series on-resistance and intermediate capacitance accumulate RC delay; feedthrough, charge injection and disabled-path leakage perturb nodes. Include source impedance, destination load, select timing and complementary-control overlap. A restoring buffer resets swing and isolates stages at area/delay/loading/polarity cost. Compare full paths across PVT with extracted routing and realistic data/select activity. Device count alone cannot establish speed, energy or noise robustness.
questions.hint: Separate rail-to-rail transmission from restoration and path delay.
questions.followup: How can slow select edges alter contention and effective resistance?
questions.trap: A full-swing transmission gate remains nonrestoring.
choices: Compare transistor count alone
Assume complementary pass devices provide unlimited regenerative gain
Evaluate accumulated on-resistance/internal capacitance, nonrestoring noise behavior, control timing and the complete loaded path
Ignore intermediate nodes because the endpoint can reach both rails at DC
choiceExplanations: Fewer transistors do not guarantee lower loaded delay or energy.
A TG passes voltage without inverter-like restoring gain.
Speed and robustness depend on the entire RC/noise/control network.
Internal nodes contribute delay, injection and leakage even if DC swing is acceptable.
questions.mcqExplanation: Restoring buffers may improve a long chain but add their own area, delay and loading. Compare complete extracted paths over operating conditions.
questions.oralPrompt: A long transmission-gate mux chain promises fewer transistors. What electrical questions determine whether it is viable?

questions.title: Translate analog debugging into digital-circuit value
questions.prompt: Your background includes analog/RF work; this role emphasizes cells and ROM. Build a technical connection without inventing direct ROM ownership.
questions.answer: **Link one actual experiment to the new circuit.** Describe how your real settling work separated RC/time constants, finite drive, load and measurement-window error, then connect that method to cell/bitline waveforms. Or describe differential/common-mode mismatch analysis and connect it to sense offset. Use only actual tools, work and measured results; do not invent specifications or tapeout ownership. Close with a boundary: “I have not owned a ROM compiler, but I can bring waveform/model/debug discipline and verify precharge, decode, sensing and margin assumptions.” Transferable reasoning is strongest when supported by a concrete artifact and clear experience limits.
questions.hint: Choose one real experiment rather than listing every project.
questions.followup: Which analog testbench assumption changes for a dynamic node?
questions.trap: Transferable skill does not imply identical signoff or undocumented experience.

questions.title: Loaded common-source voltage gain
questions.prompt: At valid saturation bias, gm=1 mS, ro=100 kΩ, RD=8 kΩ and AC-coupled RL=100 kΩ. Neglect body effect. What is low-frequency common-source gain?
questions.answer:
The gain is **−6.897 V/V**. Output-node KCL places all three resistances in parallel:

```latex
R_{out}=(100\,\mathrm{k\Omega})\parallel(8\,\mathrm{k\Omega})\parallel(100\,\mathrm{k\Omega})=6.897\,\mathrm{k\Omega}
```

Multiplying by −1 mS gives the result. Using gm·ro alone would predict −100 and ignore the resistor that dominates the output conductance.
questions.hint: Write output-node KCL and combine all output conductances.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: Intrinsic gain is not the gain after loading.
choices: −8 V/V
choiceExplanations: −100 uses intrinsic gmro and ignores both loading resistances.
The parallel resistance is 1/(1/100k+1/8k+1/100k)=6.897 kΩ; gain is −gmRout.
−8 ignores finite ro and the 100 kΩ external load.
The magnitude is right but a common-source drain output inverts the small signal.
questions.mcqExplanation: The parallel resistance is 1/(1/100k+1/8k+1/100k)=6.897 kΩ; gain is −gmRout.
questions.oralPrompt: At a valid saturation bias, gm = 1 mS, ro = 100 kΩ, RD = 8 kΩ and AC-coupled RL = 100 kΩ. What is the low-frequency common-source gain in V/V? Neglect body effect.

questions.title: Diagnose gain loss after increasing bias
questions.prompt: A common-source amplifier’s measured gain falls after bias current doubles at fixed geometry and supply. Which measurement plan best separates output-resistance loss, reduced saturation margin and a shifted pole?
questions.answer: First, output resistance may fall faster than transconductance improves; compare gm and gds at both operating points. Second, the larger resistor drop may push the device out of saturation or reduce swing; inspect VDS, VOV and a small DC input sweep. Third, the measured frequency may now lie near a changed pole because bias and capacitance changed; compare DC gain with the full AC response. Also keep the external load identical. These mechanisms require different fixes; gain loss alone does not identify the cause.
questions.hint: Separate DC operating point, low-frequency gain and frequency dependence.
questions.followup: Which change helps bandwidth while potentially reducing intrinsic gain?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Compare only one high-frequency magnitude point with a different load
Compare gm/gds, VDS versus overdrive, and DC gain versus full AC response at the same external load
Measure bias current alone and assume gm determines gain
Check only that the supply voltage is unchanged
choiceExplanations: Changing load and observing one point cannot isolate the cause.
These measurements distinguish device gain, operating-region/headroom and frequency-response mechanisms.
Gain also depends on output conductance, load and frequency.
Fixed supply does not imply fixed drain bias, swing or poles.
questions.mcqExplanation: A larger gm can coexist with lower ro, less saturation margin or different bandwidth. Gain loss alone does not identify a unique repair.
questions.oralPrompt: You double the bias current of a common-source stage at fixed geometry and supply, and its gain falls. Give three physically distinct explanations and the measurements that separate them.

questions.title: Which gain belongs to which output?
questions.prompt: A matched NMOS pair has ideal tail bias, gm = 1 mS per device and RD = 5 kΩ per drain. Define vid = v1 − v2 and vod = vd2 − vd1. Which small-signal gain pair is correct?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Each branch changes by ±gm·vid/2. Drain 1 falls by gm·RD·vid/2 while drain 2 rises by the same amount. Subtracting drain 1 from drain 2 doubles that single-ended change, giving +5 V/V differential gain and −2.5 V/V at drain 1. Reversing the differential output definition reverses only its sign.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A fixed total current still permits differential current steering.
choices: vod/vid = −5; vd1/vid = −5
vod/vid = +5; vd1/vid = −2.5
vod/vid = +2.5; vd1/vid = +5
Both gains are zero because the tail current is fixed

questions.title: Find differential-pair common-mode floor
questions.prompt: An NMOS differential pair needs VGS = 0.60 V at its bias current. Its grounded tail source requires VDS ≥ 0.15 V. What first-order input common-mode floor follows from this tail-side constraint?
questions.answer: The common-source node must remain at least 0.15 V above ground. Each input gate must sit 0.60 V above that node, so the first-order minimum is **0.75 V**. This checks the tail-source side only. A complete input range also checks the input devices, load compliance and available output swing.
questions.hint: Stack the gate-source voltage above the tail source’s required drain voltage.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choiceExplanations: This is the source-node floor, not the input gate voltage.
This subtracts compliance instead of stacking required headroom.
The source node must be at least 0.15 V, and the gate is 0.60 V above it.
This leaves no voltage across the tail source.
questions.mcqExplanation: VCM,min ≈ VGS,input + VDS,min,tail = 0.75 V. Load and input-device saturation impose additional range constraints.
questions.oralPrompt: An NMOS differential pair needs VGS = 0.60 V at its operating current. Its tail source requires VDS ≥ 0.15 V and is tied to ground. Estimate the minimum input common-mode voltage.

questions.title: Mirror error from channel-length modulation
questions.prompt: For the saturation mirror model, Iref=50 µA, width ratio=4, λ=0.10 V⁻¹, VDS,ref=0.60 V and VDS,out=1.20 V. What Iout follows?
questions.answer: The geometry-only answer is 200 µA. Channel-length modulation scales it by (1 + 0.10×1.20)/(1 + 0.10×0.60) = 1.12/1.06. Therefore **Iout ≈ 211.32 µA**, about 5.66% high. This is a deterministic bias error under the given model; it should not be labeled random mismatch.
questions.hint: Apply the geometry ratio and then the ratio of drain-voltage correction factors.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: 224 µA
200 µA
choiceExplanations: 224 µA includes the output modulation but fails to normalize by the reference modulation.
200 µA ignores unequal-drain-voltage channel-length modulation.
189.29 µA reverses the output/reference modulation ratio.
questions.oralPrompt: Use the stated saturation model with Iref = 50 µA, width ratio 4, lambda = 0.10 V⁻¹, VDS,ref = 0.60 V and VDS,out = 1.20 V. Estimate Iout in µA.

questions.title: A mirror fails only at low output voltage
questions.prompt: A mirror ratio looks accurate above 0.35 V but collapses as Vout approaches ground. Which first diagnostic is strongest?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** The voltage-dependent knee points first to output compliance: the transistor may leave saturation and cannot sustain the intended current. Inspect VDS and overdrive at the failing operating points. Random mismatch can shift the curve, but it does not by itself explain why nominal operation recovers above a consistent voltage boundary. A cascode can increase output resistance while worsening the minimum voltage requirement.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Assume a Monte Carlo mismatch failure and average more runs
Increase the intended ratio without checking device regions
Check output-device saturation and minimum compliance voltage
Add a cascode because it always improves low-voltage compliance

questions.title: Phase margin at unity loop gain
questions.prompt: For a conventional single-loop amplifier with stable open-loop behavior and one relevant unity-loop-gain crossing, loop-gain phase at that crossing is −125°. What phase margin does this indicate?
questions.answer: **55°**. Phase margin is 180° + (−125°). The measurement is of loop gain Aβ, not just the closed-loop signal transfer. It does not establish large-signal settling or guarantee adequate margin at every load and PVT corner.
questions.hint: Measure angular distance to −180° at the relevant loop-gain crossing.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choiceExplanations: 125° is the magnitude of the measured phase, not the distance from −180°.
Phase margin is 180°−125°=55°.
The phase is 55° above −180°, not below it.
Adding the absolute phase magnitude to 180° uses the wrong sign.
questions.mcqExplanation: Use the phase of loop gain Aβ at its unity magnitude. This single result does not establish large-signal settling or all-corner/load stability.
questions.oralPrompt: For a conventional single-loop amplifier with a stable open-loop response and one relevant unity-loop-gain crossing, the phase at that crossing is −125°. What phase margin does this indicate?

questions.title: Distinguish slew limiting from poor damping
questions.prompt: An amplifier has adequate small-signal phase margin but is slow on large steps. Which observation most directly supports slew limiting?
questions.answer: The amplifier may be slew limited: finite current charges a compensation or output capacitance, limiting dV/dt. Compare a small step with progressively larger steps. A roughly constant slope during a portion of large-step response and settling time that grows with step amplitude support slew limiting. Ringing on small steps instead points toward insufficient damping or another small-signal issue. Check output saturation and overload recovery too; stable linear analysis does not cover recovery from every large-signal state.
questions.hint: A capacitor charged by a current limit produces a characteristic waveform shape.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Settling time is identical for every step amplitude and output level.
Small and large steps show the same normalized damped ringing envelope.
Only a DC gain measurement changes when input amplitude is swept slowly.
Large steps show an approximately constant-slope interval whose duration grows with step amplitude.
choiceExplanations: Strong amplitude dependence is expected when a slew interval grows.
Amplitude-independent normalized dynamics suggest a linear response rather than slew limiting.
DC gain alone does not identify a transient slew-current limit.
A finite charging current limits dV/dt independently of step size over that interval.
questions.mcqExplanation: Compare progressively larger steps while checking output saturation and recovery. Small-signal stability does not bound every large-signal settling condition.
questions.oralPrompt: A feedback amplifier has adequate small-signal phase margin but settles much too slowly after a large step. Give a mechanism and a test that distinguishes it from poor phase margin.

questions.title: Integrated white-noise voltage
questions.prompt: Flat voltage-noise density is 8 nV/√Hz across an ideal 100 kHz brick-wall band. Ignore other noise. What rms input noise follows?
questions.answer: The density is multiplied by the square root of bandwidth: 8 nV/√Hz × √100000 Hz = **2.530 µV rms**. Multiplying directly by bandwidth gives incorrect units. With a real filter, use equivalent noise bandwidth or integrate the squared transfer function.
questions.hint: For flat uncorrelated noise, rms grows with the square root of bandwidth.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: 8 µV rms
2.530 µV rms
800 µV rms
0.0253 µV rms
choiceExplanations: The supplied density and bandwidth do not give 8 µV; integrate noise power before taking its square root.
Multiplying density directly by bandwidth gives wrong units and the wrong value.
This is a factor-of-100 conversion error.
questions.oralPrompt: An amplifier has flat input voltage-noise density 8 nV/√Hz. Ignore other noise and integrate over a 100 kHz brick-wall band. What is its input noise in µV rms?

questions.title: What averaging removes
questions.prompt: Repeated readings show random scatter plus a constant input-equivalent 0.5 mV bias. Which statement is strongest?
questions.answer: **Choose A.** Averaging independent zero-mean samples reduces the random standard error as 1/√N. A constant offset remains. Correlation, drift and low-frequency noise can also prevent the ideal averaging benefit, so independence must be checked rather than assumed. Calibration or a suitable offset-cancellation technique targets the constant bias.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Averaging can reduce uncorrelated scatter while leaving the offset
Averaging N samples divides both offset and noise by N
A constant offset is a white-noise density
A narrower bandwidth always removes all offset

questions.title: ADC acquisition to half an LSB
questions.prompt: A 10-bit converter with 1 V span acquires a full-scale step through an ideal 1 kΩ–2 pF RC. How long to reduce the remaining error to half an LSB?
questions.answer: The RC is 2 ns. Half an LSB relative to a full-scale step is 1/2048, so exp(−t/RC) ≤ 1/2048. Therefore t ≥ RC·ln(2048) = **15.25 ns**. This is an ideal settling floor; extra time may be required for nonlinear switch resistance and driver recovery.
questions.hint: Convert the error target into a fraction of the full-scale step.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: About 1.39 ns
About 13.86 ns
About 2 ns
About 15.25 ns
choiceExplanations: 0.693RC only halves the initial error.
13.86 ns corresponds to 1/1024, or one LSB, rather than half an LSB.
One time constant leaves about 37% error.
Half an LSB is 1/2048 of full scale, so t=2 ns×ln(2048).
questions.mcqExplanation: RC=2 ns and exp(−t/RC)≤1/2048 requires t≥15.249 ns. This excludes nonlinear switch resistance and driver recovery.
questions.oralPrompt: A 10-bit, 1 V-span converter acquires through an ideal 1 kΩ–2 pF RC. Starting one full-scale step away, how many ns are needed to settle to half an LSB?

questions.title: Aliasing versus resolution
questions.prompt: A 70 MHz interferer enters an ideal 100 MS/s sampler. Its alias at 30 MHz overlaps your desired input band. Which change directly prevents this folding?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** Reject the 70 MHz component in the analog path before sampling, or change the frequency plan/sample rate so its alias no longer overlaps the signal band. Increasing resolution preserves the ambiguous samples more precisely. Digital filtering after sampling cannot separate two original frequencies that produced the same sampled sequence in the occupied band.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Add two ADC bits
Average more output samples without changing the passband
Add appropriate analog anti-alias rejection before sampling
Treat the interferer as quantization noise

questions.title: Read the old state
questions.prompt: Initially a = 0 and b = 0. At a rising edge with din = 1, the block executes a <= din; b <= a;. What are a and b after the nonblocking updates?
questions.answer: **Choose B.** Both right-hand sides are evaluated from the pre-update state: a gets din = 1 and b gets old a = 0. The updates do not turn the source-code sequence into combinational propagation through both registers at the same edge.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: Source-code order is not a substitute for a clock-cycle model.
choices: Both values are inherently unknown

questions.title: Does a missing else imply a latch?
questions.prompt: Compare `if (en) q <= d;` inside `always_ff @(posedge clk)` with a path that leaves y unassigned inside `always_comb`. Which interpretation is correct?
questions.answer: In the edge-triggered process, q updates only when en is true and otherwise holds its registered value; this describes a flip-flop with enable behavior. In an intended combinational process, failing to assign y along a path requires its previous value to be retained, which implies level-sensitive storage or triggers a tool diagnostic because always_comb promises combinational behavior. Use complete assignments/defaults for combinational outputs. Whether hardware includes storage is determined by behavior and event control, not by the mere presence of an else keyword.
questions.hint: Start with the process’s event control, then examine unassigned paths.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: The first describes a flip-flop enable; the second requests retention in a combinational process and can infer a latch or cause a diagnostic.
Both are purely combinational because the statements use if.
The first is an unconditional flip-flop; the second implicitly assigns y to zero.
Both necessarily describe level-sensitive latches because both omit else.
choiceExplanations: Event control and assignment completeness determine storage behavior.
The clock event and missing combinational assignment both matter.
No assignment means retain behavior, not an implicit zero or unconditional update.
An edge-triggered process retains its registered value between qualifying updates.
questions.mcqExplanation: Do not diagnose storage from the presence of `else` alone. Use complete combinational assignments and intentional sequential enables.
questions.oralPrompt: Compare if (en) q <= d; inside an always_ff @(posedge clk) block with an incomplete assignment to y inside always_comb. Explain the intended or inferred storage.

questions.title: Multi-bit clock-domain crossing
questions.prompt: Eight binary counter bits each cross through a separate two-flop synchronizer. What failure remains possible even if each chain has acceptable individual metastability MTBF?
questions.answer: Different bits can be observed from different source updates, especially when several bits change together. The destination may see a word the source never produced. MTBF for individual resolution does not establish bus coherency. Use a suitable transaction handshake, an asynchronous FIFO, or a deliberately constrained Gray-coded transfer where appropriate. State the information-rate and physical timing assumptions for the chosen scheme.
questions.hint: Individual bit reliability and word-level transaction correctness are different properties.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: Eight acceptable single-bit synchronizers do not imply one coherent eight-bit transaction.
choices: The destination clock must become frequency-locked to the source
All counter words become coherent once the chains have identical RTL
A mixed word composed of bits from different source updates
Every output bit is forced to the same value by the synchronizers
choiceExplanations: Synchronizer chains do not lock clocks.
Structural identity does not establish coherent sampling across multi-bit transitions.
Different bits can be observed on different cycles, creating a value the source never issued.
They independently carry bit values and do not force a shared logic level.
questions.mcqExplanation: Different bits can be observed on different cycles, creating a value the source never issued.
questions.oralPrompt: An 8-bit binary count passes through eight separate two-flop synchronizers. What remains unsafe even if each individual synchronizer has acceptable metastability MTBF?

questions.title: When can the source change the payload?
questions.prompt: In a bundled-data request/acknowledge crossing, when may the source overwrite the current payload holding register?
questions.answer: **Choose C.** The source must wait until the acknowledgement has safely returned and the particular protocol permits the next transfer. Capturing a request in the first destination synchronizer is not confirmation that the destination consumed the payload. Holding the data until acknowledgement is part of the coherency contract.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Immediately after asserting request
After one source clock regardless of the destination
After the acknowledgement and protocol-defined completion
Whenever no individual bit appears metastable in simulation

questions.title: Asynchronous reset release
questions.prompt: Why does a design commonly synchronize deassertion of an asynchronously asserted reset within each clock domain?
questions.answer: Assertion directly forces the reset state according to the cell behavior. Release near a clock edge can violate recovery/removal requirements, leaving registers metastable or leaving related state elements on different effective release cycles. A domain-specific release synchronizer reduces this risk and makes initialization sequencing deliberate. Also satisfy the cell minimum reset pulse width and the system sequencing contract; asynchronous assertion is not permission to ignore all electrical timing.
questions.hint: Distinguish forcing a state from allowing normal clocked operation to resume.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Asynchronous assertion makes deassertion electrically independent of every clock edge
Release near an active edge can violate recovery/removal or release related registers on inconsistent cycles
The release synchronizer eliminates the cell’s minimum reset pulse-width requirement
One release clock can safely serve unrelated clock domains without separate timing analysis
choiceExplanations: Recovery/removal requirements still couple release to clock timing.
A controlled release reduces metastability and inconsistent initialization timing.
Minimum pulse width and sequencing remain separate requirements.
Each domain needs release behavior appropriate to its own clock.
questions.mcqExplanation: Asynchronous forcing of state does not imply unrestricted release timing. Respect recovery/removal, pulse width and domain-specific sequencing.
questions.oralPrompt: Why can an asynchronous reset assert safely while its deassertion still needs synchronization and timing analysis?

questions.title: Can data registers be left unreset?
questions.prompt: A datapath register is intentionally not reset. Which condition is necessary for a safe design?
questions.answer: **Choose D.** A reset, well-defined valid/control path must prevent unknown data from influencing any meaningful action until the datapath is initialized. This can reduce reset routing and implementation cost, but requires verification. Merely ignoring a displayed output is insufficient if uninitialized bits can reach an address or write enable.
questions.hint: Start by stating the model, the operating condition and the quantity being measured.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: The simulator happens to initialize it to zero
The datapath has at least eight bits
The clock is fast enough that unknown values disappear
Known valid/control state blocks every use until initialization

questions.title: A hold fix that breaks setup
questions.prompt: A path has setup slack +20 ps and hold slack −20 ps. A cell adds 30 ps minimum and 45 ps maximum delay; all other delays and clocks are fixed. What are the new slacks?
questions.answer: The maximum data delay grows by 45 ps, so setup slack falls from +20 to **−25 ps**. Hold improves by 30 ps to +10 ps. The cell therefore does not produce a fully timing-clean solution; placement or sizing must preserve enough max-delay margin as well.
questions.hint: Use the maximum increment for setup and minimum increment for hold.
questions.followup: Which assumption would you verify first in simulation, and why?
questions.trap: A correct equation is useful only within its stated operating conditions.
choices: Setup −25 ps; hold +10 ps.
Setup +65 ps; hold +10 ps.
Setup −10 ps; hold +25 ps.
Setup +20 ps; hold +10 ps.
choiceExplanations: Setup loses the 45 ps maximum increment, while hold gains the 30 ps minimum increment.
Added maximum data delay consumes setup slack, not adds it.
This swaps minimum and maximum increments.
A hold cell on the shared path also changes maximum delay.
questions.mcqExplanation: 20 − 45 = −25 ps; −20 + 30 = +10 ps. The repair fixes the stated hold check but does not make the path timing-clean.
questions.oralPrompt: A shared path has +20 ps setup slack and −20 ps hold slack. A proposed cell adds 30 ps minimum delay and 45 ps maximum delay. What is the new setup slack? Assume clocks and all other delays stay fixed.

questions.title: Clock-skew setup and hold tradeoff
